Additionally, the “deep” part of these excisions lies at the center between these two epithelial layers and may contain rigid tissue such as cartilage or tarsal plate. If the surgeon determines it is reasonable to do so, initial and subsequent layers in these settings should be excised in a manner that facilitates ease of tissue processing. It stands to reason that the easier a given piece of tissue is to process with complete representation of all epithelial and deep margins intact, the easier it will be to interpret and accurately identify and map residual tumor. Tissue specimens that are harder to process will result in more challenging interpretations and a greater possibility of incomplete treatment or unnecessary additional stages

of MMS. The best approach for easing histologic processing is to take MMS stages that require through-and-through resections at the same level or to the same depth internally versus externally such that the specimen can essentially be placed flat on a microscope slide with both epithelial layers and the deep margin in full contact with the slide immediately following excision from the patient and any division of the specimen that may be necessary.

A further challenge in these situations is accurate tissue orientation and mapping. This is especially true for wedge-style Mohs stages on the ear where the skin on both sides of the auricular cartilage is similar in histologic appearance (unlike eyelid, nose, and lip where tissue differs histologically inside vs. out). Cases such as these require excellent communication between the surgeon and laboratory staff, careful mapping, and thoughtful placement of orienting scores.

The primary objective of MMS at any site is complete tumor extirpation; therefore, it is sometimes necessary to sacrifice cosmetically or functionally important anatomic structures. However, it is important to understand the unique anatomic aspects that exist in these “special sites” so that unnecessary morbidity can be avoided. Thorough discussion of the complex anatomy of these sites has been eloquently described elsewhere and will not be the focus of our discussion. Instead, we will try to highlight some practical surgical pearls and pitfalls.

Eyelid anatomy is perhaps the most complex of any site Mohs surgeons operate (Fig. 1.14, Fig. 1.15). For a full discussion of relevant anatomy, we recommend the excellent review article by Patel and Itani.28
Fig. 1.14 Eyelid anatomy: sagittal section. Reproduced from Leatherbarrow B. Oculoplastic Surgery. 3rd Edition. New York: Thieme; 2019.

Fig. 1.15 Basic eyelid anatomy: frontal view. Reproduced from Schuenke M, Schulte E, Schumacher U. THIEME Atlas of Anatomy: Head, Neck, and Neuroanatomy. Illustrations by Voll M and Wesker K. © Thieme 2020.

• Eyelid skin is the thinnest anywhere on the body (<1 mm), with essentially no subcutaneous fat between it and the underlying orbicularis oculi muscle. • Eyelid is divided primarily into anterior and posterior lamellae; although usually not discussed as such, a “middle lamella” also exists at portions of the eyelid (see Fig. 1.14):

○ Orbicularis oculi is a muscle of facial expression → hence, innervated by branches of facial nerve (cranial nerve [CN] 7). Orbicularis oculi muscle is a sphincterlike muscle divided into two main concentric subunits. (1) Orbital— outermost

ring of muscle, under voluntary control, and responsible for forced lid closure; overlying skin is easily undermined above the muscle allowing for great mobility. (2) Palpebral—inner ring of muscle, under voluntary and involuntary control, responsible for blinking and winking, and contiguous with lateral canthal tendon (attaches laterally to Whitnall’s tubercle) and medial canthal tendon (MCT; a bifurcated structure that envelops the lacrimal canaliculi at the medial portion of the orbit). Palpebral orbicularis oculi is further subdivided into a peripheral preseptal and a central pretarsal portion. Preseptal orbicularis oculi: skin is loosely attached and mobile; deep to this layer lies the “middle lamella” consisting of the orbital septum, orbital fat pads, and the lid retractor muscles/aponeuroses (levator palpebrae superioris and Muller’s muscle superiorly, and capsulopalpebral fascia inferiorly). Pretarsal orbicularis oculi: overlying skin is tightly adherent to posterior lamella. – “Middle lamella”: Deep to the preseptal portion of the orbicularis oculi muscle lies (in order from superficial to deep) orbital septum, orbital fat pads, and the lid retractors (levator palpebrae superioris, Muller’s muscle, inferior tarsal muscle, and capsulopalpebral fascia):

○ Levator palpebrae superioris: the major eyelid elevator, innervated by oculomotor nerve (CN3), attached to the tarsal plate via its aponeurosis, and is compromised in Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis). ○ Sympathetic innervation: Muller’s muscle and inferior tarsal muscle. ○ Pearl: If a laceration to the preseptal portion of the eyelid results in a large amount of herniating fat, then you know that the orbital septum has been compromised. – Posterior lamella: conjunctiva and tarsal plate:

○ Tarsal plate: fibrous tissue, comprises the structural support of the lid, and houses Meibomian glands → provides oily secretions that prevent tear evaporation. • Lacrimal canaliculi are located deep to superficial wing of the MCT:
• Lacrimal gland is located at the superolateral aspect of the upper eyelid. • Vascular supply of the eyelid is extremely rich!

○ Notably, at the MCT, branches of the facial artery (external carotid) anastamose with the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid). – Pearl: The rich vascular supply of the eyelid makes for an excellent wound bed for skin grafts; flaps are also well vascularized and robust in this location. • Lymphatic drainage (important for understanding regional metastatic disease):
– Lateral two-thirds of upper eyelid and lateral one-third of the lower eyelid → preauricular nodes. – Medial one-third of upper eyelid and medial two-thirds of the lower → submandibular nodes.

• Chlorhexidine prep is contraindicated near the eye due to the risk of keratitis; povidone–iodine is recommended. • Chalazion clamps assist in hemostasis and facilitate Mohs excisions (especially of the lid margin). • Eye shields: use during MMS is controversial:
○ Used by up to 75% of Mohs surgeons, but only used consistently 10% of the time by those who use them.29

○ Roughly one-third of Mohs surgeons have, at some point, had a patient who experienced corneal abrasions due to eye shield use; usually self-resolves in 2 to 3 days with conservative pain- relief measures ± topical antibiotics (erythromycin ointment or quinolone drops). – Plastic (polymethyl methacrylate) eye shields are recommended over stainless steel eye shields for all nonlaser procedures30; cannot use with laser procedures due to risk of thermal-induced corneal damage:

○ Lower risk of sharp edges and burs than stainless steel → decreased risk of corneal abrasion. ○ Less likely to conduct energy from electrosurgical units. ○ Cheaper. – Must ensure the shields are properly fitted and have a smooth, intact surface → otherwise, risk of corneal abrasion. – Technique:

○ Apply proparacaine topically to anesthetize eye. ○ Inspect eye shield for scratches, burs, sharp edges, or debris. ○ Apply lubricant (methylcellulose-based lubricants are preferred over Lacri-Lube or antibiotic ointments). ○ Insert eye shield: (1) Tell the patient to look up and then retract the lower lid. (2) Insert inferior edge of the eye shield posterior to the lower eyelid, all the way down to the fornix. (3) Tell the patient to look down and retract the upper eyelid (superior edge of the eye shield will fall into place). • Tissue distortion can become problematic with high volumes of local anesthetic → use minimal required amount of anesthetic. • Breach of orbital septum → risk of retrobulbar hematoma. • Having an assistant pull the skin taut during Mohs excision is key, since periocular skin is thin and loose. One way of doing this on the eyelid margin is having an assistant keep traction, gently but firmly, with one forceps while the surgeon uses another forceps to grip the other side while taking a layer. The editors prefer to grip the eyelid margin with the forceps on behalf of the assistant first, which is a critical step with risk of causing injury, and subsequently allow the assistant to take over the forceps and keep tension. • Using a no. 11-blade or 15c blade is helpful for incisions on the floppy portions of eyelid (skin overlying the orbital portion of the orbicularis oculi):

– These sharper blades are also helpful along the free margin of the lid, which is an area where it is difficult to achieve great side-to- side tension from your assistant. • Mohs layers on the eyelid often do not need to be angled at 45 degrees, since the skin is so lax. Even vertical Mohs excisions can typically be laid down with ease. The lid margin is often relaxed with small vertical

incisions on the superficial portion due to the thickness of sebaceous tissue. • Given the thin and floppy nature of the eyelid skin, it is often more difficult to take narrow subsequent Mohs stages compared to other thicker-skinned sites. Vertical incisions using a no. 11 blade or 15c blade are helpful in this regard. • To ensure high-quality Mohs slides, extra attention is required when inking and laying down Mohs layers on eyelid skin.

– Loose, redundant skin can lead to folding artifact. – Lid margin and conjunctival layers may be confusing to lay-down for your histotechnician, since conjunctiva may be mistaken for missing epidermis → it is helpful to bring them into the room during the Mohs layer to show them the in vivo orientation of the true margin. – Editor’s note: To this extent, when a layer must be taken on the bulbar conjunctiva, it is also important to make sure the edges are not folded as this tissue is extremely thin. Typically, experienced Mohs surgeons comfortable with eyelid layers can continue to take layers from the lid margin down to the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva if needed. However, one must understand and review the unique nuances of conjunctival frozen section histology. Practically, taking a conjunctival layer, once over the sclera, allows for one chance at margin evaluation, if the histotechnician and surgeon are able to properly orient and embed the tissue for evaluation. If positivity is noted once the limbus is approached, other therapeutic options will be considered by a cornea surgeon such as excision with cryotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, or orbital exenteration.

It is important to note that once the palpebral conjunctiva layers are exhausted and the tumor extends on the bulbar conjunctiva, further surgery may risk severe eye damage and even loss of an eye. Therefore, if a severe tumor is suspected, all possible risks, alternative treatments, and outcomes, including exenteration, should be discussed with the patient in detail prior to surgery to obtain informed consent, and such surgery should be done by or in conjunction with a cornea or oculoplastic surgeon.

In Dr. Tolkachjov’s experience, taking such layers in a multidisciplinary setting and in conjunction with a cornea surgeon and anesthesia would be ideal, if a Mohs surgeon has privileges at an “eye” hospital or can supervise and guide a cornea surgeon (with the help of an intraoperative microscope) making the incisions and using blunt and sharp scissors dissection while keeping the conjunctiva taut to remove conjunctival tissue from the limbus over to the canthus if tumor involvement is suspected. Clinically, SCC (conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia or ocular surface squamous neoplasia) spreading over the conjunctiva may mimic a pterygium or a pinguecula, a yellowish, raised thickening of the bulbar conjunctiva on the sclera, close to the edge of the cornea. While pingueculae are not cancerous, rapid changes or severe overgrowth may signal a possible SCC formation.

– Excess ink can obscure true skin edge margins and impair precise tissue lay-down → carefully laying out the specimen on a piece of cardboard and applying only pinpoint amounts of tissue ink helps minimize this problem. As discussed earlier, folding artifact is common if tissue is not properly laid down prior to sectioning. – Conjunctival tissue appears different than skin histologically. Conjunctival mucosa has a very thin layer of epithelium, and usually, an underlying lymphoplasmacytic bandlike infiltrate in the superficial dermis. – Familiarity of conjunctival histopathology, especially when transitioning from palpebral conjunctiva to bulbar conjunctiva, is necessary as vasculature and glands of the bulbar conjunctiva may often resemble glandular SCC.
1.8.2 Lip The lip is a fairly simple, highly mobile anatomic structure comprising a sphincteric muscle (orbicularis oris), hair-bearing cutaneous lip skin, and mucosa.
• Similar to orbicularis oculi, the orbicularis oris muscle is a sphincteric muscle of facial expression that is innervated by CN7.

– However, orbicularis oris has no bony attachments → lip has greater laxity/mobility → easier to rearrange tissue during reconstruction. – Like the eyelid, the orbicularis oris muscle fibers attach directly to the overlying skin and mucosa, with essentially no intervening subcutaneous fat. • Vascular supply is extensive:
– Anastomosing arcades provided by labial arteries, which run deep to the orbicularis oris muscle. • Motor innervation of lip:
– Orbicularis oris is innervated by the buccal branch of CN7. – Lip depressors are innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of CN7:

○ Major danger area is where the nerve courses over the mandible.31 Typically occurs 3 cm anterior to the masseteric tuberosity (approximately one-fourth of the distance between the masseteric tuberosity and the mental midline; Fig. 1.16). • Sensory innervation of lip: • Upper lip is innervated by the infraorbital nerve (branch of V2). • Lower lip and chin are innervated by the mental nerve (branch of V3).

Fig. 1.16 Anatomic landmarks that can be used to predict the location of the marginal mandibular nerve. Reproduced with permission from Hazani R, Chowdhry S, Mowlavi A, Wilhelmi BJ. Bony Anatomic Landmarks to Avoid Injury to the Marginal Mandibular Nerve. Aesthet Surg J 2011;31(3):286–289.

• Nerve blocks of the infraorbital nerve (upper lip) and mental nerve (lower lip) are highly effective and can minimize anesthetic-related tissue distortion. • The vermilion border becomes blanched and distorted after local anesthesia injection:

– Prior to anesthesia injection, mark the vermilion border with a skin marker while it is easily seen before distortion with local anesthetic. – During your initial Mohs layer, make superficial scalpel hash marks along the previously marked vermilion border, since skin marker often washes off throughout the course of the day.

• In addition to the vermilion border, the location of the nasolabial folds and apical triangle are important landmarks in reconstructive approaches. Use a marking pen to delineate these landmarks prior to distorting the tissue with local anesthesia. • The lip is a free margin and thus can be difficult to stabilize during Mohs excision. We recommend the following methods to achieve adequate tension and stabilization during excision:

– Tell the patient, “please do not talk during this part, you don’t want me to have a moving target!” – Standard four-point lateral surface tension often works well for the cutaneous lip. – If greater tension is needed, or you are operating closer to the vermilion border, the following methods are helpful:

○ Place rolled-up gauze inside the mouth between the teeth and the inner surface of the lips and then apply surface tension. The roll of dry gauze serves as a more stable “backstop” than slippery wet teeth do; the bulkiness of the gauze also serves to evert the lip. ○ “Pinch-pull method”: the assistant uses index fingers and thumbs of both hands to pinch inside and outside the lips on both sides of the surgical site; then they stretch and evert the lip. Pinching or grasping with gauze provides better traction and grip. This method has the added benefit of hemostasis via occlusion of the labial arteries. • Consider sharp/scalpel debulking of tumor rather than curettage, as it offers many benefits and few downsides:

– Sharp debulking helps lay down/process the tissue more easily and minimizes the chance of deep tumor positivity. – Very little is sacrificed by employing sharp debulking because defect depth is not important on the lip (unless through and through):

○ Most lip Mohs defects are closed primarily or with flaps. ○ Grafts are not generally a good reconstructive option for the mobile lip. • Superficial tumors on the upper and lower lips can sometimes be curetted lightly and cleared with a thin conservative thickness Mohs
• Orbicularis muscle fibers insert directly into overlying skin with minimal or no intervening fat → difficult to establish subdermal undermining plane during reconstruction:

– Because of the muscle fiber insertion into the skin, primary closures have a tendency to heal with inversion due to the band of scar tissue in the muscle, which retracts/inverts the skin surface → it is critical to achieve hypereversion via buried vertical mattress sutures as well as epidermal vertical mattress sutures.

The ear is a highly convoluted 3D structure whose shape is dictated by the underlying cartilaginous scaffolding. The key periauricular anatomy is shown in Fig. 1.17. The ear is in close proximity to the main trunk of CN7, the parotid gland, and numerous named sensory nerves. The primary considerations during MMS are to (1) minimize damage to critical neighboring motor and sensory nerves and (2) preserve hearing by protecting the patency of the external auditory canal (EAC).
Fig. 1.17 Key periauricular anatomy. Reproduced from Janis J. Essentials of Plastic Surgery. 3rd Edition. New York: Thieme; 2022.

– Anterior surface: very thin (1 mm or less), no subcutaneous fat, difficult to undermine off of deep tissues, and relatively immobile. – Posterior surface: thicker skin with increased mobility and subcutaneous fat, and easy to undermine and mobilize for reconstructions. • Vascular supply is provided by branches off two vertically oriented vessels:
– Superficial temporal artery (STA): supplies anterior ear through horizontally oriented unnamed branches, is a terminal branch of

external carotid system that originates in parotid by the mandible, and courses 1.5 cm anterior to tragus. – Posterior auricular artery (PAA): supplies posterior ear and courses upward within the postauricular sulcus. • EAC length = 2.5 cm from conchal bowl to tympanic membrane:
– Lateral one-third of EAC = cartilage (conchal bowl). – Medial two-thirds of EAC = bone (temporal bone). • Important structures to consider:
– Main trunk of CN7 and STA are both located 1 to 1.5 cm anterior and deep to the tragus. – EAC: only 7 to 8 mm in diameter → even slight EAC stenosis can lead to hearing loss!
• For all areas of the ear, skin grafts are a valuable reconstructive option → attempt to preserve the perichondrium whenever feasible. • Palpate all ear lesions!

– If the lesion is mobile over the cartilage → tumor less likely to be invading into cartilage → make a strong attempt to preserve perichondrium on the initial Mohs stage. – If the lesion is immobile over the cartilage → cartilage likely involved. • Conchal bowl is a difficult area to take standard beveled Mohs layers, due to its concave nature:

– Angled scalpel blades can be helpful. – If a standard no. 15 blade is used, start by using the very tip of the blade to thinly incise a circle around the lesion. Then begin your Mohs layer from the lateral aspect of the ear and use a shaving motion to pass under the lesion all the way through to the opposite (medial aspect). – Have your assistant place their fingers on the posterior ear and push up on the underside of the conchal bowl to flip it outward/make it less concave. • Scissors are helpful for dissecting in the potential space between the skin and perichondrium.

The nose is one of the most common sites for skin cancer due to its anterior projection and thus direct exposure to sunlight. This is unfortunate, since the nose is perhaps the single most important facial structure from a cosmetic standpoint, due to its centrofacial location and 3D symmetry of multiple convoluted cosmetic subunits. Because of these factors, there are multiple books dedicated solely to nasal aesthetics and reconstruction. Refer to Fig. 1.18 showing the cartilaginous nasal structure.
Fig. 1.18 Cartilaginous nasal structure. Reproduced from Janis J. Essentials of Plastic Surgery. 2nd Edition. New York: Thieme; 2014.

• The nose is divided into distinct cosmetic subunits: root, dorsum, sidewall, tip, soft triangle, and ala. • Skin on the different subunits varies in texture, mobility, and risk of tension-related distortion. • Skin texture:
○ Skin grafts often are conspicuous at these sites. – Shiny, thin skin: dorsum, sidewall, dorsum, soft triangles, and columella:

○ This greater mobility is partly related to the presence of subcutaneous fat layer separating skin from underlying muscles of facial expression. – Low mobility: ala, columella, tip, and soft triangle:
○ Undermining in these areas is very challenging and unrewarding in terms of gained mobility. • Three zones of cartilage provide the nose with its shape:
○ Responsible for degree of anterior nasal projection. ○ Anchored to bone → rigid. ○ Medial boundary of internal and external nasal valves. – Upper lateral cartilages (paired):

○ Provides structural support to nasal sidewall. ○ Anchored to bone → semi-rigid (but is still subject to distortion by compressive forces). ○ Lateral boundary of internal nasal valve (susceptible to compressive forces). – Lower lateral cartilages (paired):

○ Contributes to nasal tip projection, alar crease prominence, and provides support to external nasal valve. ○ NOT anchored to bone → very mobile and easily distorted by compressive forces. • Risk of positional distortion is determined by the presence or absence of rigid underlying bone, which resists compression; the lower alar cartilages are insufficiently rigid to resist great compressive forces:

– Low risk of distortion: dorsum, sidewalls, and nasal root. – High risk of distortion: ala, nasal tip, and soft triangle. • Nasal valves allow for proper airflow and may be compromised by closure-related tension on portions of the nose NOT braced by underlying bone:

○ Pearl: Test structural integrity by occluding opposite nostril and having the patient forcibly inspire → if nostril collapses, then structural support is required. – Internal valve: the major contributor to airflow resistance; is located superior to external nasal valve.

○ Borders: inferior portion of upper lateral cartilage, nasal septum cartilage, and turbinate. ○ Increased risk of valve dysfunction: deviated septum and compression of inferior portion of upper lateral cartilage. • Vasculature: nasal skin has ample blood supply via branches of the internal (dorsal nasal artery, a branch off the ophthalmic artery) and external (facial/angular arteries) carotid systems:

– Medial canthus is location of anastomosis between angular artery (external carotid) and dorsal nasal artery (internal carotid). – Vessels are located superficial to nasal musculature → undermining in submuscular plane is a relatively bloodless plane and preserves major vessels.
• More so than at other sites, it is important to minimize not only breadth of tissue removal during Mohs, but also depth:

– Minimizing depth of defects allows for greater reconstructive options and also decreases risk of iatrogenic nasal valve incompetence. – The distal third of the nose leads itself to clearing tumors with conservative thickness layers, and these defects heal nicely by second intent. In some cases, the defect and surrounding sebaceous skin, or even rhinophyma, can be treated with wire brush dermabrasion in the same operative session as tumor clearance with a CTL.8,​9

– Because nasal cartilages are responsible for nasal contour, excision of cartilage during MMS often necessitates cartilage replacement in order to restore normal contour. • Greater degree of beveling is often required for proper lay-down of thick, sebaceous nasal skin. • Nasal skin is the most common site for subclinical “basaloid follicular proliferations” (BFPs) or “funny-looking basaloid follicular structures” → awareness of nasal BFPs/“funny follicles” helps minimize risk of overly aggressive resections. • Shape and rigidity of the alar bulb is due to fibrofatty tissue, not cartilage:

– Even if no cartilage has been resected during Mohs excision, the external nasal valve may become compromised → if so, must re- create structural support via cartilage struts or similarly rigid tissue.

○ Pearl: Folded paramedian forehead flaps and Spear’s flaps (cheek interpolation flap) often possess enough intrinsic rigidity to obviate the need for cartilage struts, but you must assess on a case-by-case basis.

1.8.5 Periosteum/Bone Performing Mohs layers near the bone is technically challenging for both the surgeon and histotechnician. Challenges include maintaining layer contiguity, mapping, tissue lay-down, and sectioning. Periosteum is extremely thin, loose tissue that is prone to folding.

• When tumors penetrate near periosteum on your initial Mohs layer, it is often difficult to accurately correlate the precise location of the tumor seen on the Mohs slides with the in vivo location where further resection is required. As such, it is common to resect periosteum broadly around the suspected area of positivity, or even to remove the entire depth of the prior Mohs defect (complete removal of the periosteum in the operative site). Tumors that approach the periosteum are highly infiltrative, by definition, and thus have an increased risk of recurrence. It is therefore critical to ensure that whatever approach you take results in a high degree of confidence that you have fully extirpated the tumor. Given the difficulty with precise localization when only the deep margin is positive, the author usually leans toward removing the periosteum from the entire depth of the surgical site. • When removing periosteum, it is worth remembering that periosteum often retracts beneath the skin edges.

– To avoid an incomplete layer due to periosteum retraction, it is helpful to excise a small margin of skin (2–3 mm) peripheral to the prior Mohs defect all the way down to bone, and then dissect the periosteum off the bone.

– In addition, including a thin rim of peripheral skin allows the surgeon to place hash marks for mapping, and provides a better area for gripping the tissue during periosteum removal. • Periosteum is delicate tissue and easily perforated with sharp tips. To avoid perforation, one should use a periosteal elevator with the curved edge facing downward. The periosteum can then be gradually freed from the bone with multiple small pushing actions.

– If scissors or a scalpel is used instead (not recommended), it is critical that the sharp tip be pointed downward toward bone in order to avoid perforation. • Transfer the tissue carefully to a small piece of moistened cardboard, which will adhere to your specimen and make it easier to maintain orientation and ink:
– Caution: do not apply too much ink, which can obscure the tissue edges and make it harder for your histotechnician to process accurately:

○ It is often preferable to have your histotechnician do the inking while being present in the room during the layer. • It is difficult for your histotechnician to evenly cut a specimen that contains both skin and periosteum, due to their vastly different thicknesses and structural properties → it is commonly necessary to separate the periosteum in order to provide quality frozen section slides. • Instruct your histotechnician to cut thin sections and avoid deeply freezing (can lead to brittle tissue and fracturing). • If deep tumor remains positive in your periosteum Mohs layer → consider referral to ENT or neurosurgery for possible bone (outer table of the calvarium) resection—the outer table of the calvarium can be burred down with a dermatome or in the office setting with a coarse diamond fraise or a dermabrading hand engine. While this technique does not allow microscopic examination of the margins, it does provide an extra measure of tumor removal below missing or torn areas of periosteum—this technique also increases the vascularity of exposed cranium for second intent healing or split-thickness grafting.
MMS is extremely valuable in the treatment of nail unit malignancies, as it can offer high cure rates and digital sparing.

• Nail unit: the nail plate overlies the matrix, nail bed, proximal and lateral nail folds, hyponychium, and neurovascular structures. • The major neurovascular structures run along the lateral and medial aspects of the digits and are easily anesthetized with nerve blocks.

– A large study of 1,111 patients undergoing digital nerve blocks for hand surgery compared use of plain lidocaine (without epinephrine) to lidocaine with epinephrine → no complications were observed when lidocaine with epinephrine was used → data support the use of lidocaine with epinephrine for digital blocks (exercise caution if the patient has a vasoocclusive disorder).32
– Combining bupivacaine with the lidocaine with epinephrine may provide prolonged anesthesia and decrease postoperative pain.33

○ Injection site: lateral and medial portions of the proximal digit, near the MCP/MTP. ○ Slow onset (15–20 minutes). ○ Risk of damage to major neurovascular bundles. ○ Does not provide hemostasis. – Distal digital blocks (“wing blocks”):

○ Faster in onset, safer, and provide hemostasis, compared to proximal digital blocks; more painful if a prior proximal digital is not done. ○ Injection site: 5 mm proximal and lateral to the lateral edges of the proximal nail fold.
– The assistant can pinch the radial and ulnar aspects of the digit to occlude blood flow. – Tourniquet can be made from gauze or penrose drain or glove.
• Understanding of the nail deformity allows you to make an educated guess as to where the tumor lies:

– Matrix lesions → pigment or thickening within the nail plate proper. – Nail bed → normal-appearing nail plate will be elevated off of the nail bed. • The 3D shape of the distal bone and the convolutions of the nail folds make it challenging to maintain a uniform, uninterrupted Mohs layer. Trying to ensure completeness of the deep margin can be particularly problematic, as there is little subcutaneous tissue separating the nail unit from the underlying bone.

– Often, your best chance of obtaining a high-quality Mohs specimen is during your initial Mohs stage. – If the deep margin is positive on your first Mohs stage, you will likely need to use similar techniques and tools as described earlier for periosteum Mohs layers. • Due to the complex 3D structure of the nail unit, be sure to bring your histotechnician into the room to show them how the specimen appeared in vivo, so they can be more confident about what represents the “true margin” during tissue relaxation and processing.

1.8.7 Anogenital Region Tissue conservation in the anogenital region is critical for preservation of function and cosmesis of this highly sensitive area. Anogenital skin presents unique challenges due to its thin nature, laxity, and its transition zones from squamatized epidermis to the mucosal epithelium of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. EMPD and SCCs of the anogenital area are not infrequent indications for MMS, due to the desire for maximal tissue sparing.
• Scrotum/vulva/penis: The thin and highly redundant nature of genital skin presents unique challenges:
– Your assistant will need to fully stretch out the redundant skin so that your incisions yield sharp margins.

– Due to the thinness of the skin and the importance of underlying fascial and soft-tissue structures, it is critical to avoid unnecessarily deep incisions. – The surgeon should aim to incise only the epidermis and dermis with their scalpel during the initial Mohs excision. To ensure a contiguous deep tissue margin and prevent perforation of the underlying structures, iris scissors are preferred for elevation and removal of the Mohs layer after the lesion has been circumferentially incised with a scalpel. – Hash marks may be extremely difficult to identify on both the Mohs specimen and the patient’s skin surrounding the Mohs site. It is often useful to suture a single interrupted stitch at each of the hash marks on the patient. It is also critical to pay close attention to the location of the hashes on the Mohs specimen before inking it and/or giving it to your lab. • Perianal region: many of the same challenges and approaches that were discussed for genital skin apply to the perianal region. Fortunately, there are fewer deep structures of concern, and therefore, less emphasis is placed on achieving super-thin Mohs excisions.

Abstract Adhering to fundamental principles of surgical reconstruction and understanding tissue biomechanics are the keys to reliable reconstruction outcomes after Mohs micrographic surgery. Disregarding these fundamental principles leads to inconsistent outcomes or noticeable scars. This chapter will review guiding principles for facial reconstruction.
Keywords: reconstruction, design principles, tissue biomechanics, systematic wound assessment, flap, facial reconstruction
This chapter will review fundamental principles of facial reconstruction design, tissue biomechanics, anatomy, and selection of reconstruction options.

– To preserve and restore free margins and contour. – To hide scars in cosmetic subunit junctions and relaxed skin tension lines. – To optimize skin color and texture match. • Fundamental principles of tissue biomechanics:

– Reconstructions to repair central facial defects favor tissue movement from lateral to medial locations. – Reconstructions to repair lateral facial defects favor tissue movement from inferior to superior locations. – Linear closures and sliding flaps have the greatest tension at the primary defect. – Transposition and interpolation flaps transfer the greatest tension away from the primary defect to the tissue donor site.
– Ideal undermining planes vary with the anatomic location of the face and affect blood supply to flaps. • Fundamental principles of anatomy:

– Blood supply to the face comes from both the external and internal carotid systems. Incorporating vessels into flap pedicles can improve blood supply and flap survival. – The superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) protects the branches of the facial nerve. • Fundamental principles to assess facial wounds and to select an ideal reconstruction:

– Define the missing anatomic layers in a defect and replace them with similar tissue whenever possible. – Preserving free margins and contour is the top priority. Hiding scars in cosmetic subunit junction lines and relaxed skin tension lines and matching color and texture are secondary priorities. – If wound edges can be approximated without tension or distortion of anatomy, linear closure or sliding flaps are usually possible. – If approximating wound edges has high tension or distorts anatomy, transposition and interpolation flaps or skin grafts may be necessary.

We observe faces as we do highways: we disregard the expected; we notice the unexpected. Just as we ignore the characteristics of the highway until painted lines are altered or we encounter bumps or holes, we do not pay attention to facial scars unless they surprise us with unexpected lines or contours. The surgeon’s job is to leave scars that blend into the background and restore the expected contours of the face. In descending order of importance, the fundamental principles of reconstructive design are to preserve and restore free margins and contour, to hide scars in cosmetic
subunit junctions and relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs), and to optimize color and texture match with imported tissue.

2.1.2 Free Margins The eyelids, distal nose, lips, and helical rim are “free margins” because they are unsupported on one side. These structures define our appearance, as demonstrated by the prominence of free margins in a facial sketch (Fig. 2.1). Preserving and restoring the free margins of the eyelids, the distal nose, the lips, and helical rim is a top priority during reconstructive surgery. Tension from reconstructive surgery or subsequent contraction from resulting scars can change the position of these delicate structures and create noticeable changes in contour and symmetry (Fig. 2.2). Strategies to preserve free margin position include orienting tension vectors parallel to free margins, transferring tension to tissue reservoirs remote from free margins,1 and tacking tissue to immobile deep structures so that dermal sutures near free margins are tension free.
Fig. 2.2 Patient with lateral ectropion of the left eye due to contracted scar tissue from prior repair. Malposition of the free margin causes conspicuous changes in appearance.

Contour determines how light reflects off our faces. Concavities (alar groove, medial canthus, philtrum) cast shadows; convexities (zygoma, tip of nose) reflect shiny light; and planar surfaces (cheek, forehead) reflect a subtle, even light. Unnatural contours on the face are noticeable because they interrupt the expected play of light. Too much volume (e.g., thick forehead flap on the nasal tip), too little volume (e.g., a skin graft in a deep defect), or failure to recreate natural contours (e.g., flaps that ablate the alar groove) will draw attention to these aberrations in facial contour (Fig. 2.3a– c). A top priority of reconstructive surgery is to recreate natural contours by filling wounds with tissue of similar surface area and thickness.

Fig. 2.3 (a) Unnatural light reflections draw attention to this bulky paramedian forehead flap. (b) This split-thickness skin graft is noticeable for both its white color and depressed contour. (c) A cheek advancement flap blunts the natural concavities of the nasofacial sulcus and alar groove.

Cosmetic subunit junction lines create natural shadows and reflections at transition zones between facial structures (Fig. 2.1).2,​3 In complex cosmetic subunits such as the nose, further subdivisions are evident between the tip, dorsum, sidewalls, alae, and soft triangles.4 For example, the alar groove separates the ala and nasal sidewall. Around the mouth, the vermilion cutaneous junction divides the shiny red vermilion from the hair-bearing

skin of the cutaneous lip. The nasolabial fold separates the lip from the cheek. Intentionally placing scars in cosmetic subunit boundaries camouflages them within natural shadows and reflections (Fig. 2.4). Wounds near the boundaries of cosmetic subunits may be expanded to hide scars in the junction lines (Fig. 2.5, Fig. 2.6).

Fig. 2.4 (a) This defect resides along the cosmetic subunit junction lines that separate the cheek from the nose and mouth. (b) Appearance immediately after a linear repair that falls within the nasofacial sulcus and nasolabial fold. (c) Weeks after surgery, the pink scar is less conspicuous because it falls in the cosmetic subunit junction lines where a viewer expects to see lines or shadows.

Fig. 2.5 (a) Tension from a local flap for this nasal tip defect risked distortion of the free margins. (b) The defect was expanded to the boundaries of the nasal tip subunit and repaired with a full-
thickness skin graft. (c) The scars along the cosmetic subunit boundaries are inconspicuous and the free margins and contour are restored.

Fig. 2.6 (a,b) The defect was expanded to the purple markings so that the edges of the paramedian forehead flap conformed to the boundaries of the nasal tip subunit: frontal view. (c,d) Paramedian forehead flap repair. (e,f) Months after surgery, the scars at the cosmetic subunit junction lines are hard to notice.

RSTLs correspond to the wrinkles that form with animation of the underlying muscles of facial expression. RSTLs run perpendicular to the direction of the underlying muscle fibers. For example, contraction of the vertically oriented frontalis muscle fibers creates horizontal rhytids on the forehead and contractions of the circumferential orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris muscles form rhytids that radiate perpendicularly from the free margins of eyelids and lips, respectively (Fig. 2.7). As we age, these lines become more visible even without animation of facial muscles. Scars are less noticeable and have less tension when they align with RSTLs. However, placing scars in RSTLs should not violate higher priority reconstruction principles. For example, if a horizontal closure on the forehead would cause asymmetric lift of the eyebrow, it is better to perform a vertical closure that crosses RSTLs but preserves brow position.

Mismatches in color and texture can make scars noticeable, a common outcome with skin grafts (Fig. 2.3b, Fig. 2.8). Linear closures and local flaps are preferred, because they recruit adjacent skin of similar color and texture. Mismatches in the density of hair and sebaceous glands can still occur with local flaps (Fig. 2.9), especially if terminal hairs are transposed to areas normally containing vellus hairs. Replacement of specialty skin, such as the vermilion lip or eyelid margin, may not be possible. When it is impossible to avoid color and texture mismatches, conforming to higher priority reconstruction principles (free margins, contour, cosmetic subunit junction lines, RSTLs) often makes these differences acceptable (Fig. 2.9).

Fig. 2.8 (a) Large defect of the left medial canthus. (b) Healing skin graft. (c) While there is good anatomical position of the eyelids, there is noticeable mismatch in color of the graft in comparison to the surrounding skin.

Fig. 2.9 (a) Large Mohs defect on the right infraorbital cheek. (b) Trilobed flap sutured in place. (c,d) Well-healed flap with excellent restoration of contour and no pull on the ipsilateral lower lid. While incision lines are fine, note that the flap is more conspicuous given terminal hair follicles were transposed to an area of normally vellus hair–bearing skin.

Surgical reconstruction moves tissue from one area to another along preferred vectors on the face. Basic principles guide tissue movement, and understanding the preferred vectors for tissue movement can make the difference between a high- and a low-tension reconstruction. The location of the defect and tension vectors relative to the primary defect will dictate reconstruction design. Undermining in an efficient tissue plane can also facilitate skin movement.

2.2.2 Preferred Vectors to Move Facial Tissue The direction in which a skin flap slides toward the defect is called the primary tissue motion, and the countermovement of the surrounding tissue to meet the flap is considered secondary tissue motion. Facial skin moves along preferred vectors (Fig. 2.10).

To repair defects of the central face (mid-forehead, glabella, nose, lips, chin), the primary tissue motion occurs along a medial or superomedial vector that recruits skin from the lateral cheek or jowl toward the midline. The horizontal/medial vector parallels the free margins of the eyelids, distal nose, and lips, and helps preserve their position.

To repair defects of the lateral face (lateral forehead, temples, lateral cheek), the primary tissue motion occurs along a superior or superolateral vector that moves skin from the neck and jowl to more superior locations on the face. The superior vector has minimal impact on the contours of the central face. In general, facial reconstructions are most successful when the primary tissue motion follows these vectors.

Primary closures and sliding flaps (i.e., advancement and rotation) recruit skin immediately adjacent to the wound and maintain greatest tension at the primary defect. When tension at the primary defect is too great for direct closure or if tension will distort anatomy, then transposition (e.g., rhombic, bilobed, and trilobed flaps) and interpolation flaps (e.g., paramedian forehead flap and nasolabial interpolation flap) or grafts may be necessary. These flaps transfer tension to a remote donor site so that tissue can be inset at the primary defect with minimal tension. Whether tension is at the primary defect or a remote donor site, all of these reconstruction options work best when the main tension falls along preferred vectors (lateral to medial in the mid-face and inferior to superior on the lateral face; Fig. 2.10).

2.2.4 Tissue Planes for Undermining and Elevating Flaps Most local reconstructions of the face require undermining to mobilize tissue. Undermining releases either the skin edges or flap from underlying attachments to gain mobility.

The ideal surgical plane for facial undermining varies based on the location (Table 2.1). If the surgeon is working in an efficient surgical plane, flap elevation and undermining should occur with ease and minimal bleeding. Undue resistance or excessive bleeding while lifting tissue usually signifies an inefficient anatomic plane (e.g., most commonly splitting the subcutaneous fat, rather than working at the junction of the fat and fascia).
Lateral face and neck Junction of the subcutaneous fat and superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS)

the face, excision deep to the SMAS is less likely to cause motor deficits (e.g., excision of midline and paramedian frontalis muscle does not leave motor deficit on the forehead). On the midline nose, forehead, and scalp, undermining deep to the SMAS is frequently desirable.

aIn areas where the muscles of facial expression are layered, for example, lip depressors and elevators, the motor nerves innervate the deepest muscles from their superficial surface. Abbreviation: SMAS, superficial musculoaponeurotic system.

On the lateral face, the ideal plane to elevate flaps or undermine tissue is at the junction of the subcutaneous fat and fascia of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) (Fig. 2.11). This plane preserves the branches of the facial nerve, which lie deep to the SMAS. On the central face, excising deep to the muscles of facial expression/SMAS poses minimal risk for motor deficits. The most common surgical plane on the nose and central forehead is deep to the SMAS (Fig. 2.12). For smaller procedures in the central face, the surgeon may choose a surgical plane superficial to the SMAS, such as a small horizontal closure on the forehead or narrow linear closure on the cutaneous lip.
Fig. 2.11 The ideal plane for undermining on the lateral face is between the subcutaneous fat and fascia of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system. SMAS, superficial musculoaponeurotic system.

Fig. 2.12 The ideal plane for undermining on the central face is deep to the superficial musculoaponeurotic system and muscles. This minimizes risks of motor defects. SMAS, superficial musculoaponeurotic system.

The vascular supply to a flap varies according to the anatomic plane and extent of undermining. Flaps elevated too superficially (e.g., immediately subdermal) may not have adequate blood supply.5,​6 To optimize blood supply, local flaps should contain at least the epidermis, dermis, and the tight columnar cells of subcutaneous fat immediately adherent to the dermis. Undermining deep to muscle or fascia improves flap blood supply but may increase morbidity, depending on the anatomic location of the surgery. For example, in the central face (e.g., nose and central forehead) and scalp, undermining deep to the muscles of facial expression or galea, respectively, is desirable in most cases. By contrast, on the lateral face, temple, and posterior triangle of the neck, undermining deep to the SMAS

Undermining too widely can threaten a flap’s blood supply or increase the risk for postoperative bleeding and hematoma.7,​8 In general, the surgeon should undermine just enough to move the flap into place. Frequent assessment of skin edge mobility helps avoid unnecessarily wide undermining. When the skin edges comfortably stretch to their desired target, additional undermining is rarely helpful or necessary.

A comprehensive discussion of facial anatomy is beyond the scope of this introductory chapter. A few guiding principles of facial anatomy are especially important for reconstruction. Understanding the blood supply of axial flaps helps ensure survival, as does a precise grasp of the depth of motor nerves in relation to facial musculature and the SMAS.

Blood supply to the face comes from both the external and internal carotid systems. The external carotid artery and its branches supply blood to the lateral forehead, temple, cheek, ear, distal and lateral nose, and lips. The internal carotid artery and its branches supply blood to the mid-forehead, upper eyelid, and central nose. Linear closures, sliding flaps, and transposition flaps typically have a random-pattern blood supply from the subdermal plexus, so the proper plane of undermining (at least under the subdermal fat) is the most important factor for flap survival. By contrast, axial flaps contain named arteries in their pedicles (e.g., supratrochlear artery in the paramedian forehead flap and labial artery in the Abbé lip switch flap). Precise knowledge of anatomy is necessary to include the artery in the flap pedicle.
2.3.3 Superficial Musculoaponeurotic System The SMAS is a term to describe the muscles of facial expression and fascia that envelope the face and protect the facial nerve branches. The SMAS is

continuous with the platysma inferiorly and the galea aponeurotica and superficial temporal fascia superiorly.9 The branches of the facial nerve are most vulnerable after they emerge from the parotid gland, because they are covered by only a thin layer of fascia until they innervate the central facial muscles from their lateral undersurface. The temporal and marginal mandibular branches are most vulnerable. Working in the tissue plane immediately superficial to the SMAS protects the facial nerve branches and is the most common plane to elevate tissue on the temple and the mandible.

A systematic approach to assessing surgical defects helps conform to fundamental principles of surgical design and tissue biomechanics. Replacing “like with like” is a principle of reconstruction (e.g., if cartilage is missing, replace the cartilage).

The first step to reconstructing facial defects is to define the missing anatomic layers. Reconstruction under local anesthesia is generally limited to soft-tissue defects that can range from superficial defects with loss of the superficial dermis to deep defects with loss of skin, muscle, and cartilage. In general, reconstructions should replace “like with like.” For example, full-thickness skin grafts may be ideal for shallow defects with missing epidermis and dermis, but they rarely restore contour for defects involving cartilage or muscle. If defects include cartilage on the nose and ear, a free cartilage graft is usually necessary to prevent contraction of an overlying flap or graft.

In addition to replacing missing anatomic layers, donor sites ideally have skin of similar color, thickness, and density of hair and sebaceous glands. Flaps that contain hair will be conspicuous if they replace normally hairless skin (Fig. 2.9). Cheek flaps with a generous layer of subcutaneous fat will look distended if they replace normally taut lip or nasal skin.

After examining the missing anatomic layers on the wound, consider the following questions to take inventory of the major principles of reconstruction. Does the wound involve a free margin? Could tension from the reconstruction push or pull on a free margin? What surface area and thickness of tissue do I need to restore contour, and will tension from the reconstruction change facial contour? Can I design a reconstruction that hides scars in cosmetic subunit junction lines or RSTLs? Can I cover the wound with skin of similar color and texture? Is terminal hair-bearing skin being moved into a normally vellus hair–bearing area?

Assessing wound tension by pushing the edges of the defect centripetally (i.e., toward the center of the wound) determines if the wound edges can be approximated and demonstrates the impact of different tension vectors on adjacent free margins and contour. Observation of this simple test can help the surgeon choose the ideal reconstruction. If the wound edges can be pushed together, then reconstructions that maintain tension at the primary defect—linear closures and advancement and rotation flaps—are usually possible. If the wound edges cannot be pushed together because of excessive tension or if doing so would distort free margins and contour, then reconstructions that transfer tension to remote tissue reservoirs— transposition flaps and interpolation flaps—are ideal. If local tissue reservoirs have too much tension for a transposition flap, a staged interpolation flap, skin graft, or second intention healing may be necessary.
This section will review fundamental principles of different reconstruction options on the face, including second intention healing, linear closure, grafts, and flaps.

Second intention healing has two predictable outcomes: (1) the scar will have a shiny texture and (2) the scar will contract. Therefore, ideal wounds for second intention healing are located in areas where the skin normally has a shiny texture and where scar contraction will not cause anatomic distortion. Areas on the face where second intention scars have reasonable texture match include the scalp, upper forehead, ear, and nasal dorsum or proximal sidewall. By contrast, scars from second intention healing may contrast against the sebaceous skin of the nasal tip and ala or the hair- bearing skin of the cheek and lip. Scars from second intention healing may also hide in or recreate concave contours, such as the alar groove and medial canthus.10 However, this strategy must be employed judiciously, since scar contraction may blunt the concavity.

Contraction of second intention wounds can change the position of nearby free margins and cause webbing of adjacent, loose skin, such as the ectropion of the eyelid. The likelihood of anatomic distortion and webbing of the scars is greater for deep wounds spanning the concave junction between cosmetic subunits. The ideal defect to minimize distortion from second intention healing is shallow and has surrounding stiff skin. Patients should expect evolving color and volume of the second intention scar. Scars that are initially pink and hypertrophic usually mature to a hypo- or hyperpigmented color with flatter contour.

Linear closure is the side-to-side approximation of the edges of a fusiform wound. Tension lies along a single vector running perpendicular to the long axis of the fusiform wound and is greatest at the center of the wound. To avoid standing cones and to maintain normal contour, the ideal angles at the apices of a fusiform excision are greater than 30 degrees, which requires a length-to-width ratio of 3:1 or greater. In some anatomic locations, such as the nasal tip/columella, helical rim, or malar cheek, standing cones may need to be elongated to reduce tension and to maintain contour.

Primary linear closure is the most common reconstruction on the face. On the central face, primary linear closures are usually oriented with a vertical long axis so that the tension vector of the wound parallels the free margins of the face. Vertically oriented closures of the central face can still distort free margin position. When the curved lines of a fusiform excision

are joined to form a straight line, the long axis of the fusiform excision elongates and can push up or down on adjacent free margins.11 Linear closures can also compress the soft tissue of free margins, creating a fat lip or a bulky alar margin. On the lateral face, primary closures are usually oriented with a horizontal or diagonal long axis so that the primary tissue motion follows a vector from inferior to superior. The scars from primary closures on the lateral face often fall within RSTLs.

Skin grafts lack an intrinsic blood supply, so their survival depends on inosculation with the blood vessels of the wound bed. Grafts will not survive on devascularized wounds, such as forehead or scalp defects that lack periosteum or nasal tip defects without perichondrium. Full-thickness skin grafts (epidermis plus full-thickness of dermis) usually have better color and texture match because they retain hair follicles and eccrine glands. Split-thickness skin grafts (epidermis plus partial-thickness dermis) can cover larger wounds, but they usually have worse color and texture because they lack adnexal structures.

Skin grafts have sufficient volume to restore contour only for shallow wounds. Skin grafts covering deep wounds will result in depressed contour or a skeletonized appearance ( Fig. 2.3b). Full-thickness wounds of the alar margin, soft triangle, and columella may require composite grafts, which contain both skin and cartilage. Composite grafts have an especially high risk for failure, due to their high metabolic demand. As a result, composite grafting is usually limited to wounds less than a centimeter in diameter. The root of the helix is a common donor site for composite grafts.

Donor skin should match, as closely as possible, the color and texture of removed skin at the defect. Skin grafts usually are less conspicuous when they replace thin, nonsebaceous skin. By contrast, grafts are usually readily apparent on sebaceous or hair-bearing skin.

Sliding flaps move adjacent skin directly into the defect, and the greatest tension lies at the primary defect. Examples include advancement flaps, V- Y island pedicle advancement flaps, and rotation flaps.

Advancement flaps are useful for wounds that could be closed with a fusiform excision, except one of the standing cones would encroach on a free margin (e.g., eyelid, lip, distal nose, and helical rim) or cosmetic subunit junction (e.g., eyebrow, vermilion cutaneous junction, and alar groove; Fig. 2.13(a–c)). Like fusiform closures, advancement flaps maintain tension along a single vector, but they displace one or both of the standing cones to preserve a free margin or hide the scar in a cosmetic subunit junction line or RSTL.

Common locations for advancement flaps are near free margins on the face, such as the upper and lower cutaneous lip, the nasal sidewall, the infraorbital cheek and lower eyelid, the forehead and temple, the preauricular cheek, and the helical rim. Advancement flaps are also useful for small paramedian nasal tip defects (e.g., East-West flap).12 For defects of the midline face, the primary tissue motion of advancement flaps is usually lateral to medial so the tension vector parallels the free margins of the eyelids, nose, and lips. For defects of the lateral face, the primary motion is usually inferior to superior.

V-Y island pedicle advancement flaps differ from the other sliding flaps (i.e., advancement and rotation) in that their entire blood supply comes from the flap’s undersurface. A triangular shaped flap is designed with its base at the edge of the defect. Incisions are made through the dermis of the two side limbs, creating the “island” that gives the flap its name. A key suture advances the leading edge of the flap toward the defect. The secondary defect at the trailing edge of the flap is closed primarily, resulting in a suture line that resembles a “Y.”
V-Y island pedicle advancement flaps on the face are most commonly used to repair defects of the lateral upper cutaneous lip (Fig. 2.14,d), nasal sidewall and alar groove, cheek, and brow.

Fig. 2.14 (a) Mohs defect on the upper cutaneous lip. (b) V-Y advancement flap sutured in place. (c,d) Patient at follow-up with well-concealed incision lines along the nasolabial fold and vermilion border.

The hallmark of a rotation flap is the arciform incision used to mobilize the surrounding skin ( Fig. 2.15 (a,b) ). Rotating the flap into the primary defect creates a secondary defect along the arciform incision. In contrast to the single tension vector of advancement flaps, rotation flaps distribute tension across multiple vectors along both the primary and secondary defects.

A simple test to choose between a rotation and an advancement flap is to push the wound edges together (Fig. 2.16). If there is a clearly preferred tension vector at the primary wound but the standing cone of a linear closure would impinge on adjacent free margins, then an advancement flap

will work. If there is no clearly dominant tension vector, but the wound edges nearly approximate by pushing in multiple directions, then a rotation flap may be ideal to distribute tension across multiple vectors at the primary defect. The scalp is a classic location for rotation flaps because wounds at this location often do not have a preferred tension vector.

Fig. 2.16 Simple test for choosing between advancement and rotation flaps. Advancement flaps work well for wounds with preferred vectors. Rotation flaps work well for wounds without a dominant vector for closure.

Rotation flaps on the face are most commonly used to repair medial cheek defects that recruit skin from the lateral cheek and neck, lateral forehead defects that recruit from the temple, and nasal tip defects that recruit skin from the nasal sidewall and glabella.13,​14

If linear closure or use of sliding flaps would result in excessive tension or distortion of free margins (e.g., eyelids, distal nose, and lips), then a transposition flap may be useful to transfer tension to a more generous tissue reservoir. Three common transposition flaps include the rhombic or banner (single-lobed), bilobed, and trilobed flaps (Fig. 2.17). As opposed to sliding flaps, which have the greatest tension at the primary defect, transposition flaps displace the greatest tension to the final donor site (i.e., secondary defect of a rhombic flap, tertiary defect of a bilobed flap, and quaternary defect of a trilobed flap). Closing the terminal donor site allows rotation of the flap into the primary defect with minimal tension. Adding lobes to transposition flaps recruits tissue from reservoirs increasingly remote from the primary defect and displaces tension to more favorable vectors.
Fig. 2.17 Three common transposition flaps (rhombic, bilobed, and trilobed), all of which transfer greatest tension to reservoir near the primary defect. Stars represent closure of the key stitch.
Because they transfer key tension vectors away from the primary defect, transposition flaps are especially useful to repair facial defects near the free

Interpolation flaps transfer skin from remote reservoirs with a pedicle that bridges an isthmus of skin between the primary defect and the donor site. The flap pedicle remains intact until the ingrowth of blood vessels from the recipient site provides sufficient nourishment to the transferred skin. The ingrowth of new vessels is usually reliable after approximately 3 weeks, at which time the pedicle can be divided during a second surgical procedure.

Interpolation flaps are ideal for defects at or near free margins of the face. The paramedian forehead flap15 (Fig. 2.6) and nasolabial interpolation flap repair distal nasal defects,16 the retroauricular interpolation flap repairs helical rim defects,17,​18; the Abbé flap repairs large defects of the lip margin19; and the Hughes and Cutler–Beard flaps repair defects of the eyelid margin.20,​21 All of these flaps transfer tension away from the primary defect and help preserve and restore free margins.

Fundamental principles of design and tissue biomechanics are the cornerstones of successful facial reconstruction. A systematic approach to assessing wounds can help choose reconstructions that adhere to these key principles.
