Mastering nasal reconstruction requires a thorough understanding of nasal anatomy, flap dynamics, and proficiency with repair options depending on defect location, skin type and nasal topography, and patient expectations. Herein, the authors begin by presenting a review of nasal anatomy, a prerequisite for any surgeon endeavoring to master nasal reconstruction. Next, the authors review repair options according to each nasal cosmetic subunit, starting with the nasal tip and ending with the nasal sidewall. While innumerable repair options exist for each particular nasal defect, those that are presented are the result of the senior author’s trove of reconstructive experience, which has allowed him to arrive at a set of repair options that, when executed correctly, consistently produce the most reproducible results. Finally, the authors review complications as well as revisions, because even the best reconstructive surgeon will encounter occasional complications despite a perfect effort and should know how to manage these should they occur. After reviewing this chapter, the reader should have a sound understanding of nasal reconstruction and a framework to approach any nasal defect he or she should encounter.

• Superficial defects on any nasal location can have an excellent aesthetic outcome when allowed to heal by second intention, especially when augmented by the use of the “shave and sand” technique. • Deeper defects on concave areas like the alar crease and nasal root/inner canthus can also achieve good results when left to heal.

• While full-thickness skin grafts are a remarkably versatile option for range of defects on the nose, defect size, depth, neighboring skin quality, and patient preference dictate when their use is most appropriate. The conchal bowl provides the best match for wounds of the lower third of the nose, whereas postauricular skin is favored for wounds on the upper two-thirds. • Primary closure is an outstanding option for small to medium midline wounds on the nasal tip and dorsum, though several modifications of the classic fusiform closure must be employed to attain an optimal result. • Local transposition flaps are the most reliable repair options for full-thickness defects on the nose not amenable to primary closure. • The bilobed transposition flap is the preeminent flap choice for small to medium full-thickness defects on the lower third of the nose, especially the tip, whereas the rhombic flap is preferred for the upper two-thirds. • The forehead flap is the ideal choice for larger defects of the nasal tip and ala, especially when used in conjunction with cartilage grafts in the cases where functional integrity of the nose is compromised. • For full-thickness perforating defects, all three nasal layers including skin, cartilaginous or fibrofatty structural support, and nasal lining must be repaired in order to thwart damaging aesthetic and functional repercussions. • Before and during repair, nasal valve competency should be assessed and restored as needed. • In order to decrease risk of pincushioning, wide undermining to promote formation of a platelike scar, aggressive flap defatting, and use of buried vertical mattress sutures to pull deep tissues back to suture line are required. • At the time of surgery, patients should be informed of their need to return in 3 months for potential dermabrasion in order to correct any visible incision lines or contour asymmetry.

Repairing the nose poses one of the greatest challenges for the reconstructive surgeon. The combination of the nose’s complex topography, unique sebaceous texture, minimal laxity, and freely mobile free margins requires a mastery of the skills necessary to repair this complex structure. The nose plays a pivotal role aesthetically as the centerpiece of the face while also having a significant role in respiration. Thus, a poor reconstructive effort may have both cosmetic and functional repercussions for the patient. Approaching nasal defects algorithmically based on size, skin type, and location can assist in selecting the most appropriate repair option for a given patient. However, because noses drastically differ among patients, one should simply not apply a “cookie cutter” approach to nasal reconstruction. The surgeon must therefore address each nasal defect individually when selecting the optimal repair option for a particular patient.

While innumerable methods to repair a particular defect on each nasal subunit have been published, in our experience, there are a limited a number of reliable repair options for each subunit that routinely achieve high-quality results. Herein, following a review of nasal anatomy, we discuss the various repair options that we believe consistently provide superb results for patients.

Possessing a thorough understanding of nasal anatomy is essential to achieve operative success and avoid complications. The unique nasal topography, an elegant synthesis of convexities, concavities, inflections, and grooves, allows its division into aesthetic subunits. These aesthetic subunits include the tip, dorsum, sidewalls, alar lobules, and soft triangles.1

It has been advocated that superior results are achieved when skin within an aesthetic subunit is repaired with like skin possessing similar texture and color. However, many flaps on the nose that do not adhere to the subunit principle will still accomplish highly aesthetic results. A quintessential example is the bilobed flap, which uses lax donor skin from the upper sidewall to repair defects on the tip. Furthermore, many, especially in

plastic surgery literature, advocate resurfacing an entire subunit even at the expense of enlarging a defect. While the authors will often employ this technique for larger staged flaps, excellent outcomes can still be attained without sacrificing more skin. Similarly, while the borders of aesthetic subunits are theoretically an ideal place for scar placement, scars placed elsewhere with the intention of preventing distortion should be a preferred goal.

The nose can be thought of as a three-layered structure consisting of skin, cartilage or fibrofatty tissue, and a mucosal lining. The nasal lining consists of a thin layer of vascular mucosa that is tightly adherent to overlying cartilage and bone. Failure to repair the mucosal portion of a full-thickness perforating nasal defect can have grim complications including flap contraction, nasal distortion, and airway obstruction.

The majority of the nasal “skeleton” consists of cartilage with a small bony base comprising the most proximal aspect (Fig. 3.1). This bony base is formed by two symmetric nasal bones, which correspond with the nasal bridge. The nasal bones are bordered superiorly by the skull’s frontal bone at an intersection point termed the nasion (corresponding to the nasal root on the skin’s surface) and are bordered laterally by the frontal processes of the maxilla. After extending anteriorly and inferiorly, the nasal bone attaches to the septal cartilage, which continues to extend in an anterior and inferior direction to form the spine of the nose. The upper lateral cartilage projects laterally from the nasal septum to form the overlying nasal sidewall. Inferiorly, the lower nose is reinforced bilaterally by the lower lateral cartilages. Each lower lateral cartilage possesses both a lateral crus, which supports the nasal tip and medial ala, and a medial crus, which supports the nasal columella. Importantly, while the bulk of the nasal ala is not supported directly by cartilage, the rigid quality of its unique fibrofatty tissue allows it to resist collapse upon inspiration. The nasalis muscle extends superiorly and medially from the maxilla and is responsible for flaring the nostrils. Its incorporation into various flaps on the nose allows for excellent flap viability.

When executing a nasal flap or graft, an understanding of the zones of skin thickness is critical when selecting ideal donor skin (Fig. 3.2). The skin on the upper half of the nose (zone I) is thin, shiny, nonsebaceous, and relatively lax. On the tip, supratip, ala, and lower sidewall, skin tends to be significantly thicker, more sebaceous, and rigid (zone II). Moving caudally down the nose, starting at the infratip and continuing onto the soft triangles and columella, the skin transitions back to being thin and nonsebaceous (zone III), similar to that of the upper nose. While it is important to understand the zones of the nose conceptually, the size of each zone on a particular patient may vary. Likewise, the degree of sebaceous composition and size of the various nasal cartilages account for the heterogeneity of nasal shapes and sizes that exist among patients.
Fig. 3.2 Zones of the nose used to describe areas of the nose with similar skin thickness and sebaceous quality.

The nose has a rich vascular system, owing to a blood supply that comes from branches of both the external and internal carotid artery systems with extensive anastomoses (Fig. 3.3). At the level of the lateral lip, the facial artery (external carotid system) gives off its two terminal branches: the superior labial artery and the angular artery. After coursing medially along the upper lip, the superior labial artery gives off septal branches to supply

the anterior portion of the nasal septum and ultimately a branch that supplies the columella. In its upward course, the angular artery gives off the lateral nasal artery and provides blood supply to the lateral portion of the lower one-third of the nose. The external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system) and provides part of the blood supply to the nasal tip. The dorsal nasal artery branches off the ophthalmic artery and pierces through the orbital septum superior to the medial canthal ligament supplying a large portion of the upper sidewall and dorsum. The nose’s extensive vascular network allows for excellent viability of both flaps and grafts.

The sensory input to the nose stems from the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) branches of the trigeminal nerve. The ophthalmic nerve gives off the supratrochlear, infratrochlear, and external nasal nerves, which supply the skin of the root, upper sidewall, dorsum, and tip. The infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve gives sensory supply to the caudal nasal sidewall and nasal alae. The nose contains no major motor nerves; however, transection of some of the aforementioned sensory nerve branches may result in anesthesia that is likely to resolve over the course of a year. Nerve blocks are infrequently used on the nose.

A review of nasal anatomy would be incomplete without mention of the internal nasal valve. The valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway and the area of greatest resistance. It is formed by the caudal border of the upper lateral cartilage, the nasal septum, the nasal sidewall, and the inferior turbinate. Because the nasal sidewall is the most mobile border, cancer extirpation or repairs involving the sidewall adjacent to the alar groove can risk collapse of the valve, resulting in impaired airflow during inspiration. Therefore, it is essential to assess patency of the valve prior to repair to determine whether correction is necessary. In the remainder of this chapter, we will review our approach to nasal reconstruction, describing various repair options for each nasal subunit.

Due to the immobility of the thick sebaceous nasal tip skin, even minimal tissue movement can lead to distortion. Therefore, a precise reconstructive plan is vital. Second intention healing, primary closure, flaps, and grafts are all reconstructive options for the nasal tip, depending on the nature of the defect.

In patients with highly sebaceous skin, superficial defects anywhere on the nose are amenable to healing by second intention (Fig. 3.4).2 Aesthetic results when utilizing alternative reconstructive approaches can be unpredictable, as healed surgical incisions are particularly prone to postoperative scar depression on highly sebaceous skin.
Fig. 3.4 (a) Superficial defects on the nose of a 68-year-old man with a sebaceous nose. (b) Results at 3 months when wounds were allowed to heal by second intention.

While many defects can heal by second intention with no additional intervention, a “shave and sand” technique can often be employed to enhance results ( ▶Video 3.1). This technique can be performed immediately postoperatively or delayed and is particularly useful for superficial defects with abrupt edges. Using a scalpel blade placed horizontally on the skin immediately adjacent to the defect, light pressure is applied removing thin shavings skin in order to blend the transition between the defect and its surrounding skin. To further camouflage the surgical site, coarse 80-grit sterile aluminum oxide sandpaper is then rubbed over the whole subunit until fine pinpoint bleeding is observed. We describe this technique to patients by comparing it to sanding a scratch on wood furniture. While this method typically yields excellent cosmetic results in those with highly sebaceous skin, very rarely patients may develop increased pore size and/or hypopigmentation. In the editors’ experience, a manual dermabrasion apparatus may also be used with a diamond fraise for younger or nonsebaceous skin and a wire brush for thick sebaceous and rhinophymatous skin. In patients with nonsebaceous skin, surgical repair consistently yields superior results and is our favored approach, unless a defect is exceptionally thin.
Primary repair on the nasal tip should be reserved for small to medium- sized midline defects (Fig. 3.5).
Fig. 3.5 (a) Defect on the midline nasal tip of a 74-year-old woman. (b) Fusiform repair utilizing a 5:1 length-to-width ratio. (c) Results at 3-month follow-up.

There are several important points in designing and executing a successful fusiform closure on the nose.3 When designing the repair, at least a 5:1 length-to-width ratio is employed with the apices ending above the bony hump of the nasal dorsum (where the nasal bone connects to cartilage) and below the inferior margin of the nasal tip about the infratip or columella. Using standard 3:1 length-to-width ratio design may increase closure tensions and result in prominent standing cutaneous deformities, significantly distorting the nasal profile.

After widely anesthetizing the area, the ellipse including the defect is incised to the level of the perichondrium and periosteum. Undermining in a submuscular plane, often as wide as the nasofacial sulcus for larger defects, is necessary to recruit sufficient skin laxity for closure under minimal tension. Hemostasis is then performed. For a nose with prominent telangiectasia, there is often a desire to cauterize superficial vessels to allow for a bloodless field. However, doing so may result in epidermal necrosis with scarring. Rather, this bleeding should be anticipated by allowing ample

time for the epinephrine in the anesthesia to work. The defect is then closed using 5–0 polyglactin 910 buried vertical mattress sutures.4 When suturing on the nose, entry points on the wound edge should be in the deep reticular dermis, as more superficial bites can leave persistent nodules. Also, underlying muscle should be included in each bite in order to prevent a depressed scar.

For defects that are slightly off-center, the inferior triangle can be displaced medially, creating a Burow’s advancement flap, sometimes called the “East-West” flap on the nose5 (Fig. 3.6). This variation should only be used on individuals with a wide infratip and columella; otherwise, closing the inferior triangle may distort the nares.
Fig. 3.6 (a) Defect on the lateral nasal tip in a 71-year-old woman. (b) Repair with a Burow’s advancement flap. (c) Results at 3-month follow-up.

If size of a nasal tip defect precludes complete fusiform closure, a superiorly based Burow’s graft can achieve an excellent aesthetic result (Fig. 3.7). Burow’s grafts have the advantage of providing adjacent skin for superb color and texture match.
Fig. 3.7 (a) Defect on a 66-year-old woman with Burow’s graft designed. (b) Repair with Burow’s graft.

3.3.3 Bilobed Flap Our workhorse repair option for defects under 1.5 cm on the nasal tip is the bilobed flap (▶Video 3.2).6 What makes the bilobed flap the ideal option for nasal tip repair is its ability to deftly recruit laxity from upper nose to close defects where the immediate adjacent skin lacks sufficient mobility to use single transposition or other local flaps. In addition, it has an inherent Z-plasty-like motion, which provides a lengthening effect that creates a downward force, preserving the position of the free alar margin.

Proper design of the bilobed flap is crucial for its success (Fig. 3.8a). For tip defects, the flap is most commonly laterally based. The dog-ear is drawn to be approximately 1.5 times the diameter of the defect and its superior arm drawn horizontally, permitting the secondary lobe of the flap to be drawn vertically along the length of the nose. Designing the secondary lobe vertically effectively places closure tension perpendicular to the ala, preventing its displacement when suturing in the flap. Our endeavor is to

match the size of the primary and secondary flap lobes to that of the defect. Designing flap lobes that are too small may cause secondary movement upon flap closure that could result in alar displacement, while lobes too large may result in pincushioning. For defects that are more distal on the nasal tip, the Burow’s triangle needs to be drawn with its apex oriented more vertically, avoiding its placement through the ala. When doing so, we will often add a third lobe, creating a trilobed flap (Fig. 3.9), in order to place the quaternary defect perpendicular to the alar free margin as discussed previously.

(f) Improper low placement of key suture causing “bulldozing” of ipsilateral ala and elevation of contralateral ala. (g) Improper high placement of key suture causing ipsilateral alar elevation. The flap is first incised to the level of the perichondrium, and the defect is deepened to the level of the cartilage if necessary. Next, the flap is widely undermined, using skin hooks intermittently to assess if the flap will cover the defect without significant tension. Like primary closure described earlier, undermining is often carried out as wide as the nasofacial sulcus. We have found that severing an unnamed ligament, which exists at the lateral junction of the nasal bone and upper lateral cartilage, provides substantial flap movement allowing it to easily fall into place (Fig. 3.8b). The primary lobe, especially the leading edge of the flap, should then be thinned and defatted as necessary to match the level of the skeletonized

defect. We have also found that trimming tissue at the point of rotation minimizes the chance of a persistent dog-ear (Fig. 3.8c). Hemostasis is then performed with care not to cauterize vessels of the superficial skin edge.

Like other transposition flaps, the distal defect is closed first, which is the tertiary defect in the case of the bilobed flap. Because the bilobed flap often traverses the alar crease, which overlies the internal valve, a tacking suture is often placed, allowing the nasal valve to remain patent (Fig. 3.8d). Next, we place what we believe is the “key” stitch. This stitch is the one that aligns the primary lobe of the flap into the defect. In addition to correct design, proper placement of this stitch is essential to preserve nasal symmetry and prevent distortion (Fig. 3.8e). If placed too low, a “bulldozing” effect of the ipsilateral ala can occur (Fig. 3.8f), while if placed too high, displacement of the contralateral side may occur (Fig. 3.8g). The remainder of the flap is then anchored into place, the secondary lobe is trimmed, and a fast gut suture is run along the scar to finely approximate the epidermis (Fig. 3.8h, i). Prior to starting the repair, we inform patients of the potential for visible incision lines, which may inevitably occur on a sebaceous nose despite immaculate suture technique, and routinely have them return to assess the need for dermabrasion in 3 months.

3.3.4 Dorsal Nasal (Rieger’s) Flap The dorsal nasal flap is a rotation flap widely used for midline defects less than 2.5 cm on the nasal tip and supratip (Fig. 3.10).7 We use this flap infrequently due to some of its limitations; we use it only in circumstances where a defect may be too large for a bilobed flap and when the patient prefers a one-staged flap. The pivotal restraint encountered with this flap is amplified compared to that faced with other rotation flaps due to the thick sebaceous quality of the nasal skin. Therefore, increased closure tension is frequently encountered, which can often lead to conspicuous scarring and distortion. Another significant limitation is that the flap rotates thick glabellar skin into the medial canthus, often requiring subsequent revision.

Fig. 3.10 (a) Design of dorsal nasal flap for defect in a 42-year-old woman. (b) Completed flap. (c) Results at 3 months showing depressed right ala. Picture included to demonstrate inconsistent results of the dorsal nasal flap despite proper design and technique.

The flap is first designed with a Burow’s triangle angled superiorly in the direction of the base of the flap. Importantly, the leading edge is extended past the defect to overcome the inherent rotational shortening that accompanies this flap. The arc is drawn in the alar sulcus, upward along the nasofacial sulcus, continued onto the medial canthus, and then terminated on the glabella. The arc should be completed superiorly on the glabella in order to facilitate closure of the secondary defect, and a generous back cut is designed downward no more inferior than the contralateral medial canthal tendon to enable ample rotation.

After anesthesia is achieved, the flap is incised and then undermined above the perichondrium and periosteum past the nasofacial sulcus. Hemostasis is achieved in preparation for flap inset. The glabellar donor site is closed first, and the remainder of the flap closed in a layered fashion, paying careful attention to avoid nasal tip elevation. The glabellar standing cutaneous deformity is amputated, and the remaining skin in this area that is rotated into the medial canthus should be thinned to overcome the skin thickness mismatch of these two areas.

For large (typically >2 cm) or complex nasal tip or alar defects not amenable to repair with local flaps, we often employ a forehead flap (FHF) to restore the subunit with a staged approach (▶Video 3.3, Fig. 3.11).8,​9 Its reliability, ease of transfer, capacity to provide bulk when lost, and excellent color and textural match make the FHF unsurpassed in its ability to repair such defects. Relative contraindications of the FHF include patients with poor mental status who may be at risk pulling the flap’s pedicle, patients who do not understand the multiple steps required of the procedure, and patients who are at risk for not returning for a second stage. Anatomic contraindications include patients with additional skin cancers or scarring on the forehead donor site or patients who do not possess adequate forehead height to generate sufficient flap length, although if other options are limited, the flap can be curved laterally, like a hockey stick, or hair-bearing scalp can be used with a plan to do hair removal.

First and foremost, informed consent should be obtained, discussing with patients the multiple stages that are required and the prospect of having a “tube” connecting their forehead to their nose for a 3-week period. We will also show patients representative cases in our atlas to facilitate their understanding of the multiple stages requisite of this flap. Proper planning of the FHF is a prerequisite for the flap’s success. The height of the

forehead is first assessed to determine if extension of the flap onto hair- bearing skin or if extension of the flap below the orbital rim is necessary to achieve adequate length. Next, attention is paid to the nose, evaluating for any loss of lining or structural integrity as well as airway patency. If any of these elements are compromised, they will need to be addressed prior to raising the FHF. There are several approaches to addressing loss of nasal mucosa10 including lining flaps, hinge flaps, or a folded FHF. For loss of structural integrity or reduced airway patency, cartilage grafts may need to be harvested. The authors prefer use of conchal bowl cartilage due to its strength, ease of harvesting, and large reservoir available. For defects that encompass greater than 50% of the nasal tip or ala, we will typically employ the subunit principle and resurface the entire subunit. Not until all of the aforementioned factors are addressed should the surgeon start the FHF.

While the traditional paramedian FHF has classically been described as an axial pattern flap based on the supratrochlear artery, our center has demonstrated that it is really a random pattern flap and that a paramidline approach provides equivalent clinical outcomes.11 As such, the authors and the editors do not use a Doppler preoperatively as the flap’s robust blood supply is a result of the dense anastomosing network of blood vessels throughout the central forehead, rather than the singular supratrochlear artery.

First, a template is crafted out of foil from a suture packet to match the defect exactly (Fig. 3.11d). One should ensure that the template reflects the three- dimensional nature of the defect. A template too large may result in pincushioning, whereas one too small may result in secondary tissue movement in order to close the wound. The template should also not be created until any extranasal portions of the defect are addressed and after any cartilage grafts are placed to ensure it reflects the true nature of the operative defect. Second, the template is then transferred to the upper forehead and transposed 180 degrees medially to account for its rotation during interpolation. Next, the pedicle is designed on the ipsilateral side of the nasal defect and drawn with the planned medial incision starting at the midpoint of the glabella and the lateral incision near the edge of the medial eyebrow, allowing for a pedicle width of 1.2 cm. Both planned incisions are

carried upward vertically to reach the flap template. Prior to making any incisions, however, appropriate pedicle length should be evaluated by using a gauze strip held at the flap’s base and pivoted onto the nose (Fig. 3.11e).

As the FHF is an arduous procedure for patients, a small dose of an oral benzodiazepine is offered for anxiolysis. We believe the minor antihypertensive effect of oral benzodiazepines also minimizes bleeding throughout the surgery. We use supraorbital nerve blocks to provide long- lasting anesthesia as well as small aliquots of numbing medication around the pedicle and donor site areas for the epinephrine effect. After allowing sufficient time for epinephrine to work, the flap and donor site are scored with the scalpel. Superficial nicks are made in the patient’s horizontal forehead lines so these lines can be readjoined at the time of donor site closure (Fig. 3.11f). Failure to do so can result in noticeable asymmetry upon healing of the flap. The templated area is then elevated in a superficial subcutaneous plane (Fig. 3.11g). Incisions for the pedicle are then carried through subcutaneous fat, muscle, and fascia to the level of periosteum and the flap is subsequently raised (Fig. 3.11h). We consistently carry incisions beyond the supraorbital ridge toward the nasal root to increase flap reach and allow inset of the pedicle within the favorable glabellar and corrugator skin tension lines. The distal flap can be thinned aggressively as needed (Fig. 3.11i), allowed for by the robust vascular supply of this flap. Diligent hemostasis is then achieved as postoperative bleeding with FHFs is quite common; however, care should be taken to avoid the deeper structures of the pedicle. Direct electrodessication of the pedicle’s skin edge is acceptable as this area will be transected with the flap takedown. The editors frequently run a locking suture (6–0 nylon) along the edge of the pedicle to further reduce bleeding from the transected edges of the connecting pedicle.

Attention is then paid to the closure of the forehead donor site. A cursory job closing the forehead can lead to an obvious scar that in many cases can overshadow an excellent result on the nose. To assist in its closure, the forehead is bluntly undermined widely in the avascular subfascial plane (Fig. 3.11j) and then closed in a layered fashion. The galea and deep fascia of the frontalis muscle are closed first in order to prevent a depressed scar, and the dermis is closed subsequently (Fig. 3.11k). Care is taken to

reapproximate the nicks previously made when incising the flap to maintain the patient’s natural forehead lines. For larger nasal reconstructions, closing the cephalic portion of the forehead may not be possible. While other surgeons employ additional flaps or grafts to close this defect, we prefer to manage this area by second intention healing. Additional procedures introduce increased costs and morbidity and are unlikely to have superior aesthetic results to second intention in this particular area.

Next, attention is paid to the nasal defect. The nasal wound margins are conservatively undermined to allow for wound edge eversion and formation of platelike scar to minimize pincushioning upon healing. The flap is sutured into place in a layered fashion up to the superior portion of the defect to avoid impinging the vascular pedicle.

Prior to bandaging the flap, the pedicle should be inspected again for bleeding and hemostasis achieved as the epinephrine effect has often started to wear off by this time. The pedicle is first covered in Gelfoam powder, wrapped in petrolatum-impregnated gauze, and then a pressure bandage is placed. Opioid and antiemetics are often prescribed to address the common complaint of pain and nausea due to the tightness of the forehead donor site. We typically have the patient return the following day for a bandage change, again redressing the pedicle in a similar fashion. One week later, as we do with most of our repairs, we have the patient return, at which point the bandage is again changed and the wound assessed. A light, flat bandage is placed over the wound at this time.

At 3 weeks postoperatively, the patient returns for flap division and insertion, allowing enough time for the establishment of sufficient collateral circulation. While others have advocated for an additional interim stage for flap refinement or delayed cartilage placement at this time prior to takedown of the flap, we have found that doing so is unnecessary to consistently generate excellent results.

After anesthesia, the pedicle is severed in the middle, before attention to the proximal and distal aspects. At the origin of the pedicle, any granulation tissue is debulked and subcutaneous tissue thinned to an appropriate depth that matches the neighboring glabellar skin. A defect is then created around the pedicle in an inverted V shape, and the pedicle is trimmed and inset here in a layered fashion (Fig. 3.11m). At the nasal defect, the superior part of

the flap is similarly debulked of granulation and subcutaneous tissue to match the surrounding nasal skin and excess skin is trimmed. A well-placed linear closure can also be used to close the pedicle origin. The flap is then inset in a layered fashion and both wounds are bandaged.

We have the patient return 3 months postoperatively for wound assessment. Additional revisions are performed at this time if the patient desires, which may include thinning or sculpting of the flap and dermabrasion. All of our patients are informed of the possibility of any revisions at the time of the initial surgery.

3.3.6 Prelaminated and Prefolded Forehead Flap When there is complete nasal tip loss, the senior author has previously described a prelaminated and prefolded FHF as a novel method for repairing this formidable defect. Performed in three to six stages, a three- dimensional nose is formed upside on the distal forehead and ultimately transferred to the nose. The main advantage of this flap is that the difficult work is performed on the forehead precluding intranasal manipulation. This allows for good visibility and is advantageous for the patient with anxiety or oxygen requirements. Additionally, there is a robust vascular supply due to the delayed pedicle formation.

While the flap is being created, the nasal defect is temporarily covered with a split-thickness skin graft. First, a template from hydrocolloid film (DuoDerm; ConvaTec, Skillman, NJ) is molded to recreate the nose. The paper backing of the DuoDerm is replaced with gauze in order to make the template more pliable. In order to recreate the three-dimensional shape of the nose, the film is folded under itself (Fig. 3.12a) by pushing both thumbs where the nasal airways would be (demarcated with dotted lines in the figure). The cartilaginous support should then be demarcated on the template (solid red lines in the figure).

Fig. 3.12 (a) Duoderm folded under itself to recreate the 3- dimensional shape of the nose. (b) First two stitches of flap that fold corners of the flap down. (c) Next two stiches that create flap’s 3-dimensional shape. (d) Defect in 62-year-old man. (e) Flap appearance 6 months post-op.

The template is flattened out upside down on the distal forehead. The distal flap is incised and lifted, but the pedicle is left. Like a conventional FHF, the distal third is raised below the deep dermis, the middle third below adipose, and proximal third below the periosteum. An entire conchal bowl cartilage is then harvested and fashioned into three separate grafts: two cupped ovals recreate the lower lateral cartilage of the nose, and a long batten rod to support the dorsum, tip, and columella. These grafts are then positioned corresponding to their position on the nasal tip and sewn into place using 4–0 Polyglactin 910. The first two stitches fold the corners of the flap down (Fig. 3.12b). The next two stitches will create the flap’s three- dimensional shape (Fig. 3.12c). First, a stitch pierces the proximal three parts of the flap, which will correspond to the lateral-most parts of both the alar groove and the septum. Once this stitch is tied, the three parts are snugged together, and the alar grooves recreated. Next, a similar stitch is placed piercing the same three portions of the flap more distally, further securing the flap’s shape. The newly created “nose” is then secured to the underlying forehead fascia, and then covered with petrolatum, petrolatum gauze, Telfa, and thermoplastic cast (Aquaplast PS; WFR, Avondale, PA).

On week 2, the pedicle is delayed by incising it down the brow, but not lifted, leaving the pedicle in place attached to the forehead. Delaying a flap refers to incising it but leaving it in its original position. This tactic has been reported to increase vascularity as a response to stress.12
On week 4, the split-thickness graft on the nose is removed and the nasal recipient bed is freshened. The FHF is lifted, transferred to the nose, and sewn into place. The forehead defect is closed.

On weeks 6 and 7, the sectioning of the pedicle is delayed by respectively only sectioning one lateral third of the pedicle at a time. These steps are optional but recommended in order to increase vascular supply of the flap. On week 8, the remaining portion of the pedicle is divided. The flap and residual pedicle are then sewn into place, similarly to a conventional FHF. Fig. 3.12d and e depict the defect after tumor extirpation and the final result of the flap several months post-op.

In select settings on the nasal tip and ala, skin grafts can rival the results obtained with flaps (▶Video 3.4, Fig. 3.13). We most commonly use skin grafts for small, shallow defects not amenable to second intention healing in our elderly patient population. The conchal bowl is routinely selected as a donor reservoir for the distal nose because of the excellent color and texture color similarity between the two areas. This similarity is owed to the comparable sebaceous gland density and pore size.13 Furthermore, the donor site reliably yields excellent results when allowed to heal by second intention.

Fig. 3.13 (a) Alar defect in a 65-year-old woman. (b) Foil template matching the size of the defect. (c) Graft harvested directly above cartilage. (d) Full-thickness suture bites are taken, otherwise failure to reappose the epidermis and entire dermis can lead to a depressed wound edge and depressed scar. (e) Graft completely sewn in. (f) Placement of bolster using 4–0 silk suture with a figure- eight knot.

A template of the nasal tip defect using the foil from a suture packet is shown in Fig. 3.13b. After anesthesia, the graft is harvested above cartilage. The inclusion of perichondrium in the graft has been shown to lead to less graft contraction and increased retention of epidermal appendages (Fig. 3.13c).14 To expedite healing of the donor site, multiple perforations are made in the cartilage using punch biopsy tool to promote granulation. If needed, the graft is thinned to match the thickness of the skin surrounding the defect. In acutely convex locations on the nasal tip, the editors find it helpful to circumferentially undermine around the defect to reduce the incidence of pincushioning. This is less important in concave locations such

as the alar groove. We use 6–0 fast absorbing gut to sew in the graft. Simple interrupted sutures anchor in the graft at four points such as at the 12, 3, 6, and 9 o’clock positions, and the remaining graft is sutured in a running fashion. While suturing the graft, one should pay careful attention to ensure reapposition of the epidermis and the entire dermis by taking full-thickness bites (Fig. 3.13d). A common error is to take too superficial of bites, only including the epidermis and papillary dermis, because the reticular dermis tends to retract toward the center of the graft. Failure to reappose the epidermis and entire dermis can lead to a depressed wound edge and depressed scar. Following graft inset, a bolster is sewn on to ensure contact between the wound bed and base of the graft in order to enhance graft imbibition. An assistant applies petrolatum to the graft, followed by a nonstick gauze like Telfa, then a folded 2 × 2 gauze on top. The bolster is secured with one or two figure-of-eight stitches using 4–0 silk (Fig. 3.13f). The patient returns 1 week later for bandage and bolster removal, at which point graft survival is assessed.

Proximity to a free margin, poor tissue mobility, and the necessity of conserving function of the external nasal valve complicate the repair of alar defects. While the tip and ala share sebaceous and thickness qualities, the ala lacks underlying cartilaginous support relying only on its fibrofatty nature to maintain its patency to allow for airflow. Thus, it is essential that the surgeon evaluate remaining structural integrity following tumor extirpation to determine the need to replace structural support.

Defects that are limited to the concave region of the ala can demonstrate excellent results when allowed to heal by second intention, regardless of wound depth. Even some wounds that straddle the concave and convex areas of the ala can produce good results, as long as the aspect of the wound on the convex alar lobule is at least 4 mm from the alar rim. Wounds near the alar rim allowed to be healed by second intention risk creation of a distracting notch, a complication that is notoriously difficult to revise. Very superficial defects on the alar lobule are an exception. We will often employ

the shave and sand technique to contour superficial wounds on the ala. Partial-thickness defects on the ala and the distal third of the nose also respond nicely to recontouring with a wire brush or diamond fraise driven by a hand engine. Especially in men with highly sebaceous skin or rhinophyma, for which the wire brush is best, the shoulders of the defect can be eliminated while the rhinophyma of the entire distal third of the nose is also treated (Fig. 3.14a–c).15

Wounds of intermediate depth on the ala can often be reconstructed with a full-thickness skin graft (Fig. 3.13). Like the nasal tip, the conchal bowl provides the most optimal donor site. We have found that for smaller wounds, utilization of a graft on the alar lobule often provides superior contour than a flap would if used to repair the same wound. The major limitation of selecting a graft is the resultant skin color discrepancy. In women, this discrepancy can be easily camouflaged with makeup.

Any time structural integrity of the ala may be compromised, a cartilage graft should be considered. Cartilage grafts can be used in conjunction with both flaps and full-thickness skin grafts. The conchal bowl is our preferred donor site, which makes it convenient when harvesting both cartilage and

skin from this location when repairing an alar lobule defect. A strut slightly longer than the inferior aspect of the defect is harvested. The cartilage is thinned as needed, and pockets are created on either site of the defect where the strut is inserted after which it is secured with sutures. If the depth of the defect is greater than the harvested skin graft, chopped up pieces of cartilage can also be placed in the bottom of the defect before the graft is sewn into position. This can help maintain the convex contour of the ala.

3.4.3 Medial-Based Bilobed Flap Partial- or full-thickness alar defects that measure ≤1.5 cm can dependably be repaired with a bilobed flap that is medially based, especially if they are situated at the anterior aspect of the ala (Fig. 3.15). A medially based bilobed flap is designed and executed in the same fashion as its laterally based counterpart, with the exception that when undermining, the plane of undermining should transition from above cartilage on the nose to a subcutaneous plane on the cheek.

3.4.4 Spiral Flap Similar-sized defects that are more proximal and may fall on both sides of the alar groove can also be repaired with a spiral flap (Fig. 3.16a, b).16 This flap is designed from the wound edge at point A and spirals upward so that “B” is the diameter of the defect and “C” is 1.5 times the diameter (Fig.

3.16c). Again, undermining is wide and below the level of the muscle. Using 6–0 polyglactin 910, the tip of the spiral is sutured onto itself. Then the remainder of the flap is advanced forward into the defect in a spiral fashion to close the defect and maintain convexity of the nasal ala.

Full-thickness defects ≥1.5 cm that are confined to the alar lobule can be repaired with the cheek-to-nose interpolation flap (CNIF; Fig. 3.17). The CNIF can be designed as either a peninsula or an island, but we prefer a peninsula as it theoretically should be better vascularized. While the CNIF is a robust flap that allows for an aesthetic repair, one must keep in mind that it is not quite as well vascularized as the FHF. Like the FHF, the subunit principle is adhered to on a situational basis, depending on the nature of the defect.

Fig. 3.17 (a) Defect in a 79-year-old man. (b) Repair with cheek-to- nose interpolation flap. (c) Results after takedown of flap at 3 weeks. (d) Results at 3 months. (e) Defect in a 55-year-old woman. (f) Repair with cheek-to-nose interpolation flap. (g) Results after takedown of flap at 3 weeks. (h) Results at 3 months.

First, a template is created to exactly match the defect. The template is placed on the cheek lateral to the melolabial fold and superior to the oral commissure. While the template should be placed inferiorly enough to allow for sufficient pedicle length, it should not be too long where there is a chance of the flap’s blood supply being compromised. Importantly, the superior aspect of the template should be placed medially, adjacent to the melolabial fold, to account for the rotation of the flap into the defect. A peninsula is drawn encompassing the flap template with the base situated above the defect. The inferior apex of the peninsula should be drawn acutely enough to allow for closure of the secondary defect without a residual standing cone deformity.

The flap is incised from the base of the peninsula to the apex. It is important to remove the Burow’s triangle inferior to the template until adequate reach of the flap into the defect is ensured. Once incised, the flap is undermined at the superficial subcutis. As undermining is continued proximately, the level of undermining is deepened to the deep subcutis to allow for a well- vascularized base. Once sufficient reach is guaranteed, the Burow’s triangle is removed, and the flap is aggressively thinned distally. Hemostasis is achieved, and the flap sewn in in a layered fashion

At approximately 3 weeks, the flap is taken down. First, the pedicle is severed distally. At this time, if following the subunit principle, the remainder of the posterior aspect of the alar lobule can be excised leaving a 1- to 2-mm rim laterally. Subcutis and granulation tissue are removed so the flap can be sewn in flush the surrounding tissue. Attention is then turned to

the base of the pedicle, which is severed and removed along with any granulation tissue. Although this site can be closed primarily or in a V-Y fashion, we prefer a primary closure because we feel a V-Y in this area tends to pincushion more readily.

3.4.6 Spear Flap For defects where there is full-thickness loss of the ala and vestibular lining extending to the lateral alar crease, the Spear flap is an excellent option to recreate the hemicylindrical convexity of the alar rim and the crease of the alar cheek fold (Fig. 3.18).17 The Spear flap is a reverse nasolabial island pedicle flap that is flipped over and turned upon itself, allowing it to recreate the missing alar skin.
Fig. 3.18 (a–c) Pictorial representation of how a spear flap is executed. (d) Defect in a 53-year-old woman with Spear island flap
designed. (e) Spear island flap incised to subcutaneous plane. (f) Flap hinged on its subcutaneous base medially and sewn into mucosal portion of defect.
Fig. 3.18 (Contiuned) (g) Flap sewn into place. (h) Results at 3 months. (i) Defect in an 81-year-old woman. (j) Repair with Spear flap. (k) Results at 3 months.

A peninsula is drawn off the lateral edge of the wound with its apex oriented inferiorly. The medial arm of the peninsula is situated in the melolabial fold. The width of the flap should match the width of the defect, and the apex should be acute enough (<30 degrees) to allow for donor site closure without resultant standing cone deformity. The base of the flap is what will ultimately be sutured to provide nasal lining.

The medial and lateral arms of the flap are incised down to the subcutis. The apex is undermined proximally to its base in a subcutaneous plane. After aggressive thinning of the flap and undermining of the donor site, the donor site can be closed, allowing for closure of the remainder of the flap under little tension. The flap is then hinged on its subcutaneous base medially, likened to flipping a page of a book. What was originally the superior/medial corner of the island is sewn into the superior/lateral corner of the nasal lining defect. The original inferior/medial corner of the island is then sewn into the inferior/medial corner of the lining defect. The lateral portion of the upper island is then sutured to the medial nasal lining with the inferior apex hanging down from the inside of the nose. The flap is then folded upon itself to form the external ala. It is important that the flap is folded upon itself at the right point in order to provide symmetry with the contralateral ala. Periosteal sutures can be used at the lateral aspect of the flap to prevent flaring of the newly created ala. The remainder of the flap can then be sewn in using a layered technique.

The soft triangle is a complex subunit of the nose, suspended between the nasal infratip and alar rim. It is composed of a vestibular lining, a very thin subcutaneous space, and nasal skin that is significantly thinner and less sebaceous than the remainder of the lower third of the nose. Although it is a small structure, loss of the soft triangle will result in an aesthetically noticeable notched appearance.

The columella can be a very difficult structure to repair. Small superficial defects can be allowed to heal by second intention with satisfactory results, while slightly larger columellar defects may be adequately repaired with a full-thickness skin graft. Complete loss of the columella may necessitate a cartilage graft in conjunction with an interpolated flap (forehead or cheek- to-nose) in order restore function and cosmesis.

The turnover flap is a simple method to repair defects of the soft triangle or correct notches that occur as a secondary complication of other flaps or grafts in the area (Fig. 3.19).18 While the turnover flap is an effective choice
for repairing defects limited to the soft triangle area, for larger defects it may also be used to provide vestibular lining for surface flaps as well as blood supply for an overlying skin graft.

Fig. 3.19 (a) Soft triangle notch in a 39-year-old woman 3 months after a repair with a full-thickness skin graft. A hinge flap is designed. (b) Illustration depicting where full-thickness skin graft will be placed. (c) Repair with soft triangle turnover hinge flap, covered with a postauricular full-thickness skin graft. (d) Results at 3 months.

The contralateral soft triangle serves as a template in estimating the amount of tissue that is required to be replaced. A triangle-shaped turnover flap is designed at the junction of the inferior nasal tip and the columella with its apex pointing toward the contralateral ala. Ultimately, the inferior arm of the triangle will become the new free margin of the soft triangle.

The flap is incised, and the apex is undermined until it can be turned over so it can reach the alar rim. The portion of the alar rim that will receive the flap’s edge (superior arm of the initial triangular flap) is freshened with excision of the skin edge to a depth that allows suturing of both the turnover flap and an overlying full-thickness skin graft. After hemostasis is achieved, the superior margin of the flap is sutured to the vestibular margin of the alar rim. The inferior margin of the flap should extend an additional 1 to 2 mm below the contralateral soft triangle to compensate for eventual wound contraction that will occur, and bilateral free margin symmetry can be established. A full-thickness skin graft from the postauricular sulcus is designed to cover both the exposed flap surface and the flap’s donor site. The postauricular sulcus is chosen because its thin skin provides a suitable match for the thin smooth skin of the soft triangle. The graft is harvested, sewn in, and immobilized with a tie-over bolster dressing.

3.5.2 Nasal Tip Rotation Flap Small partial-thickness defects at the junction of the soft triangle, lateral nasal tip, and anterior ala can present a significant reconstructive challenge. A useful repair option for these defects is the nasal tip rotation flap.19 This flap elegantly hides incision lines at the junction of the nasal tip and dorsum and is able to maintain nasal tip topography with a low risk of alar rim elevation.

A Burow’s triangle is drawn paralleling a line connecting the inferior nasal tip to the mid alar rim (Fig. 3.20). For defects that are more inferior placed, the Burow’s triangle should be angled more inferiorly toward the nasal infratip/columella. Proper placement of this triangle will prevent notching of the alar rim. When possible, the angle of flap rotation is designed within the cosmetic junction line between the nasal tip and the nasal dorsum. However, the angle of flap rotation may need adjustment depending on the

vertical dimension of the defect, nasal laxity, and the patient’s particular nasal tip topography. Defects with larger vertical dimensions, thick or inelastic sebaceous tissue, and bulbous nasal tips may necessitate a greater arc of rotation, sometimes beyond the midline, which allows for increased tissue movement. A displaced Burow’s triangle is then drawn due to the length discrepancy between the longer outer and shorter inner arcs.

Fig. 3.20 Nasal tip rotation flap. (a) Deep lateral nasal tip defect of a bulbous nose illustrating flap design (different patient). (b) Flap elevated after complete undermining of the nasal tip above cartilage and the nasal dorsum to allow a platelike internal scar to form. (c) Second key stitch (after closure of the secondary defect) demonstrating alignment of the leading flap edge to close the primary defect. (d) Immediate postoperative appearance (anterior view). The flap is incised, and both Burow’s triangles are excised. Undermining is carried out widely, mobilizing the entire nasal tip subunit above the lower lateral alar cartilage in order to recruit ample tissue. The displaced Burow’s triangle is closed first, followed by securing the leading edge of the flap into the inferoposterior aspect of the defect. The remainder of the flap is sutured in a layered fashion.

The nasal dorsum, also sometimes referred to as the “bridge” of the nose, has considerable aesthetic importance. Repair options for the nasal dorsum have been described in detail in other sections. Like other areas of the nose, superficial defects can heal adequately, although employment of the previously described shave and sand technique will often optimize the result. Primary repair can effectively close the majority of small to medium full-thickness midline defects (Fig. 3.21). Defects where size may seem to initially preclude use of primary closure can often be closed after extensive undermining to recruit lax skin on the bilateral nasal sidewalls, offering the advantage of excellent color and texture match. For defects on the lateral nasal dorsum where primary closure runs the risk of alar retraction, a local flap is preferred. The various options for these defects will be discussed in Chapter 3.8.

Very large defects on the nasal dorsum that cannot be satisfactorily closed using adjacent skin can be closed using a full-thickness skin graft (Fig. 3.22) or an FHF. A postauricular donor site is preferred as it provides an excellent match for the thinner skin of the upper two-thirds of the nose. The donor site is closed primarily in the sulcus leaving a nearly imperceptible scar. When defects are too large for a postauricular donor site, the supraclavicular fossa is preferred.
Fig. 3.22 (a) Defect on a 69-year-old man. (b) Repair with a full- thickness skin graft harvested from the postauricular sulcus. (c) Results at 3 months.

Due to its concave nature, small to medium-sized defects on the nasal root can heal wonderfully by second intention. For a deeper defect, second intention is still a good option; however, there is often enough laxity for a primary closure. For nonmidline defects, when executing a fusiform repair, the ellipse is oriented obliquely toward the inner canthus.

One situation in our experience where repair with a full-thickness skin graft is preferred over flap is for larger wounds of the nasal root area. Grafts in this area frequently yield excellent results, more so than grafts in other areas. Further, the propensity of flaps to cause webbing, contour deformity, and distortion in this area often makes grafts the better repair choice. Again, a postauricular donor site is preferred.

Like the other subunits of the nose, superficial wounds can heal by second intention, often in conjunction with the shave and sand technique. Small, full-thickness wounds can be closed primarily, with the ellipse oriented obliquely, running parallel to a line extending from the nasal tip to the inner canthus. Closing larger wounds on the nasal sidewall in a fusiform fashion runs the risk of ipsilateral alar retraction, and thus should be avoided. Instead, large defects are optimally repaired with the local transposition flap.

3.8.1 Rhombic Transposition Flap The rhombic flap is our “workhorse” for repairing small to medium-sized defects less than 1.5 cm on the nasal sidewall due to its reliability, efficiency, and cosmetic elegance (Fig. 3.23).20 In the majority of cases, the laxity of the superior nasal sidewall supports using an inferior base. Small to medium-sized defect on the lower sidewall may necessitate use of a bilobed flap in order to draw from the reservoir of lax skin on the superior sidewall.

Fig. 3.23 (a) Defect in a 39-year-old man. (b) Repair with rhombic transposition flap. (c) Results at 3 months. (d) Defect in a 63-year- old man. (e) Repair with rhombic transposition flap. (f) Results at 3 months.

Like the bilobed flap, the most crucial design aspect of the rhombic flap is vertical orientation of the donor site. Vertical orientation will prevent pull on the ala when closing the donor site. The donor site is drawn with its apex less than 30 degrees, and its width should equal the vertical diameter of the defect. The Burow’s triangle is drawn with its superior arm parallel to the arm of the flap that in not connected to the defect.

The flap is incised and undermined widely in a submuscular plane. The donor site is closed first, followed by the Burow’s triangle. Once the remainder of the flap is secured, the flap is trimmed to fit the size of the defect. While some advocate extending the defect to fit the angulated flap,
we favor conserving normal tissue, and find no difference in the ultimate aesthetic appearance as long as excellent suture technique is employed.

3.8.2 Superior-Based Bilobed Flap For vertically oriented ovoid defects on the lateral nasal dorsum or the anterior nasal sidewall, we occasionally will perform a superior-based bilobed flap.21 The vertical orientation of the defect may preclude the use of a rhombic flap, as a significantly larger flap must be designed in order to situate the donor site perpendicular to the ala. The particular use of a bilobed flap in this area utilizes lax cheek skin as a reservoir, similar to the single-stage nasolabial flap.

For the editors, nasal sidewall defects that are distal but do not cross the alar groove can also be repaired nicely with a lateral-based rotation flap that recruits laxity from the medial cheek. The flap is designed along the alar groove and lengthened out on to the cheek a distance equal to the diameter of the defect superior to the defect. Superior to the defect a Burow’s triangle is removed. The key stitch should be placed at the nasal tip crease and close the defect from side to side. The second stitch is placed in the proximal alar groove and starts with a bite in the floor to become a three-point stitch and lifts up the collapsed nasal valve. As the remainder of the donor site is closed, care must be taken to inset the cheek skin edge and prevent blunting of the alar groove.

3.8.4 V-Y Flap In some patients, the portion of the mid-nasal sidewall that extends into the nasofacial sulcus can do so with a slight convexity or hump. Defects of 1 to 2 cm situated in this location or even more proximal encroaching the medial canthus can be nicely repaired with a V-Y flap that recruits skin from the medial cheek.

The flap is designed as a V extending inferolaterally from the defect. The proximal portion of the flap is the same width as the defect and tapers to a 30-degree angle—staying above the melolabial fold.

The incision of the flap is extended into the deep subcutaneous tissue. As with any island pedicle flap, the pedicle is lengthened by blunt/sharp dissection downward and turning laterally so as to also undermine the tissue on either side of the donor site. Once hemostasis is achieved, the proximal edge of the flap is advanced in a superior direction onto the nasal sidewall. As it is advanced, it can be rotated to meet the opposite side of the defect in such a way to keep the primary tissue movement vector horizontal and not pull down on the eyelids. The corners of the leading edge of the flap are trimmed to match the shape of the defect. The remainder of the flap and the donor site can be closed with buried vertical mattress sutures and 6–0 fast- absorbing suture on the surface (Fig. 3.24).

Defects measuring greater than 1.5 cm on the lateral or inferior portion of the lateral sidewall are readily repaired with a nasolabial transposition flap (▶Video 3.5). The nasolabial flap is a superior-based transposition flap that utilizes lax cheek skin as a donor reservoir. Perforating defects and those that obliterate the alar rim can also be repaired with a nasolabial flap. The flap provides an excellent color and texture match for the missing nasal skin, and the scar is well-hidden within the melolabial fold. Although it is a transposition flap by definition in that the flap is transposed over the lateral ala, the sliding advancement of the cheek allows the nasal portion of the flap to be closed under minimal tension. However, for wounds that are greater than 2.5 cm or patients without abundant cheek laxity, an alternative repair should be chosen. Modifications of the nasolabial flap have simplified the its design and execution, precluding the need for a second stage and minimizing the standing cone deformity and trapdoor phenomenon that classically result from the original design.

The medial arm of the flap starts at the midpoint of the lateral aspect of the defect and descends along the melolabial fold. Importantly, this incision should not transect the apical triangle as this is an important structure that should be preserved. The lateral arm of the flap should extend higher than the point of transposition over the lateral ala, and the width of the flap should match exactly the width of the defect. A Burow’s triangle is drawn superiorly above the defect with its apex less than 30 degrees and directed toward the medial canthus (Fig. 3.25a).
Fig. 3.25 (a) Design of the single-stage nasolabial flap. (b) Four key periosteal tacking sutures crucial for flap’s success. (c,d) Pre-

The flap is incised down to subcutis and undermined widely to facilitate formation of a platelike scar. Success of the flap is contingent on placement of four key periosteal sutures (Fig. 3.25b), which maintain contour and relieve tension on the flap. The initial periosteal suture connects that lateral aspect of the cheek wound to the lateral alar crease at the apex of the apical triangle of the lip, reforming the contour of the melolabial fold and relieving tension on closure of the donor site. This suture has been deemed one that “separates the men and women from the boys and girls” as its successful placement deep in the alar crease requires significant technical expertise. The remainder of the donor site can then be closed in a layered fashion. The second periosteal suture is placed in the nasofacial sulcus to prevent tenting that would otherwise occur. The suture is placed from the nasofacial sulcus to a point at the base of the flap approximately 1 cm superior to the alar crease. Like the first key suture, this one also relieves tension on the advancing flap. At this point, the flap should be thinned and defatted. Any fat remaining on the underside of the flap will fibrose and contract and contribute to the trapdoor phenomenon; therefore, “fat is your enemy.” The third periosteal suture is placed at the anterior distal aspect of the flap in order to direct closure tension in a horizontal direction and mitigate pulling on the ala that would otherwise occur. The last key periosteal suture is placed connecting the distal aspect of the flap to the alar crease, which has two purposes. First, this suture recreates the alar crease that would otherwise be blunted without its placement. Second, this suture stents open the nasal valve that collapses when there is wounding in this area. Once the periosteal sutures have been placed, the distal aspect of the flap can be amputated, and the remainder of the flap sewn in slightly concave from the adjacent wound edges in a layered fashion. Fig. 3.25c, d depicts a defect suitable for this flap with immediate postoperative results.
While complications are sometimes inevitable, the vast majority can often be avoided with careful planning, execution, and meticulous attention to

surgical technique. Pincushioning, a common complication during nasal reco- nstruction, can be prevented if one exactly matches the primary flap lobes and grafts to the size of the defect, performs wide undermining to promote formation of a platelike scar, defats flaps to prevent fat fibrosis, and uses buried vertical mattress sutures to pull deep tissues back to suture line.

In the first few months postoperatively, it is important to suppress the urge to overcorrect any flap irregularities, remembering that it takes a full year for scars to fully mature. For example, flaps have the tendency to retain fluid due to the disruption of lymphatics. Compression of the flap that reduces flap “puffiness” can highlight this phenomenon. Collateral lymphatic channels eventually reform, which can be hastened by instructing patients to perform vigorous scar massage starting 1 month postoperatively. Visible incision lines or contour asymmetry can be corrected with dermabrasion. We typically perform this at a minimum of 3 months postoperatively. As mentioned previously, we always inform the patient of the need for dermabrasion at the time of surgery so that it does not appear later that dermabrasion is suggested as a cover-up for surgical incompetence. Persistent flap fullness may necessitate use of intralesional triamcinolone at a strength of 40 mg/mL. If no improvement is observed with this intervention, the flap may need to be elevated and thinned of scar and subcutaneous tissue.
