The tumor removed was a high risk and graft coverage allows easier assessment for possible recurrence compared to flap closure. (a) Rotation flap raised in the subgaleal plane with loose alveolar tissue and periosteum exposed. (b) Periosteal flap incised, rotated, and partially sutured into the primary defect. (c) Rotation flap returned to the original position and graft applied.

Other types of advancement flaps (e.g., H-plasty flaps or O-T flaps) have a limited role in scalp reconstruction due to the inelastic nature of the scalp. Similar to primary linear closures, modified advancement flaps are mainly used for small defects located on the loose regions of the scalp. Less commonly, bilateral advancement flaps (such as O-T flaps) can be used for moderate sized defects if scalp mobility is adequate (Fig. 5.18).
Fig. 5.18 (a–c) Multiple full-thickness defects of the scalp closed with one A-T advancement flap. (a) Multiple defects placed in an elongated A-T advancement flap. (b) Bilateral advancement flap
closed with a small area left to heal by second intention. (c) One- year follow-up. (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

Rotation flaps have a major role in scalp reconstruction as the natural convexity of the scalp is well suited for curvilinear incisions. Simple rotation flaps can be used for small (9 cm2) scalp defects (Fig. 5.19). Generally, incisions should be roughly four to six times the length of the original surgical defect to account for the intrinsic inelasticity of the scalp. A standing tissue cone is designed adjacent to the operative wound to create a triangulated defect, after which a curvilinear incision is designed along an arc adjacent to the defect and directed toward a tissue reservoir. The arc of rotation can be vertically oversized superiorly, so the distance from the pivot point to the flap tip equals the distance from the pivot point to the most distal aspect of the defect. This allows for compensation of pivotal restraint, minimizes tension on the flap, and eliminates the need for secondary motion around the operative defect.34 The flap should be widely undermined, particularly around the point of pivotal restraint. As the flap is elevated, it is rotated to fill the surgical defect. Once this occurs, a secondary defect is created along the entire arc of the flap, which is closed in a fashion allowing for tension to be evenly distributed along its span. Discrepancies in length between each side of the arc may be created and require the removal of standing cutaneous deformities35 or can be sewn out using the rule of halves principle. In the editor’s experience, large single- arm rotation flaps can effectively cover a large defect (Fig. 5.20).

Fig. 5.19 Small rotation flap in a 70-year-old woman with a 2.0 × 1.6 cm defect over the left parietal scalp. (a) Flap designed to encompass greatest vasculature and maintain hairline position. The length of the flap is four times the defect diameter. (b) Flap rotated into position to ensure both primary and secondary defects can be closed under low tension. (c) Primary and secondary defects closed with deep sutures. (d) Final flap trimming and epidermal sutures placed.

Fig. 5.20 (a–d) Single-arm scalp rotation flap. (a) Flap design showing a wide and long arc of at least 4 times the area as the defect width. This allows for a wide base for flap perfusion and a long arc of rotation to minimize tension along the arc path. (b) Flap undermined at the subgaleal plane. The flap can be undermined

quickly in this plane without having to use cautery during the undermining process. However, some surgeons prefer to cauterize as the flap is being incised. (c) Key sutures align the anterior end of the flap as well as a midpoint pulley suture to allow the flap to be anchored at the high tension points. (d) A few more deep 3-0 polyglactin 910 sutures on an RB-1 needle are placed to minimize tension and ensure approximation of the galea and dermis/subcutis. Epidermal sutures are then used. Running or interrupted sutures are effective. (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

O-to-Z rotation flaps are particularly wellsuited for small to large vertex defects when insufficient laxity exists for closure with a single- sided rotation flap. Rather than pure rotational movement, these flaps can incorporate varying amounts of advancement into the design. Two distinct arcs are created, each originating 180 degrees opposite one another, with both extending in the same direction. Each flap follows the same principles as the single rotation flaps. Once elevated, each flap is rotated in the same direction (either clockwise or counterclockwise), converting the circular “O”-shaped defect into a “Z”-shaped suture line.35 The key suture approximates the leading edge to each rotation flap, and then the redundancy along the corresponding area is sewn out by the ”rule of halves” technique (Fig. 5.21).

Fig. 5.21 O-Z rotation flaps in a 70 year old female with a 3.9 × 3.6 cm defect over the central parietal scalp. (a) Flap incision lines in place with each arc four times the length of the defect diameter. (b) One flap has been raised in the subgaleal plane. (c) Primary defect is closed first. (d) Primary and secondary defects closed and epidermal sutures placed.

Double hatchet flaps are a variant of O-to-Z rotation flaps incorporating further advancement into the design. Two triangular flaps that would otherwise be utilized as standing cones for a primary linear closure are created with the shape of a hatchet, with each flap originating 180 degrees opposite one another, and extending in the same direction. Once incised and raised, each flap is rotated so that the leading edge of each hatchet is approximated into the other, thus closing the primary defect. Secondary defects are then closed in a V-Y fashion.36,​37

Generally, large to very large defects or medium defects in very inelastic scalps are reserved for this indication as their implementation is time- consuming and will lead to extensive scalp scarring.

Pinwheel flaps are composed of four rotation flaps, each separated 90 degrees from one another (see Fig. 5.22). These flaps converge centrally after being raised and rotated, thereby allowing closure of the operative defect.38 In the editors’ experience, if four rotation flaps are required to close the defect rather than only two, then a better option is four rhomboid or Limberg’s flaps (as discussed in the next section) or a large single-arm rotation flap.
Fig. 5.22 Pinwheel flap. Design of the pinwheel flap drawn. This flap is used in tight scalps when a single arc or O-Z rotation flaps are not enough to close the defect.
Orticochea flaps are composed of three or four rotation and/or advancement flaps and are used for medium (10–50 cm2) or large (>50 cm2) vertex scalp

defects. The scalp is divided into vascular territories that should be included in each flap: temporal, occipital, and supraorbital/supratrochlear territories. Three to four flaps are appropriately designed around the operative wound following the same principles of single rotation or advancement flaps. Extensive undermining is undertaken to mobilize the entire scalp, and galeal releasing incisions are utilized to further expand mobility of each flap.16,​39

In the author’s experience, transposition flaps are of limited usefulness for closing operative wounds on the scalp. In selected cases where rotation flaps are not suitable, bilobed, trilobed, rhomboid, and Banner flaps can be considered. Transposition flaps can be used to cover large defects with exposed calvarium lacking periosteum while leaving an intact periosteum and some galea in the secondary defect for a backgraft, which can often be taken from the excised standing tissue cone of the transposition flap itself (Fig. 5.23).

Fig. 5.23 Scalp banner transposition flap. (a) Large vertically- oriented defect with some bone exposed. (b) Banner flap transposed to cover the defect. Note that the galea of the flap was left intact over the secondary defect allowing FTSG placement and pulley sutures to partially close the secondary defect and improve granulation. (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

Multiple Limberg’s flaps can be used in selected cases where the operative wounds are located on loose regions of the scalp, such as the frontal scalp of bald male patients. With this technique, the wound is projected into a hexagon fitting three distinct rhombi, so that three consecutive rhombic flaps allow for repair of the wound. Of note, such flaps have the disadvantage of leaving a multiplicity of scars that may be aesthetically undesirable.40

Although beyond the scope of dermatologic surgery, microvascular free flaps, also known as free autologous tissue transfers, are usually performed by plastic surgeons for the reconstruction of large to extensive defects that cannot be repaired otherwise. For scalp reconstruction purposes, free flaps may be composed of muscle only or may contain skin, subcutaneous tissue, and muscle. These flaps are completely separated from their original vascular supply at the donor site. The flap can now be moved to a distant recipient site, where the vascular pedicle is anastomosed with appropriate recipient arteries and veins through microsurgical techniques. These flaps offer the advantages of bringing a bulk of vascularized tissue allowing for appropriate contouring of the calvarium, and in the case of flaps containing muscle only, providing a healthy recipient site for subsequent skin grafts. The superficial temporal artery and vein are common recipient vascular pedicles, though facial vessels and the external jugular vein can be used as well. Donor tissues may include the radial forearm, anterolateral thigh, gracilis, lateral arm, parascapular, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi. These flaps have been shown to have a very high success rate in the literature and have been shown to be safe in the elderly population.7

Complications after scalp reconstruction are uncommon. Two primary complications in any skin surgery are necrosis and infection. The robust blood supply of the scalp reduces the incidence of both, even after large reconstructions. In the author’s practice, scalp reconstructions have a 0.6% incidence for infection and 2% for necrosis. This is in comparison to 0.8% and 5%, respectively, when all reconstructive sites are combined. Infections, when culture was possible, most commonly grew S.aureus. The patients generally respond to a 2-week course of a first-generation cephalosporin. Necrosis is treated with careful serial debridement of any fully declared full-thickness loss, followed by the use of protocols as outlined under Chapter 5.2.2.

Surprisingly, given the high scalp vascularity, hematomas after scalp surgery in the author’s practice are also uncommon, but the incidence is not tracked. The low occurrence of hematomas may relate to the higher closure tension of scalp reconstructions, which could serve as a form of vessel tamponade. Hematomas, should they arise, are treated as per standard well- defined and published protocols.

Multiple larger blood vessels supplying the scalp can increase the risk for significant intraoperative bleeding. A thorough understanding of vessel anatomy, including location and plane, is mandatory. This knowledge can alert the physician and allow visualization and ligation of the vessel, before it is inadvertently transected. The author’s preference in larger scalp reconstructions is to incise the outline of each flap in small sections, complete hemostasis, and then continue. This allows excellent visualization for undermining and accurate incision angles to preserve hair follicles.

When reconstructions are performed in hair-bearing scalps, the possibility of telogen effluvium and permanent traction alopecia exists. As previously outlined, incision angles matching the angle of hair follicles, and low-tension closures, minimize the chance of hair loss. In many cases postsurgery, differentiating temporary from permanent hair loss can only occur with the passage of time. Up to 2 years can be required for scalp hair to return to a clinically meaningful number around the surgery site. This is especially true in patients of advanced age. Hair loss can also occur in areas of previous necrosis or dehiscence. Initial treatments include changing the patient’s hairstyle, use of scalp dyes, or hair-thickening agents, all to

camouflage or give the illusion of greater hair density. Permanent improvement requires serial excisions of the alopecic scalp, or the use of internal tissue expanders with subsequent removal of the alopecic scalp and then movement of the expanded skin into the defect. Hair transplantation using modern techniques can be a very effective method to improve scarring hair loss secondary to surgery. There is a large body of evidence outlining high survival rates for follicular unit grafts in scars.

Larger incisions in the scalp to allow full flap movement and accurate undermining commonly lead to transection of cutaneous sensory nerves. This can lead to numbness, paresthesias, or dysesthesias. Patients with damage to scalp nerves generally report numbness first, primarily with hair grooming. In the majority of cases, this is not of great concern to the patient. However, as nerve repair begins, secondary paresthesias and dysesthesias can occur, with patients finding this bothersome. In the author’s experience, 85% of patients have resolution of symptoms by 1 year, without the need for active treatment. By 2 years, almost all patients have had complete resolution of symptoms, again without the need for active treatment such as oral neuroleptics.

Given the large size and higher closure tensions of many scalp reconstructions, hypertrophic and, more prominently, widened scars occur in 5 to 10% of the author’s patients. Hypertrophic scars, if still problematic 6 months postsurgery, can be treated with intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (or equivalent) at concentrations of 20 to 40 mg/mL with on average 0.05 mL deposited every 1cm of the scar length. Widened scars, if of cosmetic concern, can be serially excised or undergo hair transplantation as outlined earlier.

Milia, keratin cysts, and ingrown hairs are easily extracted with a 19- gauge needle (or equivalent), if requested by the patient for cosmetic reasons. Folliculitis of limited degree, if bothersome to the patient, can be treated with a 19-gauge needle evacuation or more aggressive scalp massage during shampooing. Larger areas will require good scalp hygiene, and less commonly a 1-month course of an oral antibiotic in the cephalosporin or tetracycline families.

In patients undergoing SIH, very uncommonly, bony sequestration can occur. This requires removal of the involved bone and application of a skin graft (or equivalent) over the diploic space. This is not commonly performed in an outpatient surgical setting. Referral to the appropriate

specialist is required. Rarely arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can occur along an incision margin. They present as subtly pulsatile red-blue nodules or plaques. If located away from prominent bony suture lines, they can be safely excised in an outpatient setting under local anesthesia. Larger AVMs or AVMs located directly over a bony suture line should be assessed radiologically or referred to an appropriate specialist to ensure there is no continuity with the dural space through the epiploic veins. Very rarely, a venous air embolus could occur in a seated patient when a large scalp resection requires removal of periosteum and air enters the CNS through epiploic veins.41 The presentation is sudden onset of neurological symptoms. Treatment requires awareness of the possibility, recognizing symptoms, supportive emergency care if required, and immediate transfer to hospital.

Abstract The cheek is a common site of Mohs surgery and subsequent reconstruction. It is a large subunit with complex topography that borders many other facial subunits. Thus, many factors must be considered while operating in this area. This chapter addresses relevant anatomy such as the facial nerve and parotid gland and duct that one must take into account prior to performing surgery on the cheek. Illustrations are shown of the vascular, neural, and glandular anatomy and in addition the relaxed skin tension lines. A unique subunit principle of the cheek, with illustration, is presented including the considerations for these different subunits. An algorithm for approaching reconstruction of a cheek defect is laid out based on location and size of the defect. Reconstructions are discussed and shown with complimentary photographs especially of the more challenging repairs. This chapter ends with a discussion of possible complications that may occur subsequent to a surgery in this area and things to consider in minimizing complication risk.

• The cheek is a large subunit bordering many other complex facial subunits that must be taken into account when performing surgery in this area. • Beware of the well-known danger zones where damage of branches of the facial nerve is of higher likelihood (Fig. 6.1). • The relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) of the cheek as well as dynamic and static lines from the muscles of facial expression run parallel and often defects are sutured in this plane to minimize appearance of scarring (Fig. 6.3).

• The cheek can be divided up into eight subunits based on location with each having different skin quality and considerations given proximity to different neighboring facial subunits (Fig. 6.4). • A reconstructive algorithm can be used as a guide when faced with a cheek defect (Fig. 6.5). • There are minimal naturally occurring lines on the cheek; if equivocal repair options, consider the repair with the least number of lines (i.e., linear repair has one). • Curvilinear repairs on the cheek are of great value given convexity and allowing one to minimize tissue redundancy and tension on the eyelid. • Advancement flaps, including the V-Y advancement flap, are very useful on the cheek given large reservoir of mobile skin on lateral cheek and superior neck. • Suspension sutures to the medial canthal tendon or periosteum of the nasion or orbital rim are of great value to minimize risk of ectropion. • The bilobed transposition flap, as utilized on the nose, can be used for very large defects on the cheek with success when reconstructive options are limited. • Eversion, while still utilized on the cheek, may take a longer time to resolve than other facial sites. • Standing tissue cones at the inferior pole of a curvilinear repair may persist, while those falling superiorly in the eyelid will often relax.

The cheek is a common area of treatment in Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) and subsequent reconstruction. It is also one of the larger subunits and borders many other complex structures and subunits (ocular, auricular, oral, nasal, temporal, neck) and defects often may have significant overlap with other facial subunits. The first thing to consider in evaluating and treating a tumor with MMS, and then ultimately the reconstruction of the
resulting defect, is the relevant anatomy of a particular area. The relevant anatomy of the cheek is discussed in the following section.

In discussing the anatomy of the cheek, we will start by addressing the anatomical structures deep to the surface of the skin. Then we will go on to discuss the superficial peripheral borders and boundaries of the cheek along with the aesthetic subunits of the area.

The superficial fascia, also known as the superficial muscular aponeurotic system (SMAS), of the cheek contains many important anatomic structures. These include the parotid gland and duct, muscles of facial expression as well as branches of the facial and trigeminal nerve, and the facial artery and vein. The parotid gland lies in the inferolateral portion of the cheek in the superficial fascia. The branches of the facial nerve and of course the parotid duct arise from the anterior border of the parotid gland. The parotid duct courses anteriorly from there lying atop the masseter muscle and can be found about 2 cm inferior to the zygomatic arch. The transverse facial artery and buccal branch of the facial nerve can often be found in close proximity to the parotid duct as well. As the parotid duct continues more anteriorly/medially, it eventually pierces the buccinator muscle of the cheek and drains into the oral cavity. The branches of the facial nerve (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical) arise from within the parotid, and a diagram of these branches, the well-known danger zones,1 and parotid gland and duct anatomy is seen in Fig. 6.1.

Fig. 6.1 Please note the above anatomy of the cheek including the parotid duct and facial nerve. Specifically pay attention to the danger zones where the temporal and mandibular branches of the facial nerve lie more superficially and are at higher risk of damage in these areas. The mandibular branch of the facial nerve is found in the cheek and its course parallels the inferior margin of the mandible.

The facial artery crosses the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle lying deep to the platysma in this location. As it progresses proximally at the angle of the mouth, it gives off the inferior labial and superior labial branches and once it reaches the lateral nose it becomes the

angular artery. The infraorbital artery enters the cheek through the infraorbital foramen of the maxilla and anastomoses with branches of the facial artery listed earlier.2 The vascular anatomy of the cheek is shown in Fig. 6.2.

Fig. 6.2 The figure above illustrates the vascular anatomy of the cheek. Relevant branches of the external carotid artery are shown including the transverse facial artery and facial artery and its branches. Please note the infraorbital artery is not shown in this illustration.
The relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) begin at the nasolabial fold (NLF) and run parallel to the NLF and eventually parallel to the inferior

lateral canthal lines upon progressing more laterally. At the lateral cheek, they begin to no longer run parallel to aforementioned lines and run vertically parallel to the preauricular crease. The RSTLs are important to consider in reconstruction given reconstruction in these planes has the least amount of tension.3 Additionally, in particular for cheek reconstruction, the RSTL plane is also the same plane that all naturally occurring dynamic and static lines (rhytids) are formed over time from movements of the muscles of facial expression. Thus, reconstructions can be performed and can be best hidden if placed within already formed lines or lines that will form in the future. These RSTLs are shown in Fig. 6.3.
Fig. 6.3 The relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) are shown above. Specially pay attention to the parallel nature of these lines to the
nasolabial fold as they progress laterally and how they change as they approach the auricular and ocular areas.

The cheek’s peripheral borders are the infraorbital rim and zygomatic arch superiorly and the border of the mandible inferiorly. The medial border is the nasofacial junction, NLF, and labiomandibular crease medially and the preauricular crease laterally.4 For the purposes of this text, we will divide the cheek up into eight subunits all approximately 3 to 4 cm2 in size. These are the superomedial cheek, medial cheek, inferomedial cheek, superior central cheek, central cheek, inferior central cheek, superior lateral cheek, and inferior lateral cheek. These different subunits have different quality of skin with medial subunits being thicker and more sebaceous and superior and lateral subunits being more thin and nonsebaceous when approaching eyelid and preauricular skin. Different repairs are considered in each of these areas primarily based on size and location but also certainly considering differing skin qualities, proximity to other facial subunits and topography of each specific area. These different subunits are displayed in Fig. 6.4.
Fig. 6.4 This figure divides the cheek into the eight different proposed subunits shown. These subunits each have unique skin

This figure nicely diagrams these different cheek subunits and the overlap and borders they have with other subunits of the face (ocular, auricular, oral, nasal, temporal, neck). This clearly is a very important consideration in reconstruction of the cheek given defects often are not contained to just one of the facial subunits. Each of the other (noncheek) facial subunits have their own considerations, which are addressed elsewhere in this text, that one must take into account when faced with a cheek defect that overlaps into, approximates, or closely approximates another facial subunit.

The reconstruction options on the cheek are vast given the diverse areas of the cheek that border many unique structures such as the nose, mouth, eye, and ear. Additionally, the cheek has a large surface area among the facial subunits, thus allowing for larger tumors solely involving the cheek and sometimes necessitating very large repairs. The algorithm shown in Fig. 6.5 has been constructed as a basic guide when approaching a cheek defect. The variables addressed are size and location of the defects, which then guide one to some possible repairs to consider given those variables. Further discussion of different repairs and other considerations are included in the text in the sections to follow.

Fig. 6.5 A basic preliminary algorithm to consider while approaching a cheek defect. This algorithm is primarily based on size and location. Of course, each cheek defect is quite unique and this should only be used as a basic starting point of repairs to consider when faced with a defect.

6.4.1 Primary Closures The most common repair for optimal outcome on the cheek is the curvilinear repair.5 The cheek has convexity with minimal other topographical changes compared to other facial subunits while having few naturally occurring lines. Since additional lines are difficult to hide, the curvilinear repair, in most circumstances, allows for the best result given the minimal cosmetic footprint of a single line. These repairs are best suited to run in the RSTLs, given most naturally occurring lines on the cheek are parallel to those lines. Fig. 6.6 and Fig. 6.7 are an example of a curvilinear closure repaired parallel to the RSTLs and dynamic facial lines.

Fig. 6.6 Moderate-sized defect approximating subunit 2. Primary curvilinear repair was chosen. Please note parallel nature to dynamic lines of facial expression and relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs). (This image is provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

Additionally, curvilinear repairs are often used on the cheek to accomplish several goals, of which the most obvious is allowing one to repair parallel with RSTLs. Additionally, they are used on the convex surface of the cheek to allow for minimizing the length of the repair due to tissue redundancy. Finally, curvilinear repairs may be utilized to minimize tension placed in the vertical direction to avoid excessive tension on the eyelid and a resulting ectropion. Fig. 6.8 and Fig. 6.9 are other examples of curvilinear repairs.

Curvilinear repairs are most often done on the medial cheek with a stepwise approach of design and execution. The concavity of the superior and inferior Burow’s triangles is directed medially and laterally, respectively, with the apex of the triangles directed vertically. After removal of the Burow’s triangles and hemostasis, an assistant can place skin hooks in the tips of defect with tension in a vertical vector. Then the first suture is placed centrally in the defect perpendicular (with a horizontal tension vector) to the now vertical orientation of the defect to prevent any tension on the lower eyelid. Skin hooks can be kept in place for placement of at least the next two sutures, and a suture can be placed at the midpoint of the remaining superior and inferior defects in the same fashion as above. This style of suturing can be continued until all dermal sutures are placed. This allows the redundancy of the unequal lengths of the medial and lateral portion of the removed Burow’s triangles to be sutured out, thus minimizing the length of the repair.
6.4.2 Flaps Advancement and/or Rotation Flaps When linear or curvilinear repairs are not an option, the next best options, in the author’s opinion, are repairs that produce only two lines. In this

situation, ideally one and/or two suture lines run in an RSTL or natural border of the cheek to minimize appearance. The most common repair to produce such is an advancement and/or rotation flap. These two flaps are very similar, especially on the cheek. The major difference is that the advancement flap movement is in the same vector along the length (advancing edge) of the flap, while the movement in a rotation flap changes vectors (“rotates”) along the course of the flap. Rotation flaps are of great utility especially when working in the periocular, perinasal, and periauricular regions. This allows for rotation around these structures, without involving them in the flap, while also sometimes allowing one to remove and hide areas of tissue redundancy in the natural cosmetic borders just lateral to the nose or in the preauricular fold. These flaps may be used for large reconstructions on the superior cheek (bordering eyelid) or lateral cheek (bordering ear). Advancement and rotation flaps are raised in the plane of the mid- subcutaneous tissue, and care is taken to avoid undermining deeper where the potential of damaging important anatomic structures is of higher likelihood. Undermining large areas should be performed while alternating between reflecting the flap and then retracting the flap over the scissors or scalpel to observe that the plane of undermining is running parallel to the surface of the skin rather than diving too deeply. After undermining to achieve flap mobility, the first few sutures are placed. It is essential that these sutures are meticulously placed especially in large flaps that are close to and/or involving the eyelid. An important point in performing flaps on the superior cheek (bordering the eyelid) is the utility of sutures to suspend the flap to the periosteum of the orbital rim, nasion, or medial canthal

tendon depending on the location.6 The size and weight of these flaps, coupled with the effect of gravity and scar contraction over time in proximity to the eyelid, can put excessive tension on the eyelid and cause ectropion over time. Thus, suspension sutures are often utilized to allow for tension to be on the periosteum and not on the eyelid itself. This was deemed necessary in several of the periocular flaps shown in this chapter.

After the periosteal sutures, if utilized, the goal of the next several key sutures is to move the flap entirely into place with the tension vectors of the sutures running parallel to the eyelid. For example, inferior to the eye the suturing tension vectors run mediolaterally, while lateral to the eye the tension is in the cephalocaudal direction. One or two sutures in both these locations do the majority of the work to place the flap in the correct location, while the remainder are placed for fine-tuning and perfect approximation.

The specific type of advancement flap known as the V-Y advancement flap has great utility on the cheek given highly mobile lateral cheek skin and robust subcutaneous blood supply for flaps in this location. This flap does have four lines associated with it, so it may have a substantial cosmetic footprint, but it can be very helpful for repair of large defects. This repair is of great benefit when the defect is bordering the nose and NLF. In this location, two of the four lines of this repair can be hidden in the naturally appearing creases of the NLF and the lateral alar groove.7,​8 Fig. 6.13, Fig. 6.14 are examples of the utility of the V-Y advancement flap for large defects or defects in challenging locations.

Placing the initial load- bearing sutures at this location minimized tension on the lip medially and the eye superiorly.

The V-Y advancement flap is incised to the deep subcutaneous tissue to take advantage of the mobility and vascularity of subcutaneous tissue in this location. Undermining is performed in all directions outwardly underneath the skin adjacent to the flap. Additionally, vertical releasing of the deep subcutaneous tissue at the leading and trailing edge of the flap can be performed if extra mobility in needed. Mobility is enhanced by dissecting down into the subcutaneous tissue of the buccal fat pad to lengthen the pedicle of the flap, allowing for greater movement. The flap can be pulled into place with a skin hook and a suture can be placed at the apex of the V where the skin adjacent to the flap can be sutured linearly. This may in effect support the flap to a degree and can minimize tension on the suture on the leading edge of the flap. Finally, the leading-edge sutures are directed with horizontal tension vectors and suspension sutures, such as those to the lateral nasal sidewall periosteum, can be used if there is concern about tension on a free margin such as the eyelid.

Transposition flaps, in the author’s hands, are used less frequently on the cheek given cosmetic footprint, but they can certainly be useful in the periocular area or for very large defects on the cheek without many other good options. The plane utilized for the flap is the same as that for advancement and/or rotation flaps. The advantage of transposition flaps is they virtually just fall into place with minimal tension other than from the weight of the flap. Fig. 6.15 is an example of a bilobed transposition flap on the cheek for a large defect. The design for the bilobed transposition flap on the cheek is the same basic design utilized for nasal defects9,​10 and recruits mobility from loose skin on the neck or jowls. The intent for this flap is to hide as many of the lines from the lobes in the naturally occurring borders between subunits, such as the jawline or postauricular skin. In some instances, the lobes are taken from the neck and moved superomedially to cover the medial cheek or superolaterally to cover the preauricular cheek. If the preferred reservoir for a large preauricular defect is postauricular skin, the first lobe of the bilobed flap can transpose over the ear, hiding the second lobe in the postauricular skin and the tertiary defect in the hairline or lateral neck. Care should be taken not to transpose postauricular hair- bearing scalp; instead, the design may originate inferolaterally or involve more than two lobes, which creates a longer arc of transposition while recruiting a more distant skin reservoir.

Fig. 6.15 (a) Large defect approximating subunits 2 and 3 for which bilobed transposition flap is drawn. (b) Flap raised showing proper plane prior to suturing into place. (c) Immediate postoperative photograph. Minimal tension on adjacent lip. Initial load-bearing sutures placed in horizontal direction to avoid tension on the eyelid.

Second intention healing is used minimally on the cheek given convexity of this subunit. It could be considered for small defects in locations that are concave such as the nasofacial junction or the preauricular crease. It should generally be avoided for defects close to the free margins of the eyelid or mouth given risk for contraction and distortion of those subunits.

The use of the full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) should be avoided on the cheek unless there are no other options for very large defects. Defects involving either an entire subunit of the cheek or highly immobile skin, especially in patients who have had several previous reconstructions on the cheek resulting in surrounding scar tissue, would be a reasonable situation in which an FTSG could be utilized. FTSGs on the cheek are often cosmetically unacceptable compared to a primary closure or flap repair. FTSGs may be used in combination with other repairs on the cheek for large defects such as in combination with primary closures or flaps that partially reduce the defect and leave a smaller area to receive a graft taken from a Burow’s triangle or from the redundancy of a point of rotation (see Chapter 11). However, if an FTSG is utilized on the cheek with a suboptimal result, revision can be done with excision of that FTSG and subsequent primary or flap closure or serial excisions to remove the FTSG entirely.

Complications on the cheek do occur, and one must be aware of them to prevent such complications. Complications can be categorized into infection, bleeding, nerve or other anatomical structure damage, and finally poor cosmetic result.

Infection prevention and infection complications will be minimally addressed given it is outside the scope of this text; however, please refer to Chapter 12 of this book for such information and also see the resources mentioned at the end of this chapter. Infection prevention and treatment are crucial to improve surgical outcomes and to minimize morbidity and even mortality.11

The importance of anatomical knowledge is crucial to effective surgery on the cheek to minimize risk of damaging vital anatomic structures. Please refer to earlier section on relevant anatomy of the cheek for further details. Appropriate consent should be obtained when working in a particular area (i.e., subunit 3 due to the superficial nature of the mandibular branch of the facial nerve). Certainly, at times, damage to relevant anatomical structures, such as the facial nerve or parotid gland/duct, cannot be avoided when operating on aggressive tumors. Extirpation of deep tumors in the mid cheek can involve removal of the superficial parotid gland and/or the parotid duct. Incision lines of flaps or primary closures of these defects can drain clear salivary fluid with gustation. Usually these temporary fistulas will close and resolve without further interception as healing continues and scar formation contracts. If it persists or sinus tract formation ensues, then referral to an otolaryngologist or other head and neck surgeon specializing in nerve damage repair would be warranted.1

Bleeding complications do occur; however, they can be minimized. Generally speaking, the smaller the defect and repair (i.e., less cut tissue), the lower the risk of having bleeding complications. In addition to repair size, sound hemostasis is probably the single most important factor to minimize bleeding complications. The cheek may have higher risk of bleeding complications than many other subunits, especially if patients are on an anticoagulant. This is likely due to the size of the subunit, potentially large tumors solely involving the cheek, and large flap repairs with broad dead spaces resulting in higher risk of bleeding or hematoma formation. Further discussion of bleeding and hematoma complications is outside of the scope of this text.12,​13

The poor cosmetic outcome can result from and may be related to any of the prior complications listed earlier. Also, it can be related to any number of other factors including the patient’s skin and postoperative care as well as surgical technique. The biggest modifiable risk for poor cosmetic outcome, outside of smoking, is surgical technique, including choosing the appropriate repair addressed elsewhere in this text. The author hopes that the algorithm in Fig. 6.5 and accompanying text will be of assistance in achieving good surgical outcomes with fewer surgical revisions.

This chapter focuses on preservation of the symmetrical projection of the ear (which is the top aesthetic concern in auricular reconstruction, followed by maintaining the nautilus shape), and preservation of the helical rim and special considerations for the same. This chapter also discusses several reconstructive options, and cartilage flaps and grafts that may be needed to prevent auricular distortion. The authors also consider here that not all wounds necessitate reconstruction; many wounds on the anterior and posterior surfaces, not involving the helical rim, heal well by second intention.
Keywords: Auricular reconstruction, cartilage flap, cartilage graft, helical rim advancement, external auditory canal stenosis, retroauricular interpolation

• Preserving the symmetrical projection of the ear is the top aesthetic concern in auricular reconstruction followed by maintaining the nautilus shape. • Preservation of the helical rim is important and special considerations should be taken to preserve it. • When there is significant structural loss, cartilage flaps and grafts may be needed to prevent auricular distortion. • When there are significant defects involving the external auditory canal (EAC), caution must be taken for stenosis. • Lastly, it is important to consider that not all wounds necessitate reconstruction. Many wounds on the anterior and posterior surfaces, not involving the helical rim, heal well by second intention.

The structure and form of the ear itself has many complex intricacies, while its functions are simple and basic. The ear has many variations in the quality of the cartilage, skin, and soft tissue that make each auricle unique to reconstruct. The two primary goals of any reconstruction are to maintain the function, and secondarily, preserve the aesthetic form. When reconstructing the auricle, preserving auditory function and maintaining the normal projection of the ear will help attain these primary goals. The cartilage of the ear provides the foundation for its structure and identifiable shape. The anterior and lateral profiles comprise each ear’s unique appearance such that their preservation is critical for a successful reconstruction. When contemplating a reconstruction of the ear, it is often simplest to approach each anatomical zone separately. Table 7.1 lists each of the anatomical zones of the ear. It is best to approach the aesthetics of reconstruction based on the hierarchy listed in Table 7.2. Each auricular defect is unique and calls for careful consideration for each reconstructive option.

The topographical anatomy of the ear is unique (see Fig. 7.1a). An interesting feature of the ear is the variation in its components. Cartilage ranges from soft and delicate to rigid. Skin ranges from elastic on the earlobe to rigid anteriorly. Therefore, it is important to assess and appreciate each ear’s unique features.
Fig. 7.1 (a) Anatomic subunits of the ear. (b) Vascular supply of the lateral and posterior ear. (c) Cutaneous innervation of the ear.

The topographical anatomy of the ear is noteworthy and unlike any other anatomical site on the body. These topographical landmarks are illustrated in Fig. 7.1a. Not only are there multiple anatomical subunits of the ear, but there are also many anatomical variations within each subunit, such as rigid and soft cartilage. The skin on the earlobe is relatively elastic while the skin on the anterior surface has no elasticity. With the multiple convexities and concavities involving the auricle, as well as varying characteristics of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, it is important to assess and appreciate each ear’s unique structure.
Despite the ear’s intricate architecture, its primary functions are quite basic: hearing, maintaining EAC patency for the conduction of sound, and holding eyeglasses.

While the ear is relatively inconspicuous in its lateral location with limited visibility from the frontal view, change of its projection from the head can lead to noticeable deformities. There is a well-established hierarchy of aesthetic concerns of the ear that are listed in Table 7.2. We recommend prioritizing each concern as listed to obtain the best cosmetic outcome.

The ear has many complexities while its framework is relatively simple. The cartilage serves as the foundation that is then draped by the perichondrium, subcutaneous tissue, then the skin. On the posterior ear, the skin and subcutaneous tissue remains relatively loose and nonadherent as compared with the anterior ear. As a result, the posterior ear has more mobility and, to some degree, can serve as a skin reservoir for flaps and grafts. When performing these procedures, the undermining plane on the ear remains superficial to the perichondrium. If undermining is necessary on the lobule, it is best to do so in the mid fat.

Relaxed skin tension lines are not important for ear reconstructive strategy. Due to the complex topography of the ear, the scars of reconstruction remain relatively camouflaged and inconspicuous and are more dependent on reconstruction design and suturing technique.

The arterial supply of the auricle is from the external carotid artery with two main branches: the superficial temporal artery and the posterior auricular artery (see Fig. 7.1b.) These two networks have extensive anastomoses providing a very rich blood supply. This makes random patterned flaps dependable and relatively low risk with appropriate execution.

Cutaneous innervation of the ear is supplied by both cranial and spinal nerves (see Fig. 7.1c). Cranial nerves VII, IX, and X innervate the conchal bowl. The greater auricular nerve, arising from C2 and C3, innervates the lower half of the ear. The superior ear anteriorly is innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of CN V3. The remainder of the superior ear posteriorly is innervated by the lesser occipital nerve (C2, C3).

Fig. 7.2 Division of the ear and reconstructive options for anatomical subunit. (STSG, split thickness skin graft; FTSG, full thickness skin graft; 1°, primary; 2°, secondary; EAC, external auditory canal; TF, transposition flap; IPF, island pedicle flap.) 7.3.1 Superior Helix

As the most iconic component of the auricle, the helix is responsible for the normal shape and position of the ear. It is comprised of delicate cartilage that can be easily deformed during reconstructions. In addition, it is the most common location of skin cancers of the ear. For these reasons, the proper reconstruction of the helix is paramount to maintaining its normal contour.

We propose the algorithm in Fig. 7.3 to approach defects on the superior helix. First, it is necessary to determine if there is infrastructural compromise. If there is none, we recommend a simplified closure. If the defect remains small (<1 cm), does not involve the helical groove, and adequate soft tissue remains, a simple primary closure may be performed with excellent results. After undermining above the perichondrium, an elongated linear or curvilinear closure oriented diagonally to the helical rim is a simple method to prevent standing vertical cones and flattening of the helical curvature. This elongated closure often has a larger length-to-width ratio than the typical 3:1 observed at other anatomic locations.
Fig. 7.3 Reconstruction algorithm of the superior helix. (2°, second intention; FTSG, full thickness skin graft.)

Additional options for the superior helix without structural deficits are second intention, full-thickness skin grafts (FTSGs), and flaps. Second intention is best reserved for wounds that are shallower and have intact perichondrium. They have a smaller risk of auricular distortion from wound contraction as compared with deeper and larger wounds. If the wound is

larger and adjacent to the less rigid cartilage of the helical rim, distortion may be more likely. If the wound is more posterior where tissue is looser and supported by underlying rigid structural cartilage, distortion is less likely. FTSGs from the postauricular area, preauricular area, or the conchal bowl are excellent options for repair of superior helical defects without extensive infrastructural compromise. Assessing the wound bed’s vascular base is also important. FTSGs are better utilized with intact perichondrium and structurally insignificant loss of cartilage. Flaps (as listed in the superior helix reconstructive algorithm) should be considered when defects are larger, the wound bed has a poor vascular base, or when larger cartilage grafts have been used for structural support.

Repairs of superior helical defects with loss of structural integrity require more careful planning and discussion with the patient. Patient discussion should detail the types of reconstructions and review the goals and expectations of each option. For example, if the patient depends on the integrity of the auricle for hearing aids, reading glasses, etc., then discussing the need to preserve this function may be necessary. In the case of a larger structural defect, cartilage grafts or struts may be used to optimize auricular restoration and cosmesis.

Donor sites for cartilage grafts are demonstrated in Fig. 7.4. For larger structural defects, there are several reconstructive options. If the nautilus shape of the auricle is compromised, harvesting the entire ipsilateral or contralateral conchal bowl cartilage can be used to recreate this shape nicely. In addition to cartilage grafts, cartilage flaps can be performed. It is possible to transpose or advance cartilage with the aid of a muscular or subcutaneous vascular base. In Fig. 7.5 and Fig. 7.6, a transposition of cartilage is utilized to provide structural support for the helical rim. For defects of the superior helical rim that are deep but remain less than 1.0 to 1.5 cm in width, a wedge closure is an alternate option for repair. If a defect is too large for an aesthetic wedge closure, reestablishing structural support with a cartilage graft and performing a multistaged flap, such as a retroauricular interpolation flap or a tube flap, may yield the most optimal cosmetic results.

Similar to the superior helix, reconstruction of the mid helix is essential to maintaining the normal curvature of the helical rim. In contrast to the superior helix, the cartilage of the mid helix may be more rigid and provides more structural support though this is variable. In addition to the structural difference, the mid helix has a more limited cutaneous donor pool for reconstruction. The superior helix, inferior helix, posterior ear, and postauricular area serve as the mid helical donor pools.

Reconstruction of the mid helix requires assessment of several key factors. First, it is important to note whether there is a structural deficit that needs repair. Second, involvement of the helical groove may necessitate special consideration for the repair of the defect. The algorithm to repair the mid helix (Fig. 7.9) is similar to the superior helix. However, the primary donor pools for the mid helix are inferior lobular, postauricular, and retroauricular skin. As a result, helical rim advancement and retroauricular interpolation flaps are more commonly performed in this location.

After assessing the wound and discovering no structural deficit, the size of the wound must be taken into account. Wounds that are smaller than 1.5 cm and limited to the rim may be considered for a primary closure as described in the superior helix section. Second intention is another option for defects

that are mostly posterior to minimize the likelihood of helical rim deformation as the wound heals and contracts. In addition, if the wound involves the helical groove, second intention may not be advisable as this may cause fusion and therefore noticeable distortion of the helical rim. An FTSG and a helical rim advancement flap are also excellent options and probably the most commonly used options for reconstruction. In addition, these may be better suited than second intention if there is more involvement of the helical rim. Both a graft and the helical rim advancement flap may help to reestablish this very important cosmetic unit of the ear if executed carefully. If the wound is larger than roughly 1.0 cm in width, primary closure may be difficult to perform, and second intention is more likely to lead to auricular deformity. We prefer FTSGs, helical advancement flaps, retroauricular interpolation flaps, or multistaged tubed pedicle flaps. Each patient has unique anatomy and tailoring the repair for each defect is crucial. For example, a helical rim advancement flap may not be the best option for even a smaller wound if the lobule is too small or nonexistent to recruit skin for the closure. Helical rim advancement flaps are an excellent option for small- to medium-sized wounds, especially when they do not cross the helical groove. A retroauricular interpolation flap is preferred when the wound is larger or if the wound crosses the helical groove. This interpolation flap provides excellent vascular supply, and therefore is very reliable.

Repair of the mid helix with a structural deficit, again, is similar in principle to the repairs of superior helix necessitating structural support. Given the iconic curvature of the helix from the most superior aspect to the lobule, irregularities of this curved contour can be quite noticeable. For optimal cosmesis, it is advised to repair structural deficits to minimize these irregularities in the curvature of the helix. For smaller defects, a helical advancement flap (unilateral or bilateral) that is inclusive of cartilage (chondrocutaneous) may help to restore the appearance of the ear. Excision of a crescentic Burow’s triangle including cartilage from the superior scapha can be utilized when advancing the superior rim inferiorly to improve reach and avoid a cupping deformity. It is important to note that this may shorten the height of the ear. As with the superior helix, a cartilage graft followed by FTSG or STSG or retroauricular interpolation flap is considered the workhorse repair for structural mid helical defects. Lastly, a wedge resection may be considered, although this will lead to size discrepancy between the patient’s ears and can cause “cupping” if not performed with extreme care.

When there is involvement of the helical groove, special considerations must be taken. If the wound is small (<0.5 cm) and involves minimal cartilaginous loss, reconstruction without structural support is an option. A flap or graft may be used; however, the helical groove should be maintained with the aid of external supports such as a bolster, thermoplastic cast, spiral suture, etc. When performing the spiral suture, we recommend the needle entering from the anterior helical groove through to the posterior aspect of the ear, then looping from the posterior aspect of the helix around the helical rim and reentering on the anterior helical groove. This spiral suture will help guide and form the appropriate shape of the healing repair. Other external stabilizing tools may be utilized to help maintain or recreate the helical groove. Defects greater than 0.5 cm that involve cartilaginous loss will likely require support with cartilage graft followed by soft tissue repair and, again, strategies to maintain the helical groove.

7.3.3 Lobule The lobule is the only anatomical subunit of the ear that is devoid of rigid infrastructure. For this reason, defects on the earlobe tend to be simpler to repair than defects on the superior and midhelix. Due to the pliability of the skin on the lobule, the tissue redundancy, and laxity of the pre-and postauricular skin, the most common reconstructions of the earlobe are relatively simple. However, when defects of the lobule are larger, they may

necessitate structural support. The most important aspect of the lobule’s reconstruction is to maintain the semicircular configuration of the earlobe. If this is maintained, the repair is often unnoticeable to the casual observer even if the lobule size differs somewhat from the contralateral lobe (see Fig. 7.12).

When defects of the lobule are small (less than one-third the horizontal width of the lobule), their repairs can remain simple. It is reasonable to let smaller, superficial defects heal by second intention; however, caution is advised when the defect is located on the anterior aspect of the lobule as they may demonstrate more noticeable scar contraction or hypertrophy. One of the most common methods to repair the lobule is with a primary or wedge closure. Approximating the remaining unaffected skin is often possible and yields excellent results. Some important concepts to remember when suturing the lobule is to maintain the natural semicircular curvature of the lobule and to create maximum wound eversion to avoid depressed scar lines.

Larger defects (greater than one-third the horizontal width of the lobule) often require more innovative and creative reconstructions. Often, a complex primary closure, such as folding the lobule upon itself to recreate the natural curvature, is sufficient (see Fig. 7.13). At times, cartilage grafts should be considered if there is a risk of significant tissue contraction and distortion of the lobule. An FTSG is a reasonable option; however, they do run the risk of contraction and may lead to shriveling or pincushioning of the lobule. Avoidance of undersizing the graft may help to mitigate this risk. Utilizing the pre-, post-, and infra-auricular skin to repair the lobule should not be overlooked. It is sometimes simple and effective to use a single-staged transposition from these donor pools to repair the lobule (see Fig. 7.14). Also, the use of a two-stage interpolation repair from the infra-auricular skin may provide excellent results and lessen the risk of contraction (see Fig. 7.15).

Due to the complex topography, defects of the antihelix can seem difficult and intimidating to repair. However, even with large defects in this region, healing by second intention often produces acceptable results. Assessing the necessity of structural repair of the antihelix and discussing reconstruction goals with the patient will help guide selection of repair options.

As with the helix, we recommend concentrating on two distinct categories of antihelical reconstruction: intact infrastructure and loss of infrastructure. Defects of the antihelix without infrastructural loss are simple. The majority of the defects heal well by second intention. If perichondrium has been lost, one may consider 3- to 4-mm punch fenestrations per 1.5 cm2 to expose vascularized tissue from the opposite side of the ear and therefore increase the vascular supply to the base of the wound. An STSG is an excellent option for thin defects. In our hands, STSGs are preferred in this area owing to their decreased metabolic requirement, their ability to survive exposed cartilage more readily than an FTSG, and their excellent skin match to the antihelix. However, an FTSG can also be considered if the vasculature of the wound base is adequate. Punch fenestrations may be considered prior to placement

of STSGs and FTSGs to increase the vascular supply. They can also be used to augment second intention healing. Skin substitute products are another option to help stimulate granulation tissue in the absence of a well- vascularized wound bed. The placement of a skin substitute may be followed up by placement of an STSG or an FTSG after adequate granulation tissue formation.

When there is loss of infrastructure of the antihelix, repairs need to be individualized to each patient’s defect, ear architecture, healing preferences, and cosmetic goals. Often, loss of cartilage on the antihelix with preservation of the helical rim does not necessitate specific repair. If healing by second intention will lead to distortion of the nautilus-like shape of the ear, then reconstruction with cartilage replacement may be necessary. Wounds with loss of cartilage that are relatively smaller (<1.5 cm) may be closed with a simple wedge excision. A stellate wedge excision may help mitigate the risk of ear cupping. Larger infrastructural defects of the antihelix may require cartilage grafts, including spoke-and-wheel, followed by a flap or graft. Flaps provide a vascular supply and are better suited for larger defects necessitating cartilage replacement. Flap options in this area include retroauricular interpolation flaps, revolving door island pedicle flaps, book flaps, etc.

Repairs of the concha are relatively simple to plan and execute with the majority of defects healing well by second intention (Fig. 7.20). It is best to simplify conchal bowl repairs into two distinct categories: involving the EAC or not. When defects do not involve the EAC and the perichondrium is intact, there is no risk of the EAC stenosis. These defects of the concha can heal well with second intention regardless of their size. One may consider STSGs or FTSGs to speed healing. Other options include placement of skin substitutes or tissue importation flaps. To augment healing, 3- to 4-mm punch fenestrations of the cartilage can be utilized. When the perichondrium is not intact, healing can be delayed. In this circumstance, an STSG and punch fenestrations through large areas of perichondrial loss, placement of skin substitutes, and/or a book page flap can be employed for speedier wound healing.

When the defect involves the EAC, there is risk of EAC stenosis, and caution must be taken to avoid this complication. For cartilaginous defects involving the EAC, it is safe to granulate when defects are <25% of the EAC circumference. Larger cartilaginous defects involving >25% of the EAC circumference will require a repair with an FTSG or flap +/− cartilage graft to prevent stenosis. For lesions that are limited to the skin, it is safe to granulate wounds involving up to 50% of the circumference of the EAC without the risk of stenosis. Defects larger than 50% would be best reconstructed by skin grafting and possibly cartilage grafting to prevent stenosis.

Patient discussion regarding the healing options of second intention or placement of a graft is critical. Grafting in the conchal bowl has several considerations. First, grafts are considered for expediting healing and inhibiting scar contraction. Assessing the size of the defect and the vascularity of the bed is important for choosing the most appropriate graft. We use STSGs on the anterior ear, given an excellent cosmetic match and tenuous vascularity of these defects. STSGs are preferred if there is exposed cartilage. FTSGs are also a good option in this area assuming there is an adequate vascular base. Punch fenestrations through the cartilage may be utilized to provide vascular base from the opposing perichondrium. In addition, thinning the FTSG may be beneficial, especially near the EAC. If there is a wound base with a large proportion of exposed cartilage, one may consider placement of a skin substitute to expedite healing or to build more of a vascular base for a delayed graft.

7.3.6 Tragus While the tragus is a relatively minor component of the ear, its absence can be quite noticeable. The primary goal of reconstruction of the tragus is to maintain projection that is symmetrical from the anterior perspective. Tragal reconstruction depends on whether or not there is compromise to the tragal cartilage. If the defect is relatively small with preservation of the cartilage, a simple primary closure can be utilized. Larger defects can be repaired with an advancement flap utilizing the preauricular skin (see Fig. 7.21, Fig. 7.22). Additional options include transposition flaps, FTSGs, STSGs, or a partial primary closure of the preauricular sulcus using a Burow’s FTSG for the tragus.

When there is substantial cartilaginous loss of the tragal eminence and optimal aesthetic closure is desired, recreating this prominence is the key for a successful reconstruction. Transposition flaps are one way of repairing this defect without the use of a cartilage graft. Superiorly based transposition flaps can recreate the prominence by intentionally designing tissue redundancy and anticipating dependent edema due to the “trapdoor defect” phenomenon. This flap can be intentionally developed with excess soft tissue located within the flap covering the tragal site. A cartilage graft may be used at the time of repair or can be delayed. Lastly, a soft tissue or adipose graft can be utilized to recreate this tragal eminence.

The majority of the defects on the posterior helix can be managed by second intention healing. Defects impinging on the helical rim or those bridging across the sulcus will require other considerations to avoid distortion of the helical rim or pinning back of the ear, respectively. Grafting may be the best repair option, when necessary. Fortunately, the posterior ear has more laxity than other subunits, and for this reason smaller defects may be closed primarily. Partial closures or purse-string closures are other considerations to help reduce the size of defect and expedite the healing process. Assuming there is an adequate vascular base, an FTSG is another option. If there is exposed cartilage on the posterior surface, often an STSG would be a superior option. A flap may also be considered when there is a poor vascular bed for grafting. Often a transposition or a rotation flap may be well utilized in this location. Superior defects are best repaired with the postauricular donor pool, and inferior defects can often utilize the laxity of skin on the
posterior ear itself or the retroauricular sulcus. Cartilage grafts are rarely needed in this location, but should be considered if there is compromise to the helical rim.

Complications of the ear are not uncommon and can be classified as during (intraoperative), immediate (first 2 wk postop), midterm (2 wk–2 mo postop), and long-term (greater than 2 mo postop). Immediate postoperative complications are mostly related to bleeding or infection. Uncontrollable bleeding is rarely a problem, given the ability to directly apply pressure and cauterize vessels. After the epinephrine from the local anesthesia wears off, patients may experience some minor bleeding from the surgical site that can be controlled with pressure in the majority of cases. Antia-Buch helical rim advancement flaps and retroauricular interpolation flaps are at the highest risk of bleeding, especially in patients on anticoagulants. Uncontrolled bleeding may lead to wound dehiscence, infection, and eventual failure of the closure (primary, graft, or flap). In addition to intraoperative meticulous hemostasis, we recommend limited activity for the first 48 hours and a pressure dressing for the first 24 to 48 hours.

Infections are another immediate complication most commonly noted about one week postoperatively. Given the unique flora on the ear, especially near the EAC, it is important to culture wound infections and have a high suspicion for gram-negative infections. Appropriate antibiotics should be prescribed depending on the culture. Some surgeons use dilute white vinegar soaks and topical gentamicin ointment as part of wound care for the ear.

As with any reconstruction within the first 2 weeks of surgery, it is also possible to see infections, skin necrosis, failed grafts/flaps, and rarely maggot infestation of wounds healing by second intention. However, there are several complications that are unique to the ear. For example, retainment

of foreign bodies in the EAC can not only lead to significant pain and discomfort, but may also cause pressure on the tympanic membrane and possible temporary conductive hearing loss. Prior to bandaging, assess the EAC for retained gauze, bleeding that may lead to thrombotic impactions, and other foreign objects. Sterile chondritis is another unique complication of auricular reconstruction. It is most likely to occur in the setting of second intention healing with exposed cartilage. We recommend petrolatum jelly or other occlusive ointments to the wound and coverage with a nonstick gauze to prevent desiccation of the cartilage. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be taken on schedule to alleviate pain and reduce the inflammation of the cartilage. A wound culture should generally be obtained in the setting of chondritis. It is imperative to rule out infectious chondritis as the two can be clinically indistinguishable. For patients that are strictly one-sided sleepers, sleeping on the affected side can compromise the reconstruction or be painful. We encourage alternate sleeping positions or a donut pillow to avoid direct pressure to the site.

Midterm and long-term complications of the ear occur between 2 to 8 weeks and 2 months after surgery, respectively. There is often overlap with the timing of these potential complications. One example of a mid- to long- term complication is the formation of a keloid. This can begin to occur as soon as 6 weeks postoperatively. It is important to obtain a history of keloids from the patient and treat early and aggressively if there is any sign of keloid formation. Other long-term complications should be considered when choosing the appropriate repair. Long-term complications include contractures and distortion of the helical rim, cupping of the ear, and EAC stenosis. With the chronic use of protective equipment masks that tightly fit around the ears having become commonplace, the Editor (SNT) recommends patients to avoid wearing masks that tie around the ear. Instead, he recommends the use of masks that tie over the head and neck, removing tension that would chronically pull down on ears after reconstructive surgery. In patients who have had superior helical rim or helical crus reconstruction, especially with limited structural support, this tension can lead to contracture and even helical rim collapse. These complications can be revised; however, an effort to avoid them proactively is the best strategy whenever possible through careful planning of the reconstruction and follow up in the early postoperative period.
