This chapter presents an algorithmic approach to reconstructive options for repairing perioral defects after Mohs micrographic surgery with a focus on cosmetic subunits. These algorithms represent common reconstructive techniques and their variations utilized within each subunit in the perioral region serving as general principles. Perioral anatomy, key principles, practical pearls, and common pitfalls are reviewed to offer a solid foundation for successful perioral reconstruction.

• Know the perioral anatomy including cosmetic subunits, neurovascular supply, musculature, and tissue reservoirs. • Restoration of the oral sphincter is prioritized, followed by preservation of motor and sensory innervation and optimizing cosmesis. • Mark cosmetic subunits, vermilion border, and favorable lines of closure with ink prior to local anesthesia. • Respect the various cosmetic subunits when designing closures. • Maintain the position and alignment of the vermilion- cutaneous junction (VCJ) and the philtrum at the midline. • Place closures along relaxed skin tension lines and at the junction of cosmetic subunits. • Do not distort the free margin. • The vermilion is not an inviolable structure. • Recruit tissue from lateral reservoirs on the lip or adjacent cheek. • Consider extending surgical defects to subunit boundaries or removing an entire subunit in order to better conceal the

incision lines of the repair. • Repair defects within a single subunit when possible. • Divide defects that bridge the VCJ into vermilion and cutaneous defects and repair each individually. • Avoid pincushioning by appropriately sizing and adequate thinning of flaps and undermining the surrounding tissue. • Achieve thorough hemostasis of the lip prior to closure. • Recreate the alar crease at the isthmus and the melolabial fold with a periosteal stitch. • Close vermilion–vermilion and vermilion–cutaneous wound edges with braided interrupted sutures. • Close full-thickness defects in four layers, starting with reapproximation of the orbicularis oris sphincter. • Always consider individual factors in selecting the best method of repair. • Limit mobility of the perioral region postoperatively to avoid complications and maximize cosmetic results.

The upper and lower lips are the predominant feature of the lower face and carry considerable aesthetic significance. Beyond this, the lips have important motor and sensory functions including facial expression, oral competence and articulation of speech, as well as the protective perception of touch, pain, and temperature. The variations in texture, color, and contour between its numerous cosmetic subunits add to the complexity of the perioral region. Given these significant functional and aesthetic considerations, perioral surgical defects present reconstructive challenges from which innovation has led to a multitude of repair options. The goal in all lip reconstructions is to preserve or restore the function and aesthetics of this unique structure. Key principles for successful perioral reconstruction are detailed in Capsule Summary and Pearls at the beginning of this chapter.

The perioral region is comprised of five distinct cosmetic subunits: two cutaneous lateral upper lip subunits, the philtrum, the cutaneous lower lip and chin, and the vermilion lip (Fig. 8.1). Together, the philtrum and two lateral subunits form the cutaneous upper lip. The nasal base, defined by alar creases, the alar sill, and the columella border the upper lip superiorly. The melolabial fold and the labiomandibular crease (marionette lines) serve as the lateral boundaries of the upper and lower lips, respectively. Although considered a single subunit, the lower lip and chin can be divided at the labiomental crease, which serves as the inferior limit to the lower cutaneous lip. A small triangle of skin, the isthmus or the hairless triangle, exists in the superolateral corners of both cutaneous lateral upper lip subunits adjacent to the nasal ala. These apical triangles warrant special consideration during reconstruction, as their preservation is essential to optimize cosmetic outcomes. Of similar aesthetic importance, the philtrum is a concave subunit bounded by parallel convex philtral columns in the medial upper lip and is defined inferiorly by the Cupid’s bow of the vermilion lip.

The transition from cutaneous upper and lower lips to vermilion takes place at the vermilion-cutaneous junction (VCJ). A well-defined line, referred to as the mucocutaneous or anterior vermilion line, and its rolled border represent an important landmark in lip reconstruction. The combination of thin, nonkeratinizing epithelium and abundant underlying vasculature gives the vermilion a characteristic pink hue. The modified

mucosa of the vermilion covers the free margin of the lip and is adapted for external exposure, with relatively few salivary glands compared to the multitude found deep to the labial and buccal mucosa.1 Its surface is divided into internal (wet) and external (dry) components and the innermost point of contact between the upper and lower lips is defined as the posterior vermilion line.

From superficial to deep, lip tissue is comprised of skin, muscle, and mucosa. The body of the lip is predominantly formed by the orbicularis oris muscle, which is concentrically oriented and inserts directly into the skin’s undersurface. The relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) of the upper and lower lips are oriented in a radial fashion about the oral stoma coursing perpendicularly to the underlying orbicularis muscle. These radial lines are accentuated with pursing and are ultimately paralleled by the wrinkle lines of older patients and enhanced by chronic sun damage and smoking (Fig. 8.2). The radial RSTLs, the melolabial fold, and the labiomental crease are favorable sites to conceal incisions in lip reconstruction.

In bilaterally paired sets, the muscles of facial expression attach radially along the outer margin of the orbicularis oris, marked by the melolabial fold and labiomental creases. Motor innervation to these lip elevators and depressors originates primarily from the buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve, respectively. Although rarely damaged due to their location beneath the musculature, injury to the marginal mandibular nerve anterior to the angle of the jaw during undermining as the nerve becomes more superficial over the bony prominence can lead to significant
functional and cosmetic deformity due to the inability to laterally depress the lower lip.2 This inability is most notable when smiling due to the resulting asymmetry but can also effect speech.

Many of these muscle fibers converge at the modiolus just lateral to the commissure and, as a group, provide the orbicularis oris with an indirect connection to the facial skeleton. This lack of direct connection allows for the advantage of lip tissue to be significantly stretched during reconstructive surgery.1 Even with larger defects slightly more than half of either lip, reconstruction can be accomplished in most cases without causing excessive microstomia. When the orbicularis oris muscle is compromised, priority is placed on restoration of the muscle sphincter. The orbicularis oris muscle sphincter of the lower lip is crucial given its greater role in the retention of intraoral contents.3

Sensory innervation of the upper lip originates from branches of the infraorbital nerve, while branches of the mental nerve provide that of the lower lip. Both infraorbital and mental nerves arise from foramens along the mid-pupillary lines in the maxilla and mandible, respectively, and can be reached percutaneously or via an intraoral route for regional blocks if needed (Fig. 8.3).

Superior and inferior labial arteries provide the principal vascular supply to the lips. Both arteries originate from the facial artery along its course beneath the orbicularis oris muscle about 10 to 12 mm from the oral commissure.4 Often with a tortuous course, the labial arteries run horizontally in the submucosal plane, just beneath the orbicularis and at approximately the level of the anterior vermilion line. While the superior labial artery gives off septal and alar branches medially, the lower labial artery anastomoses with the mental artery through a variable pattern of labiomental branches often vertically oriented across the lower lip and chin (Fig. 8.4).5,6,7

When planning reconstruction of the perioral region, great effort should be made to maximize cosmesis; however, priority should always be placed on the preservation of function. Careful marking of the vermilion border, aesthetic subunits, and favorable lines of closure, such as the RSTL and subunit junctions, is essential prior to executing any perioral reconstruction and preferably done prior to local anesthetic infiltration. One of the most important considerations in lip reconstruction is preservation of lip position. Pushing or pulling the upper or lower lip out of place, pulling the Cupid’s bow off center, or creating any misalignment of the vermilion border can be aesthetically devastating and all efforts must be made to plan reconstructive options that minimize these outcomes. Over time, the high mobility of the perioral region tends to organize tissue in this region back toward baseline positioning and, therefore, even large repairs can result in excellent final outcomes. In addition, it is better to confine reconstructive design to within a single subunit using tissue from within the respective aesthetic region of the lip. With larger defects or those that span multiple subunits, repairs are more likely to involve tissue from the adjacent regions of the cheek or chin.

Certain repairs are more commonly utilized within specific subunits as their closure lines are favorably hidden in the lines of that subunit. The location, size, shape, and depth of the defect will influence the choice of closure within a given subunit. Individual patient characteristics such as skin texture, thickness, and laxity (often influenced heavily by age and sun damage) should also be taken into consideration when choosing the optimal closure. However, an algorithmic approach based on region can be helpful as common patterns of repair within certain aesthetic subunits can serve as a guideline for reconstructive design.8

The vermilion lower lip is most commonly plagued with squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), often in the setting of actinic damage and tobacco exposure. While SCC of the vermilion upper lip tend to involve the cutaneous lip, those of the lower vermilion often have little to no cutaneous involvement, unless they are allowed to progress before treatment. For this reason, defects limited to the vermilion lower lip are considered separately (Fig. 8.5), while defects involving the vermilion upper lip are included in the algorithms described below for the cutaneous upper lip.

After tumor extirpation, second intention healing can be considered for partial-thickness defects restricted to the vermilion. Superficial defects limited to the mucosal lip are often best left to heal with granulation alone and even some larger defects with partial resection of the orbicularis can heal by second intention with satisfactory results.9,​10 With an abundant vascular supply, defects of the mucosal lip re-epithelialize rapidly. A visible stellate scar may result from and represent a disadvantage of second intention healing but can be easily revised with minimal recovery (Fig. 8.6).

The remaining vermilion after tumor extirpation often consists of actinically damaged tissue. For defects in this setting, a complete vermilionectomy, followed by repair of the entire vermilion subunit is preferred. The favored method of vermilion restoration is the mucosal advancement flap (Fig. 8.7). With any vermilion repair, the design, wet–dry line, and vermilion border should be marked prior to local anesthesia. When performing the vermilionectomy, the anterior incision lines extend laterally from the defect along the VCJ, while the posterior incision lines extend laterally from the most posterior aspect of the defect to meet the anterior incision lines at the commissures with removal of mucosal Burow’s triangles as necessary. The vermilion is then removed with care to minimize trauma to the underlying orbicularis muscle. The mucosal advancement flap utilizes the mucosa lining the inner surface of the lip and is elevated by undermining within the submucosal plane deep to the minor salivary glands and immediately superficial to the orbicularis muscle. To allow sufficient anterior advancement under minimal tension, dissection may need to be extended along the vertical length of the lip to the apex of the gingivolabial sulcus, but this is often not required. The flap is then advanced anteriorly over the free margin of the lip to the anterior vermilion line where a key suture is placed in the middle of the advancing edge. Soft braided absorbable suture, such as polyglactin 910, is used to place interrupted

sutures along the remainder of the flap’s leading edge and reestablish the VCJ. The editors often use nonabsorbable epidermal sutures only if sufficient undermining has been done to relieve tension. Accurate positioning of the VCJ is of upmost importance for optimal aesthetic outcome and can be challenging especially in the setting of an adjacent cutaneous lip defect. Inherent contraction of the mucosal flap with wound maturation may distort the anterior vermilion line despite best efforts to properly align and require subsequent revision surgery. If needed, additional excision of the normal tissue of adjacent cutaneous lip may allow for proper alignment.

In addition to accurate positioning of the anterior vermilion line, the mucosal advancement flap can present other challenges. Although the vermilion is a modified mucosal surface, the labial mucosa often results in a slightly deeper red vermilion substitute that may be disfavored, especially by male patients. Some degree of touch, pain, and temperature sensation is expected to return to the vermilion over several months following mucosal advancement flap repair; however, in some patients the restoration of sensation is inadequate. Care can be taken to preserve small neurovascular structures encountered during dissection by gentle blunt spreading rather than sharply undermining when possible. This limited undermining of the mucosal lip provides two advantages: limiting sensory disruption and minimizing subsequent flap contraction.

For small defects restricted to the vermilion where there is minimal adjacent actinic cheilitis, a partial mucosal advancement flap and a bilateral vermilion rotation flap are excellent reconstructive options. Both techniques allow preservation of the healthy vermilion and favorable placement of closure lines along the VCJ. A partial mucosal advancement flap may be favored for defects with a long axis aligned with the anterior vermilion border. An ellipse is designed that places the anterior incision along the vermilion border without extending the incisions from commissure to commissure. After removal of the vermilion cones, a partial mucosal advancement flap is elevated and brought anteriorly to meet the VCJ as described earlier.

A bilateral vermilion rotation flap is designed with bilateral incisions off of the anterior aspect of the defect along the VCJ (Fig. 8.8). The flaps are elevated superficial to the orbicularis and a mucosal Burow’s triangle is taken posterior to the defect. Incisions along the VCJ may be extended to the commissures to allow adequate rotation under minimal tension but may not be required. Soft, braided absorbable interrupted sutures allow precise VCJ and flap alignment. The main advantage of a bilateral vermilion rotation flap is the tension is largely displaced laterally and therefore does not pull the lower cutaneous lip up superiorly, making the lower lip appear smaller (as can occur with mucosal advancement flaps).
Fig. 8.8 Bilateral vermilion rotation flap. (a) Vermilion lower lip defect. (b) Bilateral rotation flaps sutured in place. (c) Final result.

The cutaneous lateral upper lip can be further divided into apical and mid- lower regions, which are helpful to consider when debating reconstructive options. Second intention healing on the cutaneous lateral upper lip is limited to superficial defects located in concavities such as that of the isthmus or apical triangle.11 Granulation of deeper defects often creates a hypertrophic scar. Full-thickness skin grafts (FTSG) are rarely used in this area as they are often complicated by pincushioning, offer a poor color and texture match, and are an unacceptable alternative for the hair-bearing upper lip of men. Primary linear closures are useful for small defects in the mid-lower lateral subunit. For apical or larger defects, a variety of local flaps can be utilized to tap into regional or distant laxity and displace tension, thereby avoiding displacement of the free margin. Local skin redundancy offers excellent texture, thickness, appendage, and color match. Most local flaps in the perioral region are advancement or rotation flaps that slide tissue, almost always, from a laterally based reservoir along natural motion vectors and stay within the cosmetic unit. Depending on the location of the defect, specific flaps are used in particular regions of the cutaneous lateral upper lip to best hide suture lines (Fig. 8.9). Ultimately, individual variation in tissue laxity and size of the cosmetic subunits will heavily influence the reconstructive method chosen.

Small defects, less than 1 cm in diameter, on the lateral subunit can be closed primarily with a linear closure without the concern of free margin distortion.8,​12 A fusiform defect is first created by removing Burow’s triangles with the optimum angle of 30 degrees at the apices above and below the primary defect. Closure lines should deliberately be placed along the radial RSTLs or at the junction of cosmetic subunits to both minimize tension on the wound and improve cosmetic results. With a linear closure, the distance between the two ends of the defect will lengthen to match that of the fusiform’s arc. The superior portion of the closure should not cross the melolabial fold, and if approaching this boundary, the scar line should be redirected along the alar crease for better camouflage. If the inferior portion of the closure ends near or on the vermilion border, extension of the incision through the upper vermilion to the mucosal portion of the lip is often required to avoid standing cones (Fig. 8.10). This is favored over the use of an M-plasty, which extends outside of the RSTLs and is therefore less well camouflaged and, with all of the very small and acute angles, is

more prone for tissue mismatch and minor step-off deformities. Minimal tension on the closure is achieved through undermining laterally above the orbicularis oris. During layered suturing, emphasis is placed on maintaining alignment of the VCJ as even small offsets yield poor aesthetic results. Once again, careful marking of this important landmark prior to local anesthetic infiltration is essential to aid in precise repositioning. Suturing technique to optimize wound eversion is critical on the upper lip, especially on the hair-bearing lip of men where decreased collagen density between hair follicles reduces suture grip and increases the risk of scar inversion.13

Apical defects are best reconstructed with flaps that hide suture lines within the perialar groove or melolabial fold. Crescentic advancement flaps are ideal for small defects in the apical region that borders the inferior alar crease or lateral nostril sill. With this repair, the inferior Burow’s triangle is placed along the RSTLs of the upper lip, identical to that in primary closure; however, the superior Burow’s triangle is displaced along the alar crease in a crescentic fashion to facilitate medial advancement of tissue (Fig. 8.11). After excision of both triangles, the flap is undermined laterally in the subcutaneous tissue and advanced medially to bring together the inferior aspect of the crescent and the superior aspect of the defect with a key suture. For larger defects that have more tension on the closure, deep

tacking sutures from the flap to periosteum below the ala help advance the flap medially without pulling the ala laterally. The crescent may be excised after advancement and closure of the lip in order to minimize the excised tissue.14 Strategic placement of incision lines within the RSTLs and the alar groove consistently results in well-concealed scars and excellent cosmetic outcomes.

Rotation flaps offer an excellent reconstructive option for similarly sized defects of the apical region that border the melolabial fold (Fig. 8.12). Once again, the inferior Burow’s triangle is designed along the RSTLs of the upper lip. The arc of the rotation flap is designed from the superior aspect of the defect and extends inferolaterally along the melolabial fold. The incision should be designed outside of the fold and then follow its curvature in order to maintain both lip height and proper position of the melolabial fold upon medial rotation and closure. Undermining takes place laterally in

the subcutaneous–orbicularis oris junction of the lip and the flap is both rotated and advanced medially to close the defect. The repair is confined within the cutaneous lateral upper lip subunit and suture lines are well camouflaged within the melolabial fold offering excellent cosmetic outcomes. A variation on this repair displaces the inferior Burow’s triangle along the lateral alar crease extending to the alar sill, offering superior camouflaging of incision lines along subunit junctions.
Fig. 8.12 Rotation flap. (a) Apical region defect bordering the melolabial fold. (b) Flap sutured. (c) Final result.

Both the crescentic advancement and rotation flaps can be utilized for larger defects of the apical region by extending the inferior Burow’s triangle through the VCJ and onto the vermilion as described for primary linear closure earlier. However, for larger defects of the apical region, specifically those that abut the nasal ala and the melolabial fold, V-Y advancement flaps, traditionally referred to as island pedicle flaps (IPF), may be better a reconstructive option.15 Unlike other advancement flaps that are pulled into place, the V-Y flap is mobilized as a subcutaneous island that is pushed toward the primary defect through closure of the secondary defect. The V-Y flap is designed with its leading edge along the inferolateral aspect of the defect and its axis parallel to the melolabial fold. The two limbs of the triangular incision should be placed along boundary lines whenever possible. The superior lateral limb of the V-Y flap is placed along the melolabial fold to preserve this boundary and for optimal camouflage. The incision should be carried outside of the fold and then mimic its curvature in order to both maintain lip height and properly position the melolabial fold upon closure. Depending on the proximity of the defect’s inferior margin to the vermilion, the inferior limb can be well camouflaged along

the VCJ (Fig. 8.13). Expanding the defect superiorly to the alar base or inferiorly to the vermilion through removal of intervening skin may be necessary to facilitate this placement and avoid transection of the RSTLs by the inferior scar line. The width of the flap should match the widest diameter of the defect and its length should be at least twice that diameter along the axis of the flap.16 Gradual tapering of the limbs to meet at an angle no more than 30 degrees minimizes any upward or lateral tension on the oral commissure upon closure.

Perforators from the facial artery as it follows along the melolabial fold prior to becoming the angular artery offer an abundant vascular supply to the V-Y flap in this region. The flap is incised and undermining of the surrounding skin just above the orbicularis muscle allows for optimal wound eversion and limits potential for a trapdoor effect.8 Because of the robust vascularity of the perioral tissue, the superior and inferior edges of the pedicle can be thinned to both match the depth of the defect and maximize mobility, without compromising the flap. The centrally located blood supply makes the V-Y flap more resistant to ischemia compared to other random-pattern flaps. A skin hook is used to carefully elevate the flap to assess mobility and ensure a tension-free reach. The advancing edge of the flap and/or the defect is rounded or squared off to create the best fit and minimize pincushioning. After meticulous hemostasis, the flap’s leading edge is first sutured to the superomedial margin of the defect with a single 6–0 polypropylene suture to ensure flap position. The dermal edges of the primary and secondary defects are then approximated with 5–0 polyglactin 910 suture. This dermal suturing pushes the flap tissue into the defect, equally distributing the tension along both limbs of the flap, supporting the weight of the flap, and minimizing upward or lateral tension on the oral commissure. The epidermis is closed with 6–0 polypropylene suture to perfect epidermal approximation. Absorbable, braided sutures such as polyglactin 910 are used to place epidermal sutures at the VCJ if applicable.

The excellent tissue match, inconspicuous placement of incisional scars, and abundant vascular supply make the V-Y advancement flap a reliable repair in both viability and aesthetic results. When not placed along the VCJ, the visibility of the scar from the inferior limb represents a potential disadvantage of the V-Y flap, as does the potential for a trapdoor effect. However, this can be minimizing with adequate undermining and debulking of the flap. Mild pincushioning can be treated postoperatively with intralesional steroid and 5-fluorouracil injections.
Defects adjacent to the vermilion border and larger defects greater than 1 cm of the mid to lower lateral subunit are best reconstructed with flaps that

hide suture lines within the RSTLs, vermilion border, and the melolabial fold. A variety of advancement flaps can be utilized to tap into tissue laxity of the lateral lip, melolabial fold, and cheek. Depending on the defect size and proximity to the vermilion border or alar crease, the defect may be expanded to these boundaries to improve flap movement and scar camouflage.

Similar to primary closure, advancement flaps involve tissue movement horizontally but almost exclusively use lateral laxity as to minimize distortion of the philtral columns (Fig. 8.14). After careful marking of the vermilion border prior to anesthetic, the advancement flap is designed with an inferior horizontal incision extending laterally from the defect’s inferior edge along the vermilion border with approximately a 3:1 length-to-width ratio. The flap is then undermined just above the orbicularis on the cutaneous lip and within the subcutaneous plane on the cheek to provide adequate flap mobility and allow closure under minimal tension as to avoid distortion of the philtrum. The superior Burow’s triangle is placed parallel to the radial RSTLs of the upper lip and can be taken prior to or after flap advancement to better exact the amount of redundant tissue. The variations of advancement flap include those with excision of both superior and inferior Burow’s triangles, which can be excised in a variety of positions and those which avoid excision of the inferior, or secondary, triangle through suturing out the tissue redundancy.17 Placement of the secondary Burow’s triangle can strategically be placed along the lower lip’s VCJ, marionette line, or taken in crescentic fashion along the horizontal incision (Fig. 8.15).

The flap is advanced medially and a key suture is place at the inferior aspect of the defect and leading edge of the flap just above the vermilion, taking care to properly align the VCJ. Dermal sutures are placed with 5–0 polyglactin 910 to bring together the subcutaneous tissues of the vertical wound edges followed by an epidermal running suture with 6–0 polypropylene. At the VCJ, 5–0 polyglactin 910 is used to place interrupted epidermal sutures using the rule of halves to evenly distribute any redundancy.

Larger defects that require significant medial advancement may require extension of the horizontal incision laterally beyond the vermilion and inferior to the commissure following the melolabial fold for adequate
movement while the superior Burow’s triangle can be carried into the perialar crease in a crescentic fashion. This allows even greater flap mobility and camouflaging of scars (Fig. 8.16; ▶Video 8.1).

Because laterally based flaps are slightly wedgeshaped, there is a tendency for the vermilion border to be pushed down with medial advancement along the vermilion border. This becomes most important with larger advancement flaps and may require trimming of their inferior edge to avoid distortion of the vermilion border. Blunting of the melolabial fold may occur when cheek skin is advanced into the upper lip. This can be limited by placement of a periosteal suture that tacks the undersurface of the flap to the underlying periosteum of the pyriform aperture of the maxilla to reestablish the melolabial fold at its original position.18,​19 In the editors’ experience, the melolabial fold does have an inherent tendency to reestablish over time; however, this is not universal.

Defects of the cutaneous lateral upper lip can often involve the adjacent vermilion and provide a reconstructive challenge. In these cases, adjunct flaps are best used to repair each cosmetic subunit and properly reposition the VCJ. An advancement flap or a V-Y advancement flap in combination with a partial mucosal advancement flap is an ideal reconstructive option to repair both cutaneous and vermilion defects, respectively. This method of closure ensures optimal tissue match for the respective subunits as well as precise recreation of the VCJ in its proper location. The advancement flap is designed in typical fashion as described earlier. After the cutaneous defect is repaired, acute Burow’s triangles are taken laterally off the vermilion defect and the mucosa is undermined just above the orbicularis oris to allow advancement of the mucosa to meet the cutaneous flap edge at the newly established VCJ. In the cases where the defect’s long axis is horizontally oriented, a superiorly based V-Y flap can be used in combination with mucosal advancement with excellent results.20 Incision lines are well hidden along the VCJ inferiorly and in the RSTLs of the upper lip and melolabial fold superiorly (Fig. 8.17). A mucosal graft can be used as an alternative to a mucosal advancement flap and is typically harvested from the wet mucosa of the lower lip. However, disadvantages of the graft include creation of an additional wound to close and heal at the harvest site and the enforcement of strict limitations in lip movements for up to 2 weeks to minimize disruption of the graft–bed contact.

A wedge repair of the lip is a modification of a primary linear closure where intervening muscle and subcutaneous tissue are excised to prevent bulging at the closure line. This technique is particularly useful for larger defects (1–2 cm) on the lower half of the upper lip that are fullthickness or deep partialthickness, especially when the vermilion is involved or closure of only the cutaneous defect will push down the VCJ. Partial-thickness wedge resection can be used for defects where the muscular defect is smaller than the cutaneous defect. A wedge of muscular tissue is removed to create straight wound edges of muscle prior to approximation with an absorbable plication suture. An advancement flap can then be used to repair the cutaneous defect.21

Full-thickness wedge repair entails a multilayer primary V-shaped closure (Fig. 8.18). This method can be safely utilized for defects up to one- fourth to one-third the width of the upper lip, depending on an individual’s skin laxity, with minimal risk of microstomia or distortion.13,​22 A composite, full-thickness wedge of mucosa-muscle-skin is resected to a varying height depending on the defect size. Larger defects may require resection extending to the gingival sulcus. Inherent elasticity of the lip tissue obviates the need for undermining during lip wedge repair. The three layers of tissue are best approximated with four layers of suture: mucosa with fast-absorbing suture, muscle with long-acting absorbable suture, dermis and subcutaneous tissue with long-acting absorbable sutures, and the dermis and epidermis with nonabsorbable sutures.23 Typically the muscle is repaired first to facilitate approximation of the wound edges and minimize tension during closure of the remaining layers. When reapproximating the muscle, it is important to incorporate the most superficial portion that lies just beneath the vermilion in order to avoid notching. Next, the subcutaneous tissue is closed with dermal sutures, followed by placement of the mucosal and epidermal sutures. As with primary linear closure, precise placement of dermal sutures to realign the VCJ is essential for an acceptable cosmetic outcome. While braided absorbable sutures are used epidermally to approximate the vermilion, nonabsorbable polypropylene sutures are used for the cutaneous closure. Disadvantages of the lip wedge repair include bleeding due to transection of the labial arteries, a time-consuming four-layer repair, and the potential for lateral distortion of the philtrum due to excess tension at closure.

Full-thickness defects that involve more than one-third the width of the upper lip represent a reconstructive challenge. Repair by wedge resection or local cutaneous flaps for these large defects risks microstomia, free margin distortion, ischemia, and dehiscence due to excessive tension. In these cases, the lip-switch flap is a better repair option, as it offers a full-thickness tissue substitution with appropriate thickness, restoration of the orbicularis oris sphincter, and its own vermilion and mucosa to match that of the recipient site (Fig. 8.19). The design, originally described by Sabattini, has undergone several modifications and is commonly referred to as the Abbe– Estlander flap.24,​25,​27

Fig. 8.19 Lip-switch flap (Abbe–Estlander flap). (a) Near full- thickness defect involving more than one-third the length of the upper lip. Abbe flap design marked along with the melolabial fold and vermilion subunit boundaries. (b) Full-thickness defect completed and flap incised. (c) Flap pivoted nearly 180 degrees on a lateral pedicle containing the labial artery. (d) Flap and donor site sutured. (e,f) Final result (after pedicle divided and flap inset at 3 weeks). Patient declined revision of upper vermilion-cutaneous junction step-off. (These images are provided courtesy of Christopher J. Miller, MD.)

For upper lip defects, the Abbe interpolation flap is designed as a triangular full-thickness segment of tissue from the lower lip with a width slightly smaller than half of the defect and a height that matches that of the defect. By designing a flap half the width of the defect, the length of the upper and lower lip remain proportional. The labial artery is left intact on one side to provide a pedicle, either medially or laterally based to best facilitate flap transfer. For very laterally located defects involving the commissure, the pedicle should be based medially and then transposed around the oral commissure so that the reconstruction can be achieved in a single stage, as described by Estlander.27 It is important to remember the

labial artery courses between the mucosa and orbicularis oris just beneath the posterior vermilion line as to not transect the vascular supply during flap incision. The pedicle includes a cuff of tissue around the artery to ensure venous drainage. The flap is rotated almost 180 degrees about its pedicle to insert into the upper lip defect. Both the donor site and the flap are sutured in the standard four-layer fashion, described earlier, to carefully approximate the tissue layers, especially the muscle, and realign the VCJ. As with other staged interpolation flaps, the pedicle is divided and the flap inset at 3 weeks. Food intake is limited to liquids and soft foods to avoid chewing while the pedicle is attached.

Although the return of quality muscle movement to the flap is variable, motor reinnervation begins after a few months and becomes increasingly normal during the first year.28,​29 By 1 year after transfer, sensory function returns to near normal with the exception of temperature detection, which can remain impaired.28 The prolonged phase of denervation and distortion of the oral commissure, often requiring commissure plasty, are major disadvantages to the lip-switch repair. Although lip-switch flaps can also be utilized for full-thickness defects of the lower lip, they are not an ideal reconstructive method in these cases due to philtral distortion if the upper lip donor site is used.

As the focus point of the upper lip, the philtrum carries significant aesthetic importance. This delicately shaped subunit is formed by the decussation of the orbicularis oris muscle and consists of a central concavity bounded by parallel convex philtral columns representing the insertion points of the contralateral muscles.30,​31 Defects involving the philtrum pose a significant challenge for the reconstructive surgeon. The philtrum is relatively void of crease lines found elsewhere on the upper lip and has a limited reservoir of available skin for reconstruction and a dynamic topography, all of which add to the complexity of its repair. The approach to defects of the philtral subunit (Fig. 8.20) and the most common reconstructive options are reviewed in the following.

Secondary intention can be an option for small defects within the philtral concavity; however, this option is rarely chosen, given the risk of excessive contraction leading to hypertrophic scarring, philtral distortion, and/or eclabium, especially near the vermilion border.

Primary linear closure can be utilized for small defects less than 50% the philtral width. The addition of an M-plasty at the inferior pole of the closure can be used to keep the incision lines within the philtral subunit, avoiding the extension onto the vermilion and preserving the Cupid’s bow (Fig. 8.21). Linear closure can be considered for larger defects; however, their use can result in blunting or flattening of the Cupid’s bow. Additionally, given the lengthening between the two ends of the defect with linear closures, larger defects closed in this fashion risk distortion of the free margin by depressing the underlying lip. This is referred to as a fish-mouth deformity if the inferior pole of the primary closure obliterates the Cupid’s bow and draws the VCJ to a point. Therefore, if a linear closure necessitates
extension past the VCJ, thereby defacing the Cupid’s bow, an alternative repair option should be chosen.

Fig. 8.21 Primary linear closure with M-plasty. (a) Small philtral defect approximating the philtral column. (b) Linear repair with M- plasty preserving Cupid’s bow. (c) Final result. (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

Similar-sized defects that are located over the philtral columns can be repaired with traditional or crescentic advancement flaps when they border the vermilion or nasal sill, respectively (Fig. 8.22, Fig. 8.23). These are performed in the same fashion described earlier for the lateral subunits with special care to accurately reposition the VCJ. Despite extension into adjacent subunits, the flap is designed so that incision lines are placed along the subunit junctions yielding excellent cosmetic results.

Fig. 8.22 Advancement flap. (a) Philtral column defect bordering the vermilion. Superior Burow’s triangle and vermilion-cutaneous junction marked. (b) Advancement flap sutured with incision lines along cosmetic subunit borders.

Fig. 8.23 Crescentic advancement flap. (a) Philtral column defect bordering the nasal sill. Inferior Burow’s triangle extending to mucosal vermilion and perialar crescent marked. (b) Advancement flap sutured in place. (c) Final result.

The Cupid’s bow of the vermilion lip defines the inferior region of the philtrum, and its intricate contour is marked by a concavity in the lower philtrum and a distinctive curvilinear vermilion border. It is a central structure at the junction of multiple subunits (vermilion, cutaneous lateral

upper lip, and philtrum), and so, defects in this area often involve more than one subunit. Importantly, when repairing defects of the central cutaneous lip that reside in or involve the lower portion of the philtrum, this distinctive landmark must be recreated. An ideal repair will restore the original contour, shape, and position of the Cupid’s bow, which vary between individuals based on age, race, actinic damage, smoking, and previous alternations including intradermal fillers and/or surgery.

A modification of the mucosal advancement flap, referred to as the “Seagull flap,” is a reconstructive option for defects involving the Cupid’s bow that are less than one-third the philtral height (Fig. 8.24).32 Design of the flap begins with careful marking of the VCJ and philtral columns for orientation, followed by a redrawing of the Cupid’s bow emanating from or incorporating the superior aspect of the defect. Bilateral apices align with the philtral columns, while the concavity is maintained at midline. Lateral incisions are extended and brought together at 30 degrees to avoid standing cones. After excision of two lateral Burow’s triangles, superficial undermining is performed predominantly above the orbicularis on the superior cutaneous flap and to less extent submucosally on the vermilion as to avoid excessive elevation of the vermilion lip. The key suture is placed midline and reestablishes the position of the notch of the Cupid’s bow. The advancement flaps are then brought together with a single layer of interrupted soft braided absorbable sutures (5–0 polyglactin 910) along the remainder of the flap’s leading edge to recreate the VCJ. Accurate positioning of the VCJ is of upmost importance for optimal aesthetic outcome, as described earlier. Increased gum showing when smiling is a potential downside to this repair.

Fig. 8.24 Seagull flap. (a) Cupid’s bow defect. Cupid’s bow redrawn with subunit borders and lateral Burow’s triangles marked. (b) Lateral Burow’s triangles excised. (c) Superficial undermining above the muscle. (d) Flap sutured. (e) Short-term result (1-week follow-up). (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

Repair of the Cupid’s bow using two opposing rhombic flaps has also been described.33 Each flap is designed with a vertical incision extending outward from the center of the superior or inferior edge of the defect and a lateral incision. The superior rhombic flap is elevated from the cutaneous lip and transposed to replace the cutaneous portion of the defect, while the inferior rhombic flap is elevated and transposed, from either the ipsi- or the contralateral side, to replace the vermilion portion of the defect. Placement of a half-buried horizontal mattress stitch (5–0 polypropylene) at the point of maximum tension is used to close the secondary defect of each flap before trimming of their abutting edges to recreate the curvilinear vermilion border. While subcutaneous sutures are placed with 5–0 polyglactin 910, epidermal sutures are placed using polypropylene for the superior flap and 5–0 silk or polyglactin 910 for the inferior flap. This repair offers an alternative approach for effectively recreating the philtral curvature and curvilinear border of the Cupid’s bow.

V-Y advancement flaps are an excellent reconstructive option for defects of the philtrum that are too wide for primary linear closure (up to 1.5 times the philtral width) but are still less than 50% the philtral height (Fig. 8.25).34 The flap is designed as a triangle extending superiorly off the defect with its apex at or even slightly onto the columella if necessary. The triangle is incised, and undermining takes place in the superficial subcutaneous plane laterally. The editors often undermine deeply with a combination of blunt and sharp undermining to achieve appropriate flap movement. The inferior and superior edges of the flap can be freed from the underlying muscular attachments to a small extent to allow movement without compromising the vascular supply. If there is still inadequate mobility, it may be necessary to eliminate the muscular attachments entirely and convert the triangular flap into a Burow’s graft rather than risk distortion of the vermilion under excessive tension. The V-Y flap is advanced inferiorly and a key suture is placed between the leading edge of the flap and the inferior aspect of the defect. If a defect lies above the VCJ, it may be necessary to first remove the cutaneous tissue between the defect and the vermilion as to optimally camouflage the suture line along the VCJ. Subcutaneous sutures are occasionally needed; otherwise, the secondary defect and lateral edges of the flap are closed primarily with nonabsorbable running or interrupted epidermal sutures (6–0 polypropylene), and the VCJ is reestablished with absorbable interrupted epidermal sutures (5–0 polyglactin 910). If the defect also involves the vermilion lip, a mucosal advancement flap should be performed in addition to the V-Y advancement, as described earlier. This ensures proper positioning of the VCJ, well- camouflaged suture lines, and optimal aesthetic results. Alternatively, a mucosal V-Y flap can be designed inferiorly to repair the vermilion defect, meeting the cutaneous flap to recreate the VCJ.35,​36 The mucosal V-Y is designed inferior to the defect onto the vermilion, and its execution is identical to the superior V-Y, except undermining is within the submucosal plane, and interrupted epidermal absorbable braided sutures (5–0 polyglactin 910) are used to close the secondary defect and secure the flap in a single layer.

Fig. 8.25 V-Y advancement with partial mucosal advancement flap. (a) Philtral defect with vermilion involvement. (b) Superiorly based V-Y advancement flap and partial mucosal advancement flap sutured into place with precise recreation of the vermilion- cutaneous junction and Cupid’s bow. (c) Final result.

As with V-Y advancement flaps in other locations, there is risk of pincushioning, which can be minimized with adequate undermining, proper sizing, and insetting, and treated with intralesional corticosteroid or 5- fluorouracil injections. Particular to philtral repair, excessive upward tension can displace the vermilion and/or cause eclabium. Limiting selection of this repair for defects less than 50% the philtral height will decrease this risk, as will adequate undermining and conversion to Burow’s graft if needed. The incision lines within the relatively smooth surface of the sulcus can sometimes be cosmetically displeasing and improved with laser resurfacing or manual dermabrasion.

A variation of the V-Y advancement flap referred to as the “pincer flap,” originally described by Dr. David Brodland, can be used to reconstruct the Cupid’s bow when defects of the lower sulcus are too large for repair by the seagull flap but still less than 50% of the philtral height (Fig. 8.26).37 The repair is designed and executed identically to that of the superiorly based V- Y flap, but the two corners of the advancing edge are rotated medially and sutured together. This both increases the size of the flap and tethers the flap down to better reconstruct the concavity of the Cupid’s bow.

Fig. 8.26 Pincer flap with partial mucosal advancement flap. (a) Cupid’s bow defect with superiorly based V-Y advancement flap and lateral vermilion Burow’s triangles marked. (b) Flap incised and lateral Burow’s triangles removed. (c) Two corners of the advancing edge are rotated medially and sutured together creating a concavity. Partial mucosal advancement with key sutures placed. (d) Flaps sutured in place. (e) Final result.

Larger defects of the philtrum, greater than 50% the philtral height, are at increased risk for eclabium development.22 When unable to be repaired with local skin flaps, FTSGs can be utilized for these defects; however, it is important to recognize several considerable limitations. Color and texture match of tissue in this cosmetically sensitive area is difficult, unless the defect is small enough to utilize a Burow’s graft, which offers an excellent match.8 In order to obtain adequate tissue, grafts are typically harvested from the pre- or postauricular skin. These sites offer a less-than-ideal match in many cases and yield an unacceptable cosmetic result for the hair-bearing upper lip in men. Although less common in the concavity of the philtrum, FTSGs are at risk for pincushioning and contraction that threatens eclabium, particularly with deeper defects.34 For this reason, the use of FTSGs is limited by the depth of the defect.

When appropriate, the defect can first be expanded to enhance symmetry or to remove the entire subunit to best conceal scar lines along cosmetic borders. FTSGs can also be used in combination with repairs of the lateral subunit to limit the recipient bed within the confines of the philtral subunit (Fig. 8.27). Once harvested, subcutaneous fat is trimmed from the undersurface of the flap and it is shaped to match the defect. Meticulous suturing with 6–0 polypropylene both secures the grafts and approximates the dermis of the graft with that of the wound edge, maximizing viability and cosmesis.38

Fig. 8.27 Perialar advancement flap with full-thickness skin graft (FTSG). (a) Philtral defect extending beyond subunit borders. Philtral columns and perialar advancement flap marked. (b) Advancement flap performed to align wound edge with philtral column. FTSG sutured in place. Note FTSG limited to philtral subunit. (c) Final result.

Large, full-thickness defects of the philtrum that are restricted to the central portion of the upper lip can be repaired with a lip-switch flap of similar size transferred from the lower lip to provide restoration of the complete aesthetic unit and restore the subunit’s cosmetic borders, as described earlier.39 Large philtral defects that extend onto the adjacent lateral lip or are too deep for FTSG can be repaired with bilateral advancement flaps. The details of their execution are also described earlier. It is important to remember that the flap is undermined above the orbicularis on the cutaneous lip and extensively within the subcutaneous plane on the medial cheek as needed for adequate mobility. With large advancement flaps, incisions may be extended inferiorly beyond the vermilion below the commissure and superiorly into the perialar crease in

crescentic fashion to both avoid distortion and camouflage scar lines. If there is vermilion involvement, a mucosal advancement flap is used to repair the vermilion subunit independently. When necessary, a periosteal stitch can be used to reestablish the melolabial fold and prevent its blunting with cheek advancement.

8.3.4 Cutaneous Lower Lip The approach to cutaneous lower lip reconstruction is relatively simplified when compared to that of the cutaneous upper lip and can be divided into defects with and without vermilion involvement and further by defect depth (Fig. 8.28). Many of the repair techniques described for the upper lip are also excellent options in this subunit.

Similar to primary linear closures of the cutaneous lateral upper lip, those of the cutaneous lower lip should be positioned along the RSTL, however, subtle they may be. The length of the incision can be shortened with the use of an M-plasty, particularly when avoiding extension past the VCJ or labiomental crease. Chin repair options are discussed in Chapter 9 of this book.
When primary linear closures cannot be contained within the subunit, advancement flaps are an ideal option. Although the tissue reservoirs on the

cutaneous lower lip differ slightly from that of the upper lip, traditional and V-Y advancement flaps similarly tap into inferolateral laxity of the cheek or chin and are designed to hide incision lines along the radial RSTL, vermilion border, and melolabial fold or marionette line (Fig. 8.29). If there is vermilion involvement of the defect, a mucosal advancement flap is used to repair the vermilion defect in conjunction with the cutaneous flap (Fig. 8.30). The execution of these flaps is identical to that described for the cutaneous upper lip. Although often unnecessary, a bilateral A-T advancement flap can also be utilized if unilateral motion is restricted resulting in excessive tension. Horizontal incisions should be placed along the vermilion border or labiomental crease for best concealment and an M- plasty can be utilized to avoid extension of the vertical incisions onto the vermilion or through the labiomental crease.

Fig. 8.29 Advancement flap. (a) Cutaneous lower lip defect bordering the vermilion-cutaneous junction. (b) Advancement flap sutured in place with inferior Burow’s triangle incision along the radial relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs). (c) Final result with incision lines well hidden along the RSTLs and vermilion border.

Fig. 8.30 V-Y advancement with partial mucosal advancement flap. (a) Cutaneous lower lip defect with vermilion involvement. (b) Inferiorly based V-Y advancement flap and partial mucosal advancement flap sutured into place with precise recreation of the vermilion-cutaneous junction. (c) Final result.

Transposition flaps can also be utilized to repair large defects on the cutaneous lower lip.40 The inferiorly based melolabial transposition flap is ideal for large defects involving the lateral cutaneous lower lip (and chin) that border the melolabial fold or marionette line (Fig. 8.31). These flaps tap into tissue laxity of the medial cheek and allow for significant tissue mobility. The flap’s medial edge extends superiorly from the defect along the melolabial fold where it meets its lateral edge at a 30-degree angle. The flap is incised and thoroughly undermined in the subcutaneous fat to allow a tension-free transposition over the oral commissure to the primary defect. A key suture is first placed to close the secondary defect. The inferior Burow’s triangle is excised and the flap trimmed to match the defect edge. Dermal sutures are placed to secure the flap position, followed by epidermal sutures to appose skin edges. Careful thinning of the flap and thorough undermining help eliminate a bulky appearance to the flap, and the resulting incision lines of the secondary defect are well hidden in the melolabial fold. When utilizing this repair, one must consider the asymmetry of the cheeks and melolabial folds that may result. Additionally, the horizontal tension vectors of this repair may blunt the ipsilateral marionette line creating another point of asymmetry. Intradermal fillers can be utilized postoperatively to help mitigate this asymmetry.

(b) Flap incised, undermined, and elevated. Inferior Burow’s triangle excised. (c) Flap transposed with minimal tension to cover primary defect. (d) Key suture in place closing secondary defect. (e) Flap completely sutured. (f) Final result. (These images are provided courtesy of Stanislav N. Tolkachjov, MD.)

A lip wedge repair is considered the standard method of reconstruction for deep partial or full-thickness defects and can be used for those involving up to one-third, or even one-half, of the width of the lower lip with minimal risk of microstomia or distortion of the subunit.1 Although these guidelines are helpful, one must consider the inherent laxity of the skin on an individual basis to avoid undesirable outcomes. If the defect is small, limited removal of mucosa and muscle no further than the VCJ may be sufficient to reduce bulging at the free margin. In general, as the defect enlarges, the height of the full-thickness wedge may increase as necessary to the height of the gingival sulcus (Fig. 8.32). A W-plasty can be incorporated into the lower lip wedge design in order to avoid extension below the labiomental crease. After composite resection of the mucosa- muscle-skin wedge, the three layers of tissue are approximated with four

layers of sutures, as described for the upper lip wedge, without the need for undermining. Priority is placed on restoration of the orbicularis muscle sphincter as the ability to retain intraoral contents relies heavily on its function in the lower lip.3 As always, precise realignment of the VCJ is crucial to ensure the best possible cosmetic outcome.

Fig. 8.32 Wedge repair. (a) Vermilion-cutaneous, full-thickness lower lip defect. (b) Wedge repair sutured in place with four-layer technique. (c) Final result. (These images are provided courtesy of John A. Zitelli, MD.)

Full-thickness defects that involve more than one-third of the lower lip represent a considerable reconstructive challenge given the risk for microstomia and free margin distortion with the use of wedge repair or local cutaneous flaps. In these cases, circumoral, full-thickness rotation- advancement flaps can be utilized to transfer adequate amounts of tissue around the oral commissure as either single or bilateral opposing flaps and restore a functional muscle sphincter. The Karapandzic technique is ideal for centrally located defects and is typically based on two sliding rotation flaps formed by bilateral partial-thickness incisions extending from the inferior border of the defect along the labiomental crease and melolabial fold, creating flaps with a uniform width (Fig. 8.33).41,42,–43 The incisions are made through the skin into the subcutaneous tissue and a separate, second incision through the mucosa on the deep surface of each flap can be reserved if additional movement is required.1,​13 For lateral defects, the contralateral flap can be made longer to avoid distortion of the central upper lip.1 Key to this reconstruction is careful preservation of the neurovascular

structures while separating the flap from the adjacent facial tissue. This allows for advancement of the myocutaneous flaps along with maximum vascular supply and optimal sensory and motor function. After medial advancement, the mucosa, muscle, and skin are closed in a four-layer fashion identical to that of the wedge repair. This reconstruction offers the unique advantage of preserving both the sensibility of the lips and motor function of the oral aperture. Additionally, the repair is performed in a single stage and suture lines are well placed in natural creases to optimize the aesthetic outcome. While in some patients the technique can be used for defects up to two-thirds the width of the lower lip, the variation in lip laxity among individuals, especially in relation to age, may result in limiting microstomia, proportional to the defect. A rounded distortion of the oral commissure and varying degrees of microstomia are major limitations of this reconstructive method. Altered sensation and tightness of the lip are the most commonly reported complications following the Karapandzic flap repair, and both have been shown to typically improve with time.44
Additionally, the Karapandzic flaps are rarely utilized for full-thickness defects of the upper lip as flap advancement past midline results in unacceptable philtral distortion.

(b) Flaps of uniform width incised to the subcutaneous tissue. (c) Myocutaneous flaps dissected with careful preservation of the

The Bernard–Burrow–Webster technique can be used for total or subtotal lip defects of the lower lip to avoid microstomia.45,​47 Two sliding flaps are formed by bilateral sets of horizontal, full-thickness incisions, both extending laterally about one-half the length of the defect, one from the commissure and one from the inferior border of the defect along the labiomental crease. The flaps are advanced medially and sutured in a layered fashion, as above, with Burow’s triangles taken along the melolabial fold and the mucosa advanced to restore the vermilion. Although the oral aperture is preserved, this technique transects the orbicularis oris muscle and obliterates the majority of neurovascular structures, resulting in sensory loss and oral incontinence.

Not unlike other areas of the face, bleeding, infection, and suboptimal scarring can complicate repairs of the perioral region. The abundant musculature and high mobility of the lip makes the perioral region especially vulnerable to postoperative bleeding and hematomas. The same factors can contribute to scar hypertrophy, inversion, or contraction leading to distortion of the free margin. Additionally, the proximity to the nose and oral mucosa increases the risk of bacterial contamination and infection. Systematic preoperative preparation, meticulous intraoperative hemostasis, and detailed postoperative instructions and wound care are essential to limit the incidence of these complications and maximize cosmetic results.

Prior to surgery, the face should be prepped with povidone–iodine solution. If the mucosal surface is breached during surgery, prophylactic antibiotics may be prescribed for 1 week starting the day of surgery. A secure pressure dressing is placed postoperatively and is left in place for 24 to 48 hours. Once removed, the patient is instructed to wash the area gently with soap and water and apply healing ointment (i.e., Aquaphor or petrolatum ointment) covered with a light dressing (i.e., Band-Aid) twice daily until suture removal at 1 week. For the first 48 hours, patients should

be instructed to limit movement, including talking and chewing, of the perioral region and encouraged to have a liquid or soft food diet. Detailed instructions on postoperative care are provided in Chapter 12.

Particular limitations and potential complications of each reconstructive technique are reviewed in the corresponding sections. However, it is worth highlighting one complication that commonly plagues some repairs of the lip, pincushioning. As described earlier, this can be minimized at the time of repair with appropriate sizing and thinning of flaps and undermining of the skin surrounding the recipient site. Postoperatively, to help flatten the bulky tissue, intradermal steroid and 5-fluorouracil injections may be administered starting 4 to 6 weeks after surgery and continued until an acceptable cosmetic result is achieved.

Abstract The chin is a midline cosmetic subunit in which cutaneous malignancies are common. Mohs micrographic surgery provides the highest cure rates and smallest defects after extirpation of these lesions. Preoperative assessment of the patient’s normal anatomy is an important part of surgical planning. Delineation of any pronounced landmarks helps with designing reconstruction. Further, understanding resting skin tension lines along the convex chin can help the surgeon fashion a repair that is cosmetically pleasing. The baseline anatomy of the patient and suspected cosmetic outcomes should be discussed with the patient as much as possible. Curvilinear primary closures are a mainstay for reconstruction. For defects spanning a large portion of the chin, advancement and rotation flaps are excellent options and likely the most commonly used flaps. While larger defects may require transposition flaps harvested from adjacent submental neck or the skin of the jaw, care should be taken to take note of typical locations of the marginal mandibular nerve. Taking care to use sufficient undermining, release from the mentalis muscle near the wound edge and appropriate eversion of the wound edge will result in the best outcomes.

• Delineate the labiomental crease and any mental cleft that is present prior to infiltration of local anesthetic. • Assess thickness and mobility of the skin prior to infiltration of local anesthetic. • Align linear closures to fit the convex contour of the chin when it is pronounced. • Elongate Burow’s triangles to account for a pronounced convex chin. This may include extending the removal of a

standing cone to the submental neck. • Avoid crossing the labiomental crease with suture lines to avoid upward displacement of the vermilion. • With deeper defects, avoid crossing the mandible to prevent tethering of the scar to the underlying menton. • Rich muscular anatomy and anastomosing blood supply allow for durable flaps if undermined in the appropriate plane on the chin. • The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve lies lateral to the chin and should be avoided for larger reconstructions utilizing this tissue reservoir.

The chin is formed by a projection in the anterior-most portion of the mandible. It is bordered by the labiomental crease superiorly and the inferior extension of the nasolabial folds (or marionette lines) laterally (Fig. 9.1). The nasolabial folds generally become more obvious in older patients with more pronounced skin laxity. The lack of significant nasolabial folds or marionette lines in younger patients makes the lateral borders of the chin more ambiguous. The inferior border of the chin is defined by the inferior border of the anterior mandible. The chin has a variably, but generally dense fibrous subcutaneous tissue mass with insertions of the mentalis muscle, which originates from the medial portion of the mandible at the lateral incisors. This muscle wrinkles the skin of the chin and helps protrude the lower lip. Other muscles in this area include the inferior portion of the orbicularis oris superiorly, the depressor anguli oris, and the depressor labii inferioris laterally. The inferior border of the chin includes the medial insertions of the platysma muscle.

Resting skin tension lines follow a generally curvilinear or sickle-shaped course curving laterally along the rounded convex axis of the protruding mental prominence. The most obvious line of the lower face is often the labiomental crease, which should be identified prior to infiltration of local anesthetic. This line is of utmost importance in designing repairs of the chin. A natural surface anatomy feature of importance is the mental cleft, when present. This too should be identified with markings prior to infiltration of anesthetic. When linear closures and scars cross this line, an obvious and lasting deformity generally ensues, pushing the lower vermilion border upward and obliterating the labiomental crease. The lateral borders include a variable nasolabial fold or marionette line.

It is important to note the convexity of the chin, which varies with age. There is some structural loss of the mandibular prominence with bone resorption and aging as well as an increase in skin laxity, which can work to the advantage of the surgeon dealing with larger defects. While second intention healing is not classically advised on convex surfaces, the size and depth of the defect should be considered when approaching these wounds. If a Mohs layer can remove a tumor superficially in the presence of a bearded man, secondary intention healing can be the best option. Finally, this convexity leads to persistent standing cones when Burow’s triangles are not long enough to account for the convexity.

Danger zones of the chin include the inferior labial arteries superiorly and the marginal mandibular nerve at the most lateral portion. These are unlikely to be encountered on the chin proper. It is also important to note that the labiomental crease is the inferior border of the lower cutaneous lip,

which has variable thickness. The oral cavity can lie less than 1 cm from the skin at this point. When considering repairs for the chin, the lateral tissue reservoirs do contain the marginal mandibular nerve, and thus it should be identified by surface landmarks during design of reconstruction. On the chin proper, one may encounter the V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve (mental nerve), which provides sensory innervation to the chin and lower lip. The presence of this nerve root offers and easy solution to anesthesia via regional block of this area and can be utilized for patient comfort.

• Second intention healing: This is reserved for superficial defects in men who normally grow beards or very broad defects where secondary intention is felt to appear superior to a full-thickness skin graft. • Primary (side-to-side) closure: Primary closures should not cross the labiomental crease if at all possible. Upward distortion of the lower lip can occur when the labiomental crease is crossed. • Bilateral advancement flap (O-T): Note this may have a component of rotation due to the convex nature of the chin and curved mental crease (this is a “go-to” flap for the chin). • V-Y advancement/island pedicle flap. • When there is lack of enough tissue laxity for above repairs:
– Unilateral or bilateral rotation flap (bilateral is reserved for defects near the midline). – Inferiorly and laterally based transposition flap/bilobed flap. – Full-thickness skin graft.

9.3.2 Healing by secondary intention The chin can heal very well when defects are shallow and broad. This may be suitable for all shallow defects but is most practical for defects that are too broad for primary closures and are shallow. If the defect is partial thickness and present in a man that normally grows a beard, it may be the preferred option for this location. If the defect includes subcutaneous fat, or obliterates follicular structures, a closure is likely the better option. Delayed repair after secondary intention healing can be a consideration for defects smaller than 1cm and no more than 3 to 5mm in depth. By allowing healing, the patient and clinician can assess the appearance and decide if closure is preferred. Facial hair preferences can change; thus, scar appearance on a clean-shaven face should be considered.

Primary closures on the chin are a mainstay for many Mohs defects. Midline or near-midline defects are common, and primary linear closures are common. Lateral defects will often appear better with a curvilinear design when oriented in a vertical fashion. This is best facilitated with the use of two concave lines on the medial side and a longer convex line on the lateral side (see Fig. 9.2). It is important to have the inner curve equal the length of the outer/broader curve by creating two concave lines on either end of the defect. Otherwise, the curve will have two skin edges of unequal length, leading to redundancy on the longer side. Undermining widely through the fibrous attachments of the mentalis muscle will facilitate movement of the edges of the defect and reduce tension on the wound. Insufficient undermining may result in a dimpled or depressed scar in this location due to the muscular attachments into the dermis.

Primary closures should not cross the labiomental crease. If a primary closure will require crossing this crease, it should be altered in some way. This will generally make an O-T flap the best option. Similarly, if the primary closure will cross the mandibular prominence inferiorly, it may

result in tethering of the scar at this prominence. A bilateral advancement flap with inferior incisions along the mandibular border will provide less likelihood of tethering at the bony prominence, which can cause an unappealing visible difference from the frontal view.

Some defects may lend themselves to closure horizontally, or slightly angled. These are generally an exception to the rule that primary closures oriented vertically have a better long-term outcome. However, patients can have differing facial contours, laxity, and defects. As with any primary closure, it is sometimes advantageous to undermine the circular defect in all directions and assess where the natural skin tension vectors “want” to close the defect. Burow’s triangles should be long enough to account for the convexity of the chin. Otherwise, standing cone deformity is visible from many angles.

9.3.4 Bilateral Advancement (O-T flap) The O-T flap (bilateral, single tangent flap) is a go-to flap for chin repairs (see Fig. 9.3, Fig. 9.8, and Fig. 9.9). Often, the convexity of the chin requires removal of longer dog-ears, and often, they will extend through the labiomental crease. Whenever the defect requires removal of a dog-ear that will cross the labiomental crease, the crease should be used as the line that defines the superior border (or the horizontal incision) for an O-T flap. This crossing arm of the “T” will often be curvilinear, following the crease. This at times will appear more consistent with a bilateral rotation flap. If a defect is closer to the inferior border of the chin, the O-T flap can be flipped so that the horizontal line of the T is along the inferior border of the mandible (see Fig. 9.6). The inferior dog-ear should ideally not cross the most inferior edge of the mandible. Crossing this prominence can lead to tethering of the scar to the bony prominence. A tethered appearance is not a certainty, and linear closures can often produce very acceptable outcomes. If a defect is sizable enough that an inferior dog-ear should cross onto the submental neck, and the superior dog-ear would cross the labiomental crease, one should consider a bilateral double tangent (O-H) flap. Horizontal lines can hide well within the labiomental crease and just under the chin on the submental neck. The O-T flap can be tailored to the site regardless of whether it is midline, or more laterally (see Fig. 9.4). The vertical arm of the T should be designed toward the central point of the chin, much like the spokes of a wheel radiating from the hub (chin midpoint) to the outer wheel

(mental crease). When defects do not fall on midline, the dog-ear should follow the curvilinear shape of the relaxed skin tension lines on the chin. Again, this is generally a sickle shape curving laterally at the most convex point.
