Fig. 10.35 (a–c) Z-plasty. Multiple triangular flaps used to correct scar contracture–induced ectropion of the lower lid. (Reproduced from Thornton J, Carboy J. Facial Reconstruction after Mohs Surgery. New York: Thieme; 2018.)

Small full-thickness marginal defects can be closed by direct layered closure depending on the laxity of the eyelid (Fig. 10.36). In the upper eyelid, marginal defects up to 25 to 30% of eyelid length can be repaired primarily. In older individuals up to 40% of the upper eyelid can be closed directly. Excessive horizontal tension is less critical in the lower eyelid, so defects up to 30 to 40% of the lower eyelid margin can be closed primarily. Defects over 30 to 40% may require canthotomy and cantholysis, i.e., LCT release to provide few additional millimeters of margin elongation (see Fig. 10.38). When performed properly, the primary closure has best cosmetic results leaving an intact eyelid margin and full lash line in a single-stage procedure. As mentioned previously, “like-for-like” lamellar reapproximation must be performed to optimize the final functional and cosmetic result.

Fig. 10.36 Direct closure of the lower eyelid marginal defect. (a) 6-0 proline or silk is used to align and evert the lash line, by placing vertical mattress suture in a far-far near-near fashion. (b) The tarsus is reapproximated using 6–0 polyglactin sutures which are placed (c) partial thickness to avoid corneal abrasion. (d) The marginal stitch is then tied and left long so the ends can be incorporated in the skin closures, with the rest of the skin approximated with 7–0 prolene suture resulting in vertically oriented suture line.

When performing direct closure, meticulous approximation of the eyelid margin is of utmost importance. Direct closure recreates smooth margin contour and reconstitutes the lash line and the tarsal plate. If edges of the defect cannot be brought together without the tension or hammocking of the

lid under the globe, canthotomy and cantholysis should be performed with or without the frost suture. If the defect involves only partial thickness of the tarsus, a pentagonal excision (Fig. 10.37a) design is preferred to avoid standing cutaneous deformities. The incisions are performed perpendicularly to excise rectangle of the tarsus to the upper eyelid crease. From there, pointed incision toward the conjunctival fornix is carried only in the anterior lamella, completing the tip of the pentagon. Next, it is important to align and evert the lash line, which will prevent notching or step-off appearance. This is usually achieved by placing 6–0 prolene or silk vertical mattress suture though the gray line (Meibomian gland orifices) in a far-far near-near fashion. This will evert the wound edges and re- establish good alignment of the eyelid margin. The tarsus needs now to be reapproximated using 6–0 polyglactin sutures, placing in a partial thickness to avoid corneal abrasion and discomfort from exposed sutures. The upper eyelid usually requires four to five and lower two to three tarsal and subcutaneous sutures. To facilitate suture passage 2 to 3 mm of OOM should be dissected from the tarsal edges. The margin suture is then tied and left long so the ends can be incorporated in the skin closures, which are tied in the final stage with 7–0 prolene suture resulting in vertically oriented scar. The correct vs. incorrect designs of the pentagon are shown in Fig. 10.37b.

Fig. 10.37 (a) Direct closure of the marginal defect after conversion to pentagonal design. (A) Establish clean tarsal edges to avoid notching, extend the skin incision to form the triangular tip of pentagon above the horizontal lid margin (superior tarsal edge); (B) sutures passed through anterior two-third of the tarsal plate to avoid corneal irritation and eyelid retractors (levator aponeurosis or capsulopalpebral fascia); (C) vertical mattress sutures are used to approximate precisely the eyelid margin; and is (D) incorporated in the skin closure to avoid corneal irritation. (b) Correct vs. incorrect design of pentagonal wedge excision. The superior triangle has to be based above the tarsus to avoid eyelid margin notching or kinking. (a: Reproduced from Chen W. Oculoplastic Surgery: The Essentials. New York: Thieme; 2001.)

Lateral canthotomy (Fig. 10.38a, b) is performed by cutting horizontally through the canthus to the lateral orbital rim using Stevens tenotomy scissors. This splits the tendon in the inferior and superior components. Cantholysis is then performed by grasping the inferolateral eyelid (lower eyelid defects) or superolateral eyelid (upper eyelid defects) and pulling superiorly or inferiorly for the release of inferior crus (lower eyelid repair) or superior crus (upper eyelid repair). The canthotomy incision is typically left unclosed or can be sutured with 7–0 prolene in continuous manner.

Fig. 10.38 (a,b) Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis of the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (LCT) (above) incorporated in pentagonal design of the direct lower lid margin closure to release lateral tension (below). (Reproduced from Freitag S, Lefebvre D, Lee N, Yoon M. Eyelid Reconstruction. New York: Thieme; 2020.)

Initially described by Tenzel in 1978, the semicircular myocutaneous flap remains a valuable technique for closing defects occupying up to two-thirds of the lower eyelid (33–75%) (Fig. 10.39a–d, h–j; ▶Video 10.3) and upper eyelid (30–66%) (Fig. 10.39e–g, k–m). This flap is used when canthotomy and cantholysis do not provide sufficient mobilization to permit tension-free primary closure. The Tenzel flap is most successful when there is adequate lateral, canthal skin laxity and availability of at least a small segment of full-thickness eyelid on the lateral side of the defect. In cases where there is no tarsus on the lateral side of the wound, it is advisable to perform periosteal flap or posterior lamella graft for optimal results (see following text). With Tenzel flap, the canthotomy incision needs to be angled upward and outward starting following the curve of the opened lower eyelid margin below the lateral extent of the eyebrow approximately 2 to 3 cm lateral to the canthal angle. The design for the upper eyelid repairs is the mirror image of the one for the lower lids, and the curve follows the opened upper eyelid margin, and continues downward and laterally at the point 2 to 3 cm below the lateral extent of the brow. As with the primary closure the tarsal edges need to be smoothened vertically, and lateral canthotomy and cantholysis is performed. The flap is undermined and advanced medially to cover the defect. Lid margin sutures and tarsal sutures are placed in similar manner as with direct closure, to avoid conjunctiva penetration and globe irritation. The skin is closed with 7–0 prolene (eyelid) or 6–0 prolene (periocular skin and temple) as described before.

Fig. 10.39 Tenzel semicircular rotational flap design for lower (a–d) and upper (e–g) eyelid full-thickness marginal defects with cantholysis of the lower (b) and upper crus (f) of lateral canthal tendon. (Continued)

Fig. 10.39 Continued Fully executed Tenzel flap for post Mohs surgery defect after removal of left lower eyelid basal cell carcinoma (h, i) and right upper eyelid squamous cell carcinoma (k, l), with six-month follow-ups (j, m).

Lateral sagging of the eyelid can be prevented by fixation of the lateral flap tissue for superolateral orbital rim periosteum with 4–0 polyglactin suture. If there is need to improve lower eyelid contour, additional support may be necessary by performing periosteal flap (Fig. 10.40). The base of the flap is designed high at the arcus marginalis (midpupillary level), extending laterally at the 45-degree angle, approximately 8 to 10 mm wide to the length corresponding to the distance from the remaining tarsus to lateral orbital rim. This maneuver will recreate tight lower eyelid with proper posterior contour. Larger defects, without any tarsus left at the wound edge, would require stronger backing of the repaired anterior lamella by using auricular cartilage, hard palate mucosa, nasal chondromucosa, or tarsoconjunctival graft from the upper eyelid. With the periosteal flap, a mucosal graft or conjunctival advancement is not necessary. Mobilization

from the inferior fornix should be performed and sutured to the superior skin margin of a myocutaneous flap with 7–0 chromic gut or polyglactin sutures. Reconstruction of the canthal ligaments is less important with the upper eyelid procedures because the effects of gravity enhance upper lid position rather than opposing it as with lower lid. As with direct repair, meticulous reconstruction of the eyelid margin is critical to exclude keratinized epithelium, and prevent notching and trichiasis.

Fig. 10.40 a–c Periosteal inversion flap for the posterior lamella reconstruction of the temporal lower eyelid. The flap is angled 45 degrees so that the lower eyelid contour is maintained after the strip is reflected inferomedially. (Reproduced from Leatherbarrow B. Oculoplastic Surgery. 3rd ed. New York: Thieme; 2019.)

This pedicle flap described by William Hughes in 1937 is considered for large lower eyelid defects encompassing two-thirds to total lower eyelid loss (Fig. 10.41a–h). Vascular autogenous tarsus lined with conjunctiva is relatively ideal replacement for loss posterior lamella. The anterior lamella can be reconstructed with a myocutaneous flap or FTSG. The drawback of this repair technique is temporary obstruction of the vision for 7 to 45 days, i.e., until the second-stage procedure with pedicle division is performed. Nevertheless, it continues to be a highly effective and popular technique for reconstruction of large eyelid defects. The flap is harvested from the ipsilateral upper eyelid, always leaving 4 mm of the marginal tarsus intact. After retracting the upper eyelid over a Desmarres retractor, a caliper is used to mark the 4 mm of tarsus to remain attached to the lid margin. The caliper may then be used to measure the width of tarsus needed to reconstruct the lower eyelid, designed to be slightly less than the width of the defect on the lower eyelid and using the maximum height of the tarsus available. A 15c blade can be used to create the full-thickness tarsal incision, leaving the superior conjunctiva attached to the tarsus. The dissection then goes at the anterior side of the tarsus until the superior tarsal margin using blunt scissors. Then the scissors should be directed more posteriorly, i.e., behind the Müller’s muscle and anterior to conjunctiva to avoid incorporation of the muscle into the flap. The visualization of the plane of dissection can be facilitated by infiltration of local anesthetic. Care should also be taken to avoid injuring the vascular arcade at the superior tarsal border. The dissection continues until the conjunctival pedicle can be advanced inferiorly without the tension and sutured in the lower eyelid defect by using 6–0 polyglactin suture. Relaxing incisions can be made vertically at the medial and lateral conjunctival edges of the flap. Conjunctiva and retractors are advanced from the inferior fornix and secured for the lower border of the tarsoconjunctival flap. The superior tarsal border of newly reconstructed posterior lamella should approximate the presurgical eyelid margin. At this point the cornea will be covered and protected by conjunctival pedicle of the flap and the upper eyelid will rest roughly at midpupillary height. With the total lower eyelid loss, the Hughes flap will be secured with lateral or medial (or both) periosteal grafts which
will replace lost LCT or MCT. The anterior lamellar replacement may be fixated to the superior edge of the tarsus using a 7–0 polyglactin suture in a horizontal mattress fashion.

Fig. 10.41 (a–h) Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap for lower eyelid reconstruction. Full-thickness defect of the medial lower eyelid with the flap harvested leaving at least 4 mm distance superior to posterior upper lid margin (a); upper border of the tarsus in the flap aligned with the lower eyelid margin and sutured to remaining tarsus on the sides of the loser eyelid (b); anterior lamella reconstructed with full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) with the superior border of the conjunctiva sutures 1 to 2 mm above the border of the tarsus and pedicle divided after 2 to 4 weeks (c). (Continued)

Fig. 10.41 Continued Hughes flap planning and execution (d–f) with pedicle division and final result (g–h). (a–c: Reproduced from Codner M, McCord C. Eyelid & Periorbital Surgery. 2nd ed. New York: Thieme; 2016.)

Postoperatively, patient is instructed to use ophthalmic eye drops four times a day (gentamicin, ciprofloxacin). Because peripheral vision is obviously reduced, use of a metal eye shield is helpful to prevent inadvertent injury of the flap, graft, and eye itself from blunt trauma. Chromic sutures are left to dissolve, while silk or prolene nonabsorbable sutures must be removed in 1 week.

Second-stage reconstruction of the tarsoconjunctival flap is performed at 2 to 4 weeks. A narrow malleable retractor is inserted under the flap to protect cornea. The flap is separated at the intended position of the new lower eyelid margin where mucocutaneous margin is ideally placed anteriorly to the apex of the reconstructed eyelid. The transected edges can be left to heal by secondary intent at this point.

Tarsal transposition flap (Fig. 10.42a–c), described by Kersten in 1986, is a good option for defects involving lateral upper eyelid. It is an alternative to Tenzel flap, composite graft, and even Cutler-Beard flap (see Fig. 10.42) when the defect is predominantly lateral. It is a single-stage procedure, using local vascularized eyelid tissue rather than creating additional comorbidity from the donor site of the contralateral upper eyelid as a donor site for composite graft, or other options of replacing posterior lamella with chondromucosal graft, or ear cartilage. The remaining ipsilateral tarsus presents the source for the reconstruction of lost upper eyelid posterior lamella in this case. The anterior lamella can then be repaired with FTSG or myocutaneous flap. The flap is designed from superior, placing the incision from superior tarsus, at the 3 to 4 mm width, down to 1 to 2 mm above the upper lid margin. The flap is divided from OOM, and then pivoted 90 degrees and attached to LCT, or periosteal flap, whichever was the method used to reconstruct lateral canthal angle, with 5–0 polyglactin suture on S- 14 spatula needle using the “cross-sword” technique. Conjunctiva can now be advanced from superior fornix and be approximated to the flap with 7–0 chromic gut. The manipulation of the levator is not necessary since the existing attachments to medial part of the tarsus are adequate for proper eyelid elevation.

Fig. 10.42 Tarsal transposition flap. Superior border of the tarsus incised horizontally (a) followed by vertical tarsal incision creating inferiorly based transposition flap (b) which is then fixed to lateral canthal tendon (LCT) or lateral orbital rim (c).

Horizontal tarsoconjunctival transposition flap (Fig. 10.43a–e) is a way to mobilize more ipsilateral tarsus for lateral upper eyelid defects and is harvested by placing horizontal conjunctival incision parallel and approximately 3 to 4 mm from the eyelid margin. The width of the flap corresponds to the size of the defect, and the wound should be closed under mild tension. Incision is continued toward the fornix, LA is cut as well as the Müller’s muscle, and the incision completed further in the subconjunctival plane. Then, the flap is transposed horizontally into the defect and sutured to the tarsal edge of the remaining eyelid with interrupted 6–0 polyglactin stitches, without compromising the conjunctiva as explained before. The opposite side should be sutured for the remnant of lateral canthal ligament or periosteal flap as discussed above. The LA has to be engaged and advanced to be sutured to the superior part of the transposed tarsal flap. It is essential that the LA be advanced without retraction of the eyelid. If that is not possible, the aponeurosis should be allowed to retract and sutured to the conjunctiva above the tarsus. The patient should be asked to look up, so that appropriate height of the eyelid margin is confirmed. The anterior lamella can then be repaired as already explained above.

Fig. 10.43 Horizontal tarsoconjunctival transposition flap. (a–c) Flap harvested with the conjunctival incision 3 to 4 mm away and parallel to eyelid margin (a), separated from Müller’s muscle (b), transposed and sutured to medial tarsal border (c). Lateral side of the flap connected to remaining lateral canthal tendon (LCT) (d) and anterior lamella repaired with full thickness skin grafts (FTSG) (e). (Reproduced from Chen W. Oculoplastic Surgery: The Essentials. New York: Thieme; 2001.)

The reconstruction of the large defects of the upper eyelid is very challenging and no single operation can achieve all goals satisfactorily. Cutler-Beard flap is one of the best available techniques for total upper eyelid reconstruction (Fig. 10.44a–e). As already emphasized for the maintenance of corneal integrity, crisp vision, and patient comfort, the upper eyelid must have a 5- to 10-mm range of movement and dynamic blink. This flap does not provide rigid posterior lamella which may result in instability of the reconstructed eyelid margin over time. Hence, free tarsoconjunctival graft or free hard palate mucosal grafts, auricular cartilage, or donor sclera can be used for the support. The flap is designed on the lower eyelid along the inferior tarsal border and extended laterally to correspond the defect on the upper eyelid, which should be reshaped in the rectangular fashion. The flap is then extended inferiorly 15 to 20 mm toward the inferior conjunctival fornix, with the lid pulled superiorly over the Jaeger plate or similar lid guard to protect the cornea. After full- thickness blepharotomy is performed, the composite flap is now brought below the lower eyelid margin bridge and sutured to the defect of the upper eyelid. This composite flap consists of skin, OOM, lower lid retractors, and conjunctiva. First the conjunctival flap should be approximated using 6–0 plain gut. Then the posterior lamella replacement, i.e., auricular cartilage, should be placed and sutured with remnants of tarsus or canthal ligaments on each side of the upper eyelid defect. LA should be advanced and attached to the upper edge of the graft using 6–0 polyglactin suture. Finally, the skin muscle flap which was already separated from the conjunctiva should be attached to the anterior side of the graft, replacing anterior lamella.

Fig. 10.44 Cutler-Beard flap—full-thickness incision on the lower lid (a), anterior and posterior lamella separated with conjunctiva sutured to upper lid defect (b); ear cartilage graft in place (c) and skin-muscle part attached (d). The division with recreation of the upper lid margin occurs in 2 to 4 weeks. (Reproduced from Codner M, McCord C. Eyelid & Periorbital Surgery. 2nd ed. New York: Thieme; 2016.)

Inset of the flap can be performed in 2 to 4 weeks with the division cut about 2 mm below the desired upper eyelid margin. Upon resection, the longer piece on the conjunctival side is draped and sutured to the skin with 7–0 chromic gut suture, ensuring that the new upper eyelid margin is not keratinized. The inferior edge of the lower eyelid bridge is then freshened, and the bases of the lower eyelid flap sutured to the bridge in a layered fashion using 6–0 polyglactin for conjunctiva and retractors and 6–0 polypropylene for the skin. If there is a risk of lower eyelid ectropion, the
skin and orbicularis may need to be undermined and any horizontal laxity should be repaired with lateral tarsal strip procedure (see following text).

In 1983, Leone published a procedure similar to Hughes flap (“reverse Hughes flap”) but designed for the upper eyelid reconstruction up to the size of 70% of the margin. Here, the tarsoconjunctival flap is harvested from the lower eyelid posterior lamella, approximately 1.5 mm below the margin of the lower lid. Upon the flap release from retractors, tarsoconjunctival advancement flap (Fig. 10.45a–d) is brought upward and sutured to remaining tarsus of the upper eyelid, while inferior tarsal margin of the lower lid flap will become the lid margin of the upper eyelid. The anterior lamella is repaired by FTSG (postauricular skin) which adheres firmly to the tarsus, preventing the skin from overhanging against the globe. The advantage of this flap compared to Cutler-Beard flap is that it requires only tarsal/conjunctival portion and not full thickness of the lower eyelid for bridging the defect on the upper lid. Hence, 1.5 mm of remaining tarsal height on the lower lid should be enough to prevent ectropion more commonly seen with Cutler-Beard technique. The tarsal flap, regardless of being only several millimeters, provides enough stability to upper eyelid to keep the skin from rolling inward. It also eliminates the need for harvesting donor tissue for eyelid support like nasal chondromucosal graft or ear cartilage, as already described with Cutler-Beard technique. The division of the pedicle is planned in 2 to 4 weeks as with Cutler-Beard flap.

Fig. 10.45 Leone tarsal-conjunctival advancement flap. Incision made 1.5 mm from the posterior lid margin (a); flap is brought upward and sutured to remaining lid margin (b) and defect repaired with full-thickness skin grafts (FTSG) (c) donor site postauricular skin (not shown).

We have already emphasized that lower eyelid laxity can be present upon removal of skin cancer and if not properly addressed can result in ectropion and dry eye syndrome. One of the most common procedures used to tighten lower lid is lateral tarsal strip (Fig. 10.46a–g). A lateral canthotomy and cantholysis of the lower crus of LCT is performed as explained before. A free tarsal strip is created from the lateral edge of the lower eyelid by splitting it at the gray line for the distance of 5 to 10 mm (depending on the amount needed for lid shortening) and denuding it from superior and anterior skin and OOM, and posteriorly from the conjunctiva and retractors.

If excessive eyelid laxity is noticed, extra 2 to 4 mm of tarsus may be removed; otherwise the tarsus length should be left intact, since in most situations its attachment to inner lateral orbital wall is sufficient to produce desired amount of eyelid tightening. A 6–0 polydioxanone (PDS), polypropylene or nylon is passed first through the superior aspect of the tarsus, then LCT remnant and continued to grasp periosteum (approximately 2 mm inside at the superior position of the lateral orbital rim) and finished by going through the inferior aspect of the tarsal strip. Before tying it, use 6–0 chromic gut through the gray line of the lateral upper and lower eyelid to prevent blunting and recreating the lateral canthal angle. After this the skin incision can be closed as described before.

Fig. 10.46 The lateral tarsal strip procedure. After canthotomy (a) and cantholysis (b) are performed the lateral tarsal strip is created by dividing anterior and posterior lamella at the gray line removing the skin and conjunctive (c–e); lateral tarsal strip attached to the periosteum of the lateral orbital rim. (f) Lateral canthal angle recreated with interrupted absorbable suture through the gray line with the skin closed with nonabsorbable interrupted sutures (g). (Reproduced from Cheney M, Hadlock T. Facial Surgery: Plastic and Reconstructive. New York: Thieme; 2014.)

After any surgical procedure on the lower eyelid, it is also important to assess medial canthal laxity by laterally displacing the lacrimal punctum. If the punctum lacrimale moves beyond medial limbus, there is a risk of
disruption of normal lacrimal drainage and subsequent epiphora. Hence, the laxity of medial canthus needs to be addressed and patient referred for prophylactic canthopexy of medial eyelid.

Wound dressing1,2,3,4,​20,​24 consists of erythromycin or gentamicin ophthalmic ointment. Cotton gauze is not necessary but if used it should be in the form of an eye pad and carefully applied over the closed eyelid to avoid risk of corneal abrasion. It may help prevent hematoma and should be removed in 1 to 2 days. The frequent application of the icepacks for 20 minutes several times a day in the first few postoperative days may decrease bruising and swelling. Antibiotic ointment should be applied twice daily at the incision site and in the eye at the bedtime until suture removal in 5 to 7 days. Most patients do not tolerate application of the ointments during the day since it blurs the vision. The use of artificial tears three to six times a day may be needed. Contact lenses cannot be worn while ointment is used during daytime hours.

Current ocular medications20,​24 such as glaucoma eye drops should be applied in the preoperative and postoperative periods prior to application of the ointments. Frost sutures are usually removed in 3 to 5 days, and the vertical mattress eyelid margin suture in 2 to 3 weeks. If FTSG is covered with a bolster dressing, the sutures are never affixed to eyelid tissue but instead at the brows, nose, or arcus marginalis. The bolster is removed in one week as in the other areas. After suture removal, ophthalmic antibiotic ointment is applied for additional 3 to 7 days. Patients should avoid strenuous physical activity for the first 2 weeks after the procedure.1,​2,​20,​24

Defects in the medial upper and lower eyelid and medial canthus may frequently involve the lacrimal drainage system, especially puncta and canaliculi. Primary reconstruction of these structures will usually prevent
epiphora and the need for more extensive procedures like conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy with Jones tube.

First it is important to determine if the punctum or the canaliculus have been violated. After punctum dilation a Bowman probe (Fig. 10.47a–e) is inserted in the punctum and ampulla perpendicular to the eyelid margin for a distance of 2 mm. Then it is rotated 90 degrees medially so that it is parallel with the eyelid margin. Gentle lateral tension is now applied to the eyelid and probe smoothly directed toward the nasal sidewall (“hard stop”). If the probe is not visible, and reaches the nasal sidewall and slides easily without tension or force, the canaliculus and lacrimal system are intact.

Fig. 10.47 (a–e) Technique of Bowman lacrimal probe insertion. Punca dilated with sterile safety pin (a) and lubricated Bowman probe inserted first vertically—J form (b) and then horizontally and medially (c) until reaching the end of lacrimal sac (d). Probe is then engaged downward and 15 degrees posteriorly for additional 15 to 20 mm until it reaches nasal cavity (e). (Reproduced from Gallin Pediatric Ophthalmology: A Clinical Guide. New York: Thieme; 2000.)

The canaliculi run through MCT (see ocular anatomy earlier in the chapter) which provides an anchor and horizontal support for the medial eyelids. If violated, MCT needs to be approximated to allow proper eyelid function by placement of the pericanalicular sutures (Fig. 10.48).

Fig. 10.48 5–0 Vicryl pericanalicular sutures (anterior and posterior) ensure repair of the medial canthal tendon, as the canaliculi run through the middle of it. (Reproduced from Chen W. Oculoplastic Surgery: The Essentials. New York: Thieme; 2001.)

If there is partial damage of one or both canaliculi, mono or bicanalicular silicone stenting (Fig. 10.49a, b) with a Crawford stent needs to be performed. Once the probe is passed through vertical and horizontal parts of the canaliculus (see earlier in the chapter), it is directed toward lacrimal bone; once the bone is reached, medially, the probe is redirected inferomedially until it passes into the inferior nasal meatus. Finally, the probe is retrieved with Crawford hook or any other clamp and cut from the silicone, with two silicone ends being tied together so that there is neither tension on the nostril nor on the medial canthus. The probes are left for 3 to 6 months and pulled out after the securing sutures are cut. If more extensive damage of the canaliculi and lacrimal system is anticipated or evaluated, consultation with an oculoplastic surgeon and subsequent conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy with Jones tube is required. One should bear in mind that epiphora is not as common in individuals more than 60 years old as well as in cases where the lower canalicular system is intact.
Fig. 10.49 Bicanalicular (a,b) and monocanalicular stents (c). (Reproduced from Freitag S, Lefebvre D, Lee N, Yoon M. Ophthalmic Plastic Surgery: Tricks of the Trade. New York: Thieme; 2019.)

One of the most common complications of periorbital surgery is lower eyelid ectropion and eyelid retraction. It occurs as a result of anterior lamellar shortening, vertical tension from the flap, and medial punctal ectropion. Common errors that lead to this outcome are poor fixation of the lateral canthal ligament to the lateral wall of the orbit, improper fixation of the posterior portion of the medial canthal ligament, undersized graft or flap, or improper deep fixation of a flap. The shortening of anterior lamella is usually remedied by complete scar lysis and its replacement by full- thickness skin graft. It is essential to ensure sufficient graft size and provide vertical support to lower eyelid margin by applying a “frost suture” (see earlier in the chapter). In addition to the skin graft, it is important to assess lateral and medial canthal angle laxity and consider lateral canthal tightening (tarsal strip) or fixation of the medial canthal ligament if cicatricial ectropion is more pronounced medially.

Other common complications to be avoided when operating in the periorbital area are corneal abrasion, lagophthalmos, and trichiasis. When using upper eyelid skin as a donor site for the FTSG, at least 20 mm of the skin (from eyelid margin to the brow) should be left in place to have proper closing of the eyelids and avoid postoperative lagophthalmos.

Plastic corneal eye shields are often used during periorbital procedures to prevent corneal and scleral abrasion, severing of extraocular muscles and corneal or globe perforation. Many Mohs surgeons (81.8%) report the use of internal eye shields in their practices. Apart from preventing operative injuries, corneal eye shields help patient relax by preventing the patients from seeing the operation itself and facilitate the take of the eyelids skin incision by tautening the skin.

Before insertion, cornea is anesthetized by 0.5% proparacine and lubricant applied over concave surface of the eye shield. The eye shield is inserted in the superior fornix with the patient positioning the eyes in the downward gaze. The removal follows the steps of the insertion in the
reverse and with the use of suction cup unless the corneal shield has built in handle (▶Video 10.4).34

The most important goals for eyebrow reconstruction are to achieve (a) shape, hair direction, and thickness appropriate to race and gender; (b) closure within the same cosmetic units; (c) hide incisions parallelly above and below the brows; (d) maximize preservation of the hair follicles; (e) avoid notching/elevation/ptosis; (f) preserve symmetry by having height of the reconstructed and contralateral eyebrow within 3 to 5 mm of each other.

The medial brow is far more aesthetically significant than the lateral brow. In general, one should move tissue more from lateral to medial, and avoid lateral displacement of the medial brow. During reconstruction, follicular transection should be avoided by creating beveled incisions parallel to the hair direction and also undermine the flaps in the subcutaneous fat to protect dermal papillae. Rotation flaps should generally be avoided, since they produce brow distortion. The use of local flaps is preferred over hair-bearing grafts, since there is about 25 to 50% of hair follicle loss in the latter.

For smaller defects options include primary closure, advancement flaps, transposition flaps, and subcutaneous pedicle flaps. For larger defects besides using the grafts and flaps there is net loss of follicular tissues. These can be addressed with follicular unit transplantation, tattooing, or make-up. Alternatively, hair-bearing skin can be recruited by using flaps from the scalp, contralateral brow, or by harvesting composite skin-hair grafts from the scalp depending on the size of the defect.

Horizontal ellipse can nicely match the curvature of the brows, immediately below and above the brows. However, the risk of brow elevation does exist. This can be assessed by pulling inferior and superior border of the defect together using the skin hooks. Using vertical closure, the risk of brow elevation can be avoided (Fig. 10.15 and Fig. 10.51a–e). This approach is recommended for defects affecting one-fifth to one-fourth of the eyebrow length.

Fig. 10.51 Direct vertical closure suitable for defects 1/5 to ¼ of the brow length. Vertical orientation eliminates brow malposition and shortening. Melanoma in situ of the R brow with corresponding defect after excision (a,b). Closure with vertical orientation (c) and subsequent cosmetic result 4 and 11 months after the procedure
(d,e). (Reproduced from Freitag S, Lefebvre D, Lee N, Yoon M. Eyelid Reconstruction. New York: Thieme; 2020.)

A variety of the advancement flaps can be utilized for the brow reconstruction like unilateral (O-L) (Fig. 10.53a–c), bilateral (A-T, O-T, or O-Z) (Fig. 10.52 and Fig. 10.54a, b), unipedicle (O-U) or bipedicle (O-H) closures (Fig. 10.55a, b). The design of the flap depends on the location and should be executed in such a way as to not disturb the position of the brow. For small- to medium-sized defects the scar can be very well hidden at, below, or above the brows. Horizontal incisions are drawn immediately beneath, above, or in the eyebrow itself from inferolateral border of the defect. Superiorly located standing cones can be removed after the approximation of the flap edges. Unilateral advancement flaps are generally preferred over bilateral since they involve less movement of the skin from medial to lateral.

Fig. 10.52 A-T closure (defect, design, flap sutured in place and cosmetic result in 1 month). (Reproduced from Thornton J, Carboy J. Facial Reconstruction after Mohs Surgery. New York: Thieme; 2018.)
Fig. 10.53 O-L closure: defect and design (a), flap in place (b) and one-month cosmetic result without eyebrow malposition (c).

The subcutaneous island pedicle flap or V-Y flaps (Fig. 10.56a–e) may be used for lateral, central, or medial defects. For medial defects, the flap can be designed to include the whole brow as reported by Bakkour et al,37

where the flap is moved medially and positioned for symmetry with contralateral eyebrow. Lateral displacement of the brow is less likely since glabellar skin is not that lax and moves less. To reduce lateral displacement tacking suture to the frontal bone periosteum may be considered. For larger defects affecting up to half of the brow the flap should be based on the preparation of the deep pedicle based on superficial temporal artery for medial locations or supratrochlear artery for lateral brow, respectively.
Fig. 10.56 Island pedicle flap. Flap design (a,c); flap sutured in place (b,d) and 6 months cosmetic result (e).

Double Z-plasty (Fig. 10.57a–c) described by Cedar38 can close midbrow defects horizontally like accordion, and may hide scars within the brow. However, it can be used only for smaller defects in the central location. Otherwise, the whole contour of the brow may be compromised.
Fig. 10.57 Double-Z rhombic flap. The rhombus is excised (a), and additional excisions are made and transposed (b) and flap sutured in place as demonstrated (c).

For isolated lateral or medial defects, as well as for the total brow defects, sometimes pedicle flaps from contralateral eyebrow, or adjacent scalp can be considered. However, there are the risks of ischemia, venous stasis, and thrombosis, in cases where pedicle is designed too narrow and the perfusion pressure is not adequate.

Pedicle flap from contralateral brow (Fig. 10.58a, b) is designed on the glabellar pedicle and is used for medial brow defects. The flap is split longitudinally and transposed to fill the medial defect on the contralateral brow. The flap should be designed approximately 30% larger to compensate for the shrinkage and follicle lose on the edges.
Fig. 10.58 Pedicled sharing flap from contralateral eyebrow design (a) and execution (b) for medial brow defect reconstruction.

Temporal flap is designed from temporal scalp, must extend to the midline for adequate blood supply, and is used for reconstruction of the lateral part of the brow. The pedicle inset occurs after 3 weeks, and the donor site is closed primarily. Distal end of the new brow may be at risk for ischemia due to lower perfusion pressure.

Temporal flap based on superficial temporal artery (Fig. 10.59a–d) can be designed as cutaneous flap (requires pedicle division in 3 wk) or tunneled flap through the subcutaneous space of the upper forehead, beneath the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve and OOM. Besides carefully creating subcutaneous vascular pedicle, one should be meticulous about choosing the suitable scalp donor site and the establishment of the correct orientation of the hair shafts at the donor site.
Fig. 10.59 Superficial temporal artery-based flaps: cutaneous pedicle transposition flap (a,b) and tunneled pedicle transposition flap (c,d).

Other free flap options include secondary vascularized hair-bearing island flaps based on ipsilateral retroauricular hair (for female brows) or free supraorbital artery pedicled flap from contralateral midbrow. Scalp
donor site can be improved by tissue expanders, hence reducing the follicle density to match the recipient skin at the brow defect.
Fig. 10.60 Orientation of donor strips from the scalp (a) and from contralateral eyebrow for composite skin-hair grafts for brow repair (b). Graft in place (c) and 6 months follow-up (d).

These composite grafts are usually harvested form postauricular temporoparietal region. The graft at the donor site is designed with the vertical long axis so that the hairs have superolateral orientation when transferred to the eyebrow. Incisions are made at the subcutaneous level just above the galea to ensure that hair follicles are obtained. Recipient skin is excised down to the frontalis and OOM. Recipient bed hemostasis is critical

for graft survival. Original hair falls from the graft in the first 2 weeks, and if successfully transplanted, new hair will grow in the next several months. Satisfactory results can be seen at 6 months.
The summary of different types of brow reconstruction based on the size of the defect is presented in Fig. 10.61.

The function of the eyelids and brows is critical for ocular health, vision, and cosmesis. Mohs micrographic surgery is ideal for the cancer removal in these delicate regions where tissue conservation is of utmost importance. The prerequisites of successful functional and aesthetic outcomes of the reconstruction in these delicate areas depend on surgeon’s knowledge of the eyelid and brow anatomy and his or her ability to assess repair requirements and execute appropriate procedures from the plethora of different reconstructive techniques available. Constant education with improvement of the experience and techniques through studying, performance, and collaboration with other surgical specialties will ensure that our patients receive optimal outcomes, restore the function of their eyelids, and obtain best aesthetic results.

Reconstructive surgery blends the knowledge of proper techniques, a framework of when these techniques should be used, execution, foresight of the healing process, as well as vision, creativity, and the art in medicine. Planning out a proper reconstruction involves evaluating the defect, cosmetic subunits involved, tissue properties (thickness, actinic damage, appearance of pores, presence or absence of hair), anatomic landmarks and danger zones, tissue reservoir, and free margins. With experience and proper evaluation of tumors and patient selection, a potential defect and reconstructive options may be planned prior to surgery. The majority of this book has focused on an algorithm and framework for reconstruction; however, large defects, defects involving multiple subunits, and multiple defects in the same patient may require a combination of reconstructive techniques and creativity.

This chapter focuses on using reconstructive techniques like combinations of primary closures, full-thickness skin grafts and Burow’s grafts, and flaps to reconstruct large or difficult, multisubunit defects and multiple defects on patients on the same surgical day. Keys to the evaluation and management of these defects are discussed, and pearls on how to best execute these reconstructions are highlighted. A case-based approach is used to illustrate these concepts. The “Combo-Z” flap is introduced to close two defects in close proximity using a combination of flap movements. The “West by East-West” flap combination is also introduced for large or multi-subunit nasal defects including the tip, supratip, and nasal sidewall. Mastering these key principles allows for a comfort level and confidence in approaching any defect(s) and broadening the reconstructive armamentarium of early career and seasoned surgeons.
– Removing a standing tissue cone at the edge of previous positivity or inflammation. – Taking a deeper base to help clear tumor stroma or inflammation.
• Combinations of flaps, grafts, linear repairs, and second intention healing allow for preservation of cosmetic subunits and decreasing tension of improperly designed reconstructions.

– Periocular full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) to avoid ectropion or eyelid tension. – FTSG after cheek advancement flap for large nasal sidewall defects (see Fig. 11.5a–c). – Second intention healing or mucosal advancement flap for mucosal lip combined with reconstruction of the cutaneous lip defect (see Fig. 11.11a–c).

– See how tissue moves when larger defect is repaired. – Determine the direction and repair type of remaining adjacent tissue. – Alternating orientations of primary repairs avoids tissue pull in the same direction.
– Make sure to obtain informed consent, and discuss the removal of adjacent lesions prior to doing so.
• Consider using another flap or “back-graft” to close a secondary or tertiary defect (see Fig. 11.2a–n; Fig. 11.7a–c).

– FTSG or O-T advancement flap for a secondary defect created by a forehead flap. • Keep standing tissue cones or any excised tissue (may be used as Burow’s grafts). • Don’t repair an area from which a graft may be taken until you determine the size of the graft needed (see Fig. 11.2c, j; Fig. 11.15f, g).
– Extending a longer incision inferiorly on a cheek or preauricular area may help prevent pucker. – Allows for reaching a tissue reservoir.
○ Forehead flap, cheek advancement flap, cheek rotation flap, FTSG. – Actinic damage and pore density (preauricular vs. retroauricular vs. conchal bowl):

○ Conchal bowl pore density matches the distal nose and alae. ○ Retroauricular sulcus skin has less actinic damage than preauricular. ○ Thin retroauricular sulcus tissue matches superficial helical or canthal defects. ○ Non-hair-bearing preauricular skin matches the actinic damage and thickness of the nasal dorsum or sidewall. – Supraclavicular skin and the inner upper arm allow for large reservoirs of free tissue.
• When harvesting an FTSG, trim tissue to the desired depth accounting for atrophy and metabolic demand.

– Even mild sloughing after incomplete FTSG thinning may allow a better long-term outcome than extensive immediate thinning causing a “skeletonized” appearance of the nose. – Dermabrasion, intralesional corticosteroids, serial excisions, or scar revision can be done at a later time to improve aesthetic outcome.

• Suturing considerations. – Create extra eversion when sewing from flap to flap (see Fig. 11.9d). – Consider pulley sutures for key tight areas that can later be removed or left. – Epidermal (top) pulley sutures may be used to bring adjacent tissue together over an FTSG allowing basting of the FTSG and gradual guiding contraction of the adjacent tissues (tie-over sutures) (see Fig. 11.17c, d). – “Set in” graft or flap to surrounding tissue or base, respectively, to account for pincushioning.

○ Sew from graft or flap to surrounding tissue. ○ Take a more superficial bite of graft or flap and a deeper bite of the target tissue. ○ Exiting the needle at the base farther from the graft allows for a better inset of the graft (especially for FTSG of the nasal ala).

Patients with cutaneous malignancies often have multiple lesions requiring treatment. Single-site surgery is most common; however, the following reasons may lead to treatment of several tumors in a single day: patient preference, difficulty traveling for treatment, and multiple tumors in one cosmetic subunit or anatomic area which would encroach on a potential reconstruction. Treating more than one tumor at a surgical visit allows

“cleaning up” the tumor burden on a patient analogous to field therapy treating actinic keratoses. To spare normal tissue, a combination reconstruction or using one reconstruction for multiple defects may be chosen.1,2,3

Inaccurate estimation of tissue laxity and reservoir can hinder a planned reconstruction and create aesthetically or functionally unsuitable results. This is often seen when overestimating the mobility of inherently tight forehead tissue, working in a scar, or approaching a free margin. Sometimes, a well-designed flap fails to close the defect. Even seasoned surgeons have elevated a large flap and realized it just won’t reach. In these cases, a comfort level with combination reconstructive techniques may improve outcomes.

As primary or linear repairs are commonly used reconstructive options, they should be the first reconstructive consideration after second intention. While the 3:1 length-to-width ratio of elliptical excisions with 30-degree angles of the standing tissue cones is frequently used, certain anatomic sites allow for lengthening or shortening of this ratio and widening or “cheating” the vertex angle of the standing tissue cones. For example, the hairless triangle of the lip, the medial canthus, and the back often allows for shortening of the excision and widening the vertex angle. However, ellipses on the nasal dorsum and columella, the scalp, the vermilion lip, and the helical rim are often extended past the 3:1 ratio, with angles that are even more acute, in order to lengthen the incision over a curved surface for a smooth transition and avoid a pucker.

In combination reconstruction, this extension of an ellipse allows for harvesting a graft without creating a new incision. Burow’s grafts are full- thickness skin grafts (FTSG) obtained from adjacent tissue from a standing cone of a primary repair, allowing for a better color, thickness, and texture match when used for adjacent tissue reconstruction.4–7 Traditionally, they are used on the nasal dorsum or tip with the proximal nose closed primarily providing the grafted tissue distally.8,​9 However, they can be used in almost
any location. In addition, FTSG from other locations can be used in combination with primary repairs.

1. Determine the appropriate tissue properties for the graft site. 2. Determine if the reservoir available in the standing tissue cone is sufficient for the defect after accounting for partial closure of the defect with a primary reconstruction. 3. If a unilateral or bilateral Burow’s grafts do not allow for sufficient tissue, FTSG may be harvested from a matching tissue reservoir (retroauricular, preauricular, conchal bowl, supraclavicular, inner arm, and femoral canal) depending on the amount of tissue needed. 4. Don’t discard tissue until the reconstruction is finished. 5. Don’t harvest the graft until you determine the area needed to be grafted. 6. Extend the primary repair from which a Burow’s graft may be harvested where an extended incision may best heal (inferior curvature of the cheek as opposed to zygoma, proximal nasal dorsum as opposed to distal nose).8,​9
7. Consider tissue match (thickness, color, texture, hair density, pore density). 8. Suturing from graft to the surrounding base and “setting in” the graft helps limit pincushioning.

The dorsal hand or large forearm defects are great for FTSG/primary repair combinations. While granulation, purse string repairs, single arm rotation flaps, O-Z double rotation flaps, and the “Mercedes” flap are used in these locations, Burow’s grafts offer an acceptable reconstruction, especially on tight and often atrophic skin.10 If the defect is too large to use a Burow’s graft without significant tension, it may be prudent to repair much of the defect primarily and use a supraclavicular or axillary upper arm FTSG to close the remaining part of the defect.

Horizontally and vertically oriented primary repairs, rotation flaps, and advancement flaps are typically used to reconstruct the temple. While FTSG of the forehead often lead to an atrophic appearance, Burow’s grafts of the temple and lateral suprabrow offer an acceptable repair option (Fig. 11.1a–c).

Fig. 11.1 Combinations of full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) and primary linear repairs of the forehead/temple. (a) Defect involving the lateral eyebrow, lateral forehead, and lower temple. (b) Burow’s graft and primary repairs bilaterally and superiorly causing slight elevation of the brow. This is often called a “Mercedes” flap when a Burow’s graft isn’t used. The brow elevation settles back to baseline within weeks to months of the repair. (c) Four-month follow-up with settling of the eyebrow and continued fading of the FTSG.

Primary curvilinear reconstruction or flaps are used on the cheek. In instances when a primary repair may not close the defect without significant tension on the oral commissure or a flap is unnecessary, a Burow’s graft may be used.

As we approach defects with regard to subunits involved and wound tension, a flap may be the reconstructive choice. If the flap is unable to appropriately repair the entire defect, a graft may be used in combination. Donor sites for grafts are discussed in other chapters and earlier in this chapter. Below are some specific examples of flap and graft combination reconstruction.

11.3.1 Lateral Infraocular Cheek The bilobed transposition and rotation flaps, such as the Mustarde cheek rotation flap, are used to close large infraocular defects. However, this cheek rotation flap is difficult to execute with the goal of avoiding any tension on the lower eyelid and preventing an ectropion. Keys to this flap include oversizing the flap (especially in the temple area), tacking the flap superolaterally from the lateral canthus with sutures to the taught temporal skin in the vertical vector or the orbital rim, and tacking the anterior edge of the flap in a horizontal direction to the medial portion of the defect or the nasal sidewall in order to avoid tension to the eyelid itself. However, if the cheek defect is large and too lateral to allow the secondary defect of the flap to be sewn out, other modifications must be made (Fig. 11.2a). Even with a maximum amount of tissue rotated starting immediately preauricularly and stretching superiorly to the lateral temple, the secondary defect may be too large. An FTSG may be taken out inferiorly from the flap standing tissue cone and purposely sized to close the secondary defect. The keys to the flap are similar to those previously discussed; however, an inferior tissue cone should not be removed until the secondary defect is maximally closed without giving too much pull to the flap or the lower eyelid. Subsequently, a template may be made of the remaining secondary defect and used to outline the area of the inferior standing tissue cone (Fig. 11.2b). This can then be sewn in to close the secondary defect without greatly changing the tissue vectors of the flap (Fig. 11.2c–e). In the case of medial or extremely large defects, a wider rotational arc maximizing the preauricular cheek availability and additional FTSGs may be needed (Fig. 11.2f–n).

11.3.2 Periauricular Cheek/Ear Large defects in the preauricular area lend themselves to a cheek advancement flap. However, the involvement of the tragus or crura of the helix may require additional closure with an FTSG. This may come from the excised infra-auricular skin needed to pull up the cheek advancement flap, the anteriorly excised standing tissue cone, or from a separate retroauricular FTSG. For a larger residual defect, a supraclavicular FTSG may be used.

In addition, if the postauricular area is involved along with the proximal superior ear, and a single-stage reconstruction is desired, the scalp and preauricular skin can be used in combination. Combinations of rotation

from the postauricular scalp and transposition flaps from either the preauricular or postauricular skin are good sources of tissue (Fig. 11.3a–f). Preauricular rotation is not ideal, as the rotated edge may blunt the superior crus of the helix.

Fig. 11.3 Combination auricular reconstruction with a superiorly based scalp rotation flap and a preauricular transposition flap. (a) Defect involving the proximal helical crus and superolateral temple/scalp. (b) Superior view of the defect. (c) Flap undermining done at the mid fat anteriorly and under the hair follicle bulbs posteriorly. Note the course of a temporal vessel branch that is avoided in undermining. (d) Key deep sutures placed to close the majority of the defect. Care must be taken to evert the helical rim edges. The preauricular transposition flap should be folded to recreate the normal rolled contour without compromising flap vascularity. (e) Final repair. (f) Three-week follow-up. Slight
sloughing is noted at the transposition flap surface; however, the distal flap survival avoided any step-off.

11.3.3 Upper Cutaneous Lip/Philtrum/Alar Sill When an upper cutaneous lip defect also involves the nasal ala, hairless triangle, and the alar sill, a combination of an advancement or rotation flap and FTSG may be used. The crescent excised to freely move the flap is an obvious reservoir for the nasal portion of the defect (Fig. 11.4a, b). Attention must be paid to the possible need for cartilaginous support, and meticulous suturing and appropriate basting must be used as FTSGs on the columella or the distal nasal ala have a high risk of failure. In the case of graft failure, this may become the patient’s best “biologic bandage,” but additional revision may be needed if a significant step-off is created.

Fig. 11.4 Combination reconstruction with a paranasal crescentic advancement flap (CAF) and full-thickness skin graft (FTSG). (a) Large defect involving the upper cutaneous lip, nasal sill, and the inferolateral nasal ala. Note the inferior standing tissue cone of the CAF is drawn as a triangle under the lateral portion of the vermilion at the oral commissure in order to better hide the scar. Original designs of the flap use a large triangle standing tissue cone in the

The suture lines are well hidden in the natural subunit junctions, and the FTSG is firmly tacked to buttress the nasal ala and tacked down to the nasal sill to replace the junction of the mucosal and cutaneous lining of the alar sill. Swelling and lateral oral commissure drooping is normal due to local anesthetic infiltration. (c) Similar large defect of the upper lip of a cosmetically sensitive patient. Note the involvement of the philtrum. (d) Flap elevated after crescents removed by the ala and the inferior lip corner. If the philtrum is involved, the subunit approach is important to consider. While Karapandzic, bilateral crescentic advancement, and Abbe flaps are designed to repair large defects involving multiple subunits of the upper or lower lips, an FTSG from adjacent skin such as the excised crescent or marionette standing cone may be combined with the crescentic advancement flap to cover similar defects when muscle is preserved (Fig. 11.4c–h).

11.3.4 Medial Cheek/Nasal Sidewall Advancing or rotating the cheek to partially close a commonly seen defect involving the medial cheek and lateral nasal sidewall allows an FTSG to be placed on the lateral nasal sidewall portion (Fig. 11.5a–c). Attention must be paid to tacking the cheek portion to the nasal periosteum to avoid tenting and blunting of the nasofacial sulcus. However, a slight malar curve recreates the natural appearance depending on the age of the patient and the level of the malar fat pad loss. Tacking of the FTSG to the nasal sidewall

and possible nasalis muscle hinge or sling may be needed for the FTSG to survive. The reservoir for this may be the superiorly excised standing tissue cone on the nasal sidewall, the standing tissue cone from the rotated cheek, or a combination of both.

Fig. 11.5 Combination reconstruction with a laterally based cheek crescentic advancement flap (CAF) and a full-thickness skin graft (FTSG). (a) Frontal view of the defect. Note the design of the flap allows for potentially closing the entire defect with a single flap; however, surgeons with a purely cosmetic subunit approach would argue against solely using this flap for this defect. (b) Frontal view of the reconstruction showing mild nasal ala pull. (c) One-month follow-up demonstrating return of the nasal ala to its original position and nice camouflaging of the scar lines in the cosmetic subunit junctions of the melolabial fold, alar groove, and the nasofacial sulcus.

While FTSG on the forehead may have aesthetically displeasing results, the immobile nature of forehead skin may require a combination repair.11,​12 For a large defect, an O-T advancement flap may be chosen. However, if the defect is located laterally on the forehead, one must be careful in undermining to avoid branches of the temporal nerve and arteries, and therefore, potentially limiting mobility. The defect may be partially closed with the bilateral advancement motion and the closure of the superiorly
based standing tissue cone. The standing cone tissue can then be used to graft the central portion of the defect (Fig. 11.6a, b).

Fig. 11.6 Combination reconstruction of an O-T advancement flap and a full-thickness skin graft (FTSG). (a) Wide defect of the central superior forehead. (b) Combination repair with an O-T advancement flap and an FTSG from the superior standing tissue cone. Of note, some authors would design the “T” superiorly in an arciform fashion and take an extended inferior tissue cone. Wide defects of the forehead are sometimes tricky due to the underestimation of the rigidity of the medial forehead skin.

11.3.6 Large Nasal Defects For certain nasal defects, the bilobed flap is a “workhorse.” However, when the flap is pushed for larger defects or inappropriately designed, there may be too much elevation of the alar rim, significant pull on the medial canthus, or inability to close the tertiary defect. While we often say hindsight is “20/20,” when a preventable complication occurs or a flap doesn’t move as predicted, and a trilobed transposition or another flap altogether should have been used, a “back graft” may be a good option, especially if the defect is greater than 2 centimeters (Fig. 11.7a–c). The

reservoir for this graft may be the trimmed tissue from the secondary lobe or other tissue previously discussed to match the nose. Similarly, a graft to “buttress” the alar rim may be used with meticulous attention paid to suturing and basting. Dermabrasion or carbon dioxide (CO2) laser may be needed for postoperative finessing at long-term follow-up.

Fig. 11.7 Combination reconstruction of a bilobed transposition flap and a back graft. (a) Defect greater than 2 centimeters involving the nasal ala approaching the alar rim, nasal alar groove, and inferior nasal sidewall. (b) Combination reconstruction of a bilobed transposition flap and an FTSG (back graft) to avoid excess pulling on the medial canthus and too much alar rim elevation. Graft reservoirs may be the trimmed tissue from the secondary lobe or the tissue cone of the primary defect. The author removed this tissue cone first to see the full movement of the bilobed flap. Mild alar rim elevation tends to resolve, and the alar groove often re- forms naturally or may be guided with tacking suture to the nasal valve or sidewall, depending on the defect depth. (c) Three-month follow-up demonstrating normal alar rim position, appropriate graft appearance, and reformation of the nasal alar groove and nasofacial sulcus.

In a similar manner, the dorsal nasal rotation flap may be used to repair a large portion of the nasal tip and dorsum; however, some defects with large lateral portions require additional tissue transfer in the form of a cheek- based flap (Fig. 11.8a–d) or an FTSG.

The nose is a common site where a combination repair is needed. While FTSG often serve to close a portion of the defect with a flap, a secondary flap may be used instead. The common flap reservoirs for nasal tissue are adjacent nasal tissue, forehead/glabella, and cheeks.

A dorsal nasal rotation flap (previously described) can be used in combination with a bilateral or unilateral cheek advancement flap(s) (Fig. 11.8a–g) and a glabellar transposition flap (Fig. 11.9a–e).

To illustrate the principle of subunit reconstruction, which is crucial on the nose, a combination of melolabial interpolation flaps (MLIF), cheek advancement and rotation flaps, and V-Y advancement flaps has been described.14 In the case of defects involving portions of the ala, the nasal sidewall, and the cheek, an MLIF or even an FTSG can be used once the other cosmetics subunits are repaired. The superiorly-based V-Y advancement flap is used when the defect is wider than it is tall. The laterally based rotation (crescentic cheek advancement) flap is used when the defect is taller than it is wide (Fig. 11.10q).

In the case of a forehead flap, the secondary defect is often granulated or closed linearly; however, if a large defect is left and granulation is not preferred, an O-T advancement flap or a W-plasty may be used to close the secondary defect.

Defects involving the inferior cutaneous and mucosal lip may pose difficulty. A bilateral V-Y advancement flap may be used; however, for large asymmetric defects, a transposition or a rotation flap from the cheek or chin can repair the cutaneous portion and a mucosal advancement may then repair the mucosal defect (Fig. 11.11a–c). A Burow’s advancement flap with a mucosal extension or partial mucosal advancement to the vermilion border allows for closure of large and difficult defects while hiding scars in the melolabial fold, Marionette lines, and the vermilion border.15

Some patients may come from long distances and present with multiple tumors. It is not uncommon to treat several tumors on the same day. Sometimes, a second tumor is found in the adjacent tissue planned to repair a primary defect. In such cases, a repair may be designed to reconstruct multiple defects together or use redundant tissue from one repair to close a second defect.

If a primary linear or curvilinear repair can close multiple defects, this is often preferred, given it does not cross multiple subunits that should otherwise be respected. The addition of an FTSG to a linear repair has previously been discussed.

A bilateral advancement flap such as the Burow’s advancement flap or the “East-West” flap (EWF) can be designed to close two defects; in a similar manner it is used to shift the standing tissue cone deformity as described in nasal reconstruction.11–14 This concept is not unique to the nose and may be applied to any anatomic site.

The author described another take on the nasal EWF.16 When the defect involves a large part of the lateral sidewall, nasal tip, and/or dorsum, and multiple adjacent defects are involved, a crescentic advancement flap (CAF) is combined with the EWF to create the “West by East-West” (WEW) flap (Fig. 11.12a–f).

Fig. 11.12 “West by East-West” (WEW) combination flap for large or multiple lateral nasal defects. (a) Two defects involving the proximal nasal tip/ala, lateral nasal dorsum, and nasal sidewall. Note the design combining the standing cones from both flaps to encompass both defects. Burow’s advancement flap (“East-West” flap) is drawn medially and the crescentic advancement flap (CAF)

is drawn laterally. (b) Undermining done at the level of the perichondrium on the nose and mid cheek fat laterally. (c) Flap undermined. (d) WEW flap repair. (e) Frontal view at 2 months. (f) Closer lateral view at 2 months demonstrating nasal-alar groove preservation and fading of the scar line.

The key steps to the WEW flap are as follows: 1. Design the flap standing cone to include the entire defect or the combined multiple defects. 2. Design the CAF portion to include enough laxity to at least close half of the defect while removing enough of a crescent to avoid blunting the nasofacial sulcus or nasal groove and possibly getting enough of a pivotal rotational motion after the advancement to close some of the nasal tip. 3. Design the EW portion to close the medial half of the defect without “beaking” the nasal tip or columella. 4. Remove the standing tissue cone and undermine above the perichondrium on the nose medially and in the mid cheek fat laterally. 5. Excise and close the columellar defect first, followed by the standing tissue cone of the nasal dorsum to align the flap edges. 6. Close the crescent of the CAF taking meticulous care to preserve the nasal groove, avoid pushing down on the ala, and preserve nasal valve patency. 7. As always, preserve the standing tissue cones in case an FTSG is needed.
11.5.3 O-T Advancement Flap, Scalp/Forehead Rotation Flap, and Paramedian Forehead Flap The O-T advancement flap also demonstrates versatility for repairs of multiple defects.

When used for multiple nasal defects, the O-T advancement flap may cause significant elevation of the nasal tip and possible depression of the nasal dorsum; however, the nasal tip elevation improves over time with natural age-related ptosis and settling of the scar tissue.
In a similar manner, multiple or large scalp defects may lend themselves well to advancement or rotation flaps. The scalp rotation flap is useful for
tapping into a reservoir of mobile occipital or parietal scalp skin to close large scalp or forehead defects.

The key steps to a scalp rotation flap (SRF) are as follows: 1. Design the arc of an SRF at least double to four times the size of the defect and laterally enough for the leading edge to cover the entire defect to rotate comfortably without flap blood flow compromise once the standing tissue cone is removed anteriorly and contralaterally from the flap leading edge (Fig. 11.13a, b). 2. In order to spare needle sticks and avoid lidocaine toxicity, numbing can be done with lidocaine and epinephrine in the areas of the defect, around the flap incision design, and the proposed standing tissue cones anterolaterally and posteriorly. The bulk of the flap does not need numbing as undermining will be done in the bloodless and “mostly” painless subgaleal plane. Touch-ups are sometimes needed intraoperatively if the galea is stuck to the periosteum due to previous surgery or radiation, as this can be extra sensitive. Tumescent anesthesia can also help avoid excessive bleeding expected with scalp flaps. 3. The flap is incised all the way to the subgaleal plane, and the flap should be undermined in this plane to minimize bleeding and freely and quickly undermine. This should be done efficiently, as bleeding from the flap edges can be significant, and heavy cautery is expected for actively bleeding vessels. Cautery of the entire edge is not needed as the small oozing vessels will stop once pressure from flap inset and sewing create a tamponade effect. 4. After undermining and elevating, the flap should be rotated into the desired direction and key sutures placed. The author uses 3–0 polyglactin 910 or deep sutures is appropriate to close the defect with the leading flap edge.17 Pulley sutures may be needed if the defect is large or the flap is undersized (Fig. 11.13c, d). 5. The rotated incised edge of the flap is then sewn out with the rule of halves balancing tension out over the entire flap arc. Again, top, deep, or a combination of both sutures may be used (Fig. 11.13e). 6. If the flap is insufficient to cover the entire defect without compromising its viability, an additional incision and flap can be made to meet the leading edge of the initial flap or an FTSG can be taken from the standing tissue cone (Fig. 11.13f, g).

In the case of multiple deep or large defects on the nose, a paramedian or paramidline forehead flap may be used after removing adjacent tissue and extending both defects in a similar manner as extending the nasal defect to the size of the entire subunit to allow forehead flap reconstruction while hiding the flap lines in natural subunit junctions.

11.5.4 “Combo-Z” Flap One of my favorite reconstructions of two adjacent defects is a bilateral motion flap, something I like to call the “Combo-Z” flap.18 While the Burow’s advancement flap uses an advancing motion to shift the direction of a standing tissue cone, when applied to multiple defects, a central diagonal incision may be made, and the entire surrounding tissue may be undermined to elevate flap edges. Once the flap tissue is elevated, skin hooks may be used to displace tissue with different motion types to estimate the optimal outcome. The flap edges may be advanced to slide into both defects; they may be rotated in the direction of the diagonal incision or may be transposed across each other to close the defects while shifting the direction of the standing tissue cones to adjust for surrounding free margins (Fig. 11.14).

These movements are analogous to the Burow’s advancement flap if horizontally advanced and the Z-plasty, if transposed.19–26 However, the key differences of the “Combo-Z” with these flaps are the utility of this flap with multiple defects, the ability to not remove standing tissue cones until the desired direction/movement is achieved after undermining and flap elevation, and the ability to utilize multiple aforementioned flap movements to create the desired direction. The desired direction itself is determined by any free margin (such as the eyelid) (Fig. 11.15a, b) ( ▶Video 11.1 and ▶Video 11.2), the natural movement of the elevated tissue, and the skin lines which would best camouflage the scar.

undermining was deemed better for transposition, allowing the tension to be toward the eye rather than away. A diagonal line is incised between the adjacent defects, and the entire area around the defects is undermined. As the flaps are elevated, skin hooks can be used to advance or transpose the flap edges in the desired direction. This is often guided by the natural tissue movement or the desire to avoid displacement of a free margin. The advancement motion is that of a Burow’s advancement flap while the transposition motion is similar to a Z-plasty with the flap edges transposed over one another prior to trimming the standing tissue cones. Another option to closing two defects in close proximity, if there is at least a separation area of similar size to one of the defects, is to use this area of separation as a rhombic flap transposed into one of the defects and closing the other defect primarily.

11.5.5 Multiple Defects Repaired with Burow’s Grafts When defects are not in close proximity due to multiple surgeries being performed on the same day, the creativity and vision at the onset of surgery will allow one to look at the surgical sites and find a way to avoid wasting tissue and close all defects with minimal extra surgery. Burow’s grafts, previously discussed in this chapter, are the easiest way to achieve these goals. Frequently, a patient presents with a tumor on the ear as well as another site. If a full-thickness epidermal/dermal repair is needed on the ear, the second site’s standing tissue cone may serve as the donor for an FTSG to the ear.

In a similar manner, patients with multiple defects on the nose or those presenting with a tumor on the nose and another site may be good candidates for FTSG. As previously discussed, FTSG are good reconstructive options for the lateral alae, soft triangle, and the columella. If a primary linear reconstruction is done on a dorsal nose defect, the remaining standing tissue cones can be used to close the alar defects (Fig. 11.16a–h). Similarly, if a flap is needed to close one of the defects, any

The nose and ear are not the only anatomic sites in which Burow’s grafts may be used.6 This concept may be used on several defects which may not be closed as separate simple reconstructions or using one reconstruction for defects.

In this chapter, combination reconstruction has been introduced with combinations of primary repairs, grafts, and flaps. Some defects require that extra creativity allowing a surgeon to use baseline knowledge of combination repairs and apply it while pushing the limits of local reconstructive options. Concepts of flap and graft combinations, Burow’s grafts from primary repair standing tissue cones, pulley tie-over sutures, and granulation (second intention healing) can be used in conjunction. As granulation of wounds was once the primary “reconstructive” method after
Mohs micrographic surgery, one must not forget to think of granulation as a viable primary or an adjunct option for combination reconstruction (Fig. 11.17a–e).

Combination reconstruction may be used when multiple defects are created, when one defect may be too large for one reconstructive option or encompasses multiple cosmetic subunits, or when a repair may not be properly planned or executed. In other words, a combination reconstruction may help a surgeon to get out of a jam and still create functionally and cosmetically appropriate results for the patient. This chapter uses select cases and anatomic examples of combination reconstructions to demonstrate key principles when approaching such defects and situations. Combinations of primary linear reconstructions, FTSG, and multiple flap types are discussed. The “West by East-West” combination flap is introduced to close large or multiple lateral nasal defects. The “Combo-Z” flap is also introduced to close two defects in close proximity using a combination of flap movements. Mastering these key principles allows for a comfort level and confidence in approaching any defect(s) and broadening the reconstructive armamentarium of early career and seasoned surgeons.

Structured perioperative management and wound care is essential to successful surgical outcomes during Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS). At the authors’ institution, these structured protocols focusing on perioperative antibiotics, anticoagulation, conscious sedation/analgesia, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICD)/implantable devices are closely followed to ensure patient safety. A discussion of these protocols in a step-wise fashion with a review of the current literature is included in the following chapter to help the dermatologic surgeon use evidence-based medicine to support their decision-making process. Furthermore, an in-depth focus is provided on the management of dressings based on the following closure or procedural types: second intention wound healing, porcine xenografts, biologic dressings, dermabrasion, primary closure, postflap care, and postgraft care. These step-by-step dressing recommendations will help to provide a framework on the management of wounds following MMS. Even in the most skilled dermatologic surgeon’s hands, complications can arise including hematoma, infection, and postprocedural pain. A brief discussion on these postoperative complications with management recommendations is included.
